Pedro mi S.r”). The part transcribed carries no date; its content points to 1676–1677. Where Biblioteca Nacional de España, Mss/2043 (formerly G. 85; BNE Digital, BDH bdh0000042925), PDF view 0496, left and right pages. There is no DECODE record and no edition. The cipher A mixed syllabic cipher, called S1 here: numbers of one or two digits for letters and syllables, letter-shaped signs read with a shifted consonant ( te = de , ga = la ), a few simple signs, some nulls and a sign for V.E. How it was deciphered The key was learned by EM alignment on 14 cipher and clear pairs from the same volume, frozen by hash, and measured once on this page: 0.742 of characters against 0.422 for the best of 200 shuffled keys. That clears the control but not the 0.85 threshold set in advance, so the key is partial. What it says The suspension of arms by which “lo de Sicilia” would be put in the Pope’s hands; orders to Your Excellency “as they stand” at Melgar; the writer fears Medina and the conferences of Oropesa; Valencia is “still very entrenched”. Still open 13 of 95 margin words are restored from the margin, not given by the key, and six cipher stretches have no counterpart. The page was deciphered at the time, so no solution is claimed. Credit Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée , with Claude Opus 5.5 agents) found the volume, transcribed the page, learned and tested the key and read it; his result reached the repository as pull request #276. The decipherment in the margin is the work of a contemporary hand.

Mss/2043 holds the letters of Cardinal Pascual de Aragón, archbishop of Toledo, to his brother Pedro Antonio de Aragón, 1675–1677, among the Aragón and Villahermosa papers. About 90 to 110 pieces are in one mixed syllabic cipher. Several carry a contemporary decipherment in the margin, and a separate gathering, “Descifrado de las cartas…” (about f. 353), holds clear copies of about fifty letters. This write-up covers a single page: PDF view 0496, left and right pages (about f. 493), with 20 cipher lines of 273 signs. View numbers are image ranks in the PDF, not folios. The facing margin carries the decipherment of the time, which is what the key was measured against. The cipher lines on the left page sit under two short lines of that clear. The left page: six lines of cipher, and on their left the contemporary hand’s decipherment (“en la suspension de armas con que se pusiese lo de Sicilia en manos de su Santidad…”). Image: Biblioteca Nacional de España, Mss/2043, PDF view 0496, left page (cipher lines 1–6 and their margin decipherment), via BNE Digital (BDH).

S1 mixes several kinds of sign. Numbers of one or two digits stand for letters and syllables (13 e , 16 a , 15 y , 25 que , 22 se , 21 pa , 26–30 sa to su , 31–35 ma to mu , 36–40 ta to tu ). Letter-shaped signs read with a shifted consonant ( te = de , ga = la , po and go = no , pa = na , ca = ua ). Simple signs give single letters (a = n, + = s, x = r, ø = o, a+ = l, r = u, ue = h, ) = d). A few three-digit numbers and some nulls (916, 296, 316, 331) complete it, and 281 stands for V.E. The key, CLE_C08c, is the last of a series. It was learned by EM alignment on 14 cipher and clear pairs of the same volume: the margins of views 0138–0139 and 0484–0485, and ten letters of views 0318–0355 paired with the “Descifrado” gathering. It was frozen by SHA-256 before p. 0496 was opened. Brice Dudout settled the confusable sign shapes on blind plates, choosing the shape he saw with no values or words shown: three forms of one family (crozier 20 = c , compact 10 = i , round 6 = p ), a U-shaped tracing that is one sign with 21 (= pa ), and one occurrence on view 0344 that is 28 (= si ). The full key is in the repository ( key.tsv ).

The test used one held-out page, opened only after the key was frozen. The cipher was transcribed and hashed before its margin was looked at. The score is the longest common subsequence between the decryption and the margin clear, set against the best of 200 shuffled keys. Run 2, the official result: 0.742 against 0.422 (margin +0.320); the second control, the share of letters covered by Spanish words of five letters or more, gave 0.281 against 0.186. Margin met, absolute threshold of 0.85 missed: partial . Run 1 gave 0.392 against 0.344 and failed. The measuring script skipped “#” note lines in the cipher file but not in the clear file, and 7 of our own note lines were scored as clear. Run 2 was agreed before it was launched, declared as the official result with no third run, and changed only those 7 lines. Both runs are in validation.txt . An earlier key (CLE_C06), measured once on p. 0504 left, gave 0.778 against 0.424: partial as well.

The decryption was cut into words and read against the margin. In the text below, square brackets mark letters restored from the margin clear, round brackets mark letters corrected from one sign, and [..] marks letters neither decoded nor in the margin. Left page. [en la su]spension de (a)r(m)as [con que] se (pu)siese [lo de] s(i)cilia en (m)anos de [su] santid(a)d y proporc[io]nando se en todo (pa)ra [hando ?] la reso[luc]ion de car(pi)o y c[ierto] Right page. [de ahi no] se [..]uian las (h)orde(ne)s [..] V.E. q(u)al se halla[n] [a] Melgar y en [el c]laro es Medelli[n] [yo] [con]fieso que q(u)anto me(n)os cor(r)esponden [es] con el; es el mejor esta(do); temo a Medina, que el no (c)ontentarse juzgo le tiene en este estado, y las (c)onferen(c)ias de Oro(p)esa y el no se [qu]e efec[tos] [pue]den pro[du]c[ir]; y Valen[cia] [se] deue de ha[llar] [mui] encastillad[o a]u[n] In English: “In the suspension of arms, whereby the Sicily affair would be placed in the hands of His Holiness, and accommodating oneself in everything, for [—] the resolution of Carpio and [certain…] … the orders are sent to Your Excellency as they stand at Melgar; and what is clear is Medellín. I confess that the less they correspond with him, the better the state of things. I fear Medina, whom discontent, I judge, keeps in this state; and the conferences of Oropesa, and I do not know what effects they may produce; and Valencia must still be very entrenched.” Gaps are marked in the full translation below. The suspension of arms and Sicily fit the Messina war of 1674–1678, and Carpio, Medellín, Medina, Oropesa and Melgar are Spanish grandees or titles of the court of Charles II. We do not identify the individuals. The count. Of the 95 words of the margin clear, 41 are certain (every letter aligned with the decryption), 41 probable (at least half of the letters aligned, including “suspension de armas”, which the head cut of the measurement leaves out although the decryption has it), and 13 restored (under half aligned). That makes 82 of 95, or 86% without the restored words, under the 95% bar, so the extent is partial. The count was made by script on the alignment of the official measurement. Where the cipher corrects the margin. The margin was checked again after the measurement, without re-running it. Three places give the better reading to the cipher: the margin’s “burgo” is juzgo (“juzgo le tiene en este estado”), its “mel ar” is Melgar , and its “tado”, twice, is estado . At line 13 of the right page the decryption has “ualenzuela” where the margin has “valencia”, and the adjective is masculine (“encastillado”). It may be Fernando de Valenzuela, the queen mother’s favourite, who took refuge in the Escorial at the turn of 1676–1677. That is a hypothesis only: it is not counted and it does not date the letter.

13 margin words are restored, not given by the key: “en”, “la”, “con” at the head, “que” (three times), “lo”, “hando”, “cierto”, “ahi”, “se” (twice) and “mui”. Six cipher stretches have no counterpart in the margin: tararahasii , hsmir , enne , eyseco , prohcp and lapide . The transcription is less secure than the training pieces: pale ink and crossing interlinear writing give 7 doubtful signs (as A|B) and 3 illegible ones. The margin on the right page is partly cut by the binding. The key is partial by our protocol (0.742, under 0.85), and no held-out page with a clear is left for a new test. One reader only, an AI agent, did the transcription and the reading. Brice Dudout answered the shape plates, not the reading, and no palaeographer has checked either. A glimpse of the margin before the hash: the first overview strip of the left page showed the right edge of the margin clear, a few word endings, before the cipher was hashed. Not part of this reading: the interlinear clear on the right page, which was left unread so that the test stayed clean, the other pieces of S1 in the volume, and the date and the persons behind Carpio, Medina, Oropesa and Valencia.

A letter of the duke of Ferrara to his secretary in clear Italian, with runs of Greek- and Latin-shaped signs under small raised vowel digits. Brice Dudout recovered the key from the signs alone, tested it once on held-out lines (0.605 of letters in Italian words against 0.155 for the best of 200 shuffled keys) and read 357 of 402 cipher words (88.8%). Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (89% of the cipher) Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · WAINUT (pointer to a source) · Daniel Bourdeau (pointer to a source) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (89% of the cipher) The letter Ercole II d’Este, duke of Ferrara, to his secretary Claudio Ariosto, Ferrara, 23 April 1559, with a postscript. The letter is in clear Italian, and the passages about the countess, her husband and their affairs are set in cipher. Where Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Modena, Autografoteca Campori, Lettera E, Este (d’), Ercole II d’Este, duca di Ferrara, cc. 39–41 (IIIF manifest 8d50f9af-95d8-405e-a3a4-f66933e69af1). Catalogue 2159 here, from WAINUT’s sweep of the Estense collection. No DECODE record, no entry at Cryptiana, no edition found. The cipher Consonant signs of Greek and Latin shape, each followed by a small raised digit that gives the vowel: 2 o, 3 i, 4 e, 5 a, 6 a, 7 e, 8 i, 9 o, 1 u. A raised ring doubles the consonant, a dot is a null, & is qu , and a few code numbers under a bar stand for words. About 1,830 signs and raised marks in 77 cipher lines. How it was deciphered Brice Dudout froze a protocol and the transcription with SHA-256 hashes, held out 22.1% of the signs, learned the key by annealing on the rest and measured it once: 0.605 of the held-out letters fall in Italian words of five letters or more, against 0.155 for the best of 200 shuffled keys. The keys of four neighbouring Este ciphers do not fit. What it says A countess asks the duke to pay her debts out of arrears of censi (rents). He refuses those that fell due during her husband’s rebellion, “a causa della sua ribellione non s’ha da haver nulla”, and offers to pay the future ones to her rather than to him. The peace of 1559 will lessen the husband’s credit. Still open 39 of 402 cipher words are unresolved, mostly in five stretches where both blind transcriptions read the same unreadable shapes; the code numbers 22, 24 and 25–27; and who the countess, her husband and the count are. Credit Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée ), working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents: the blind transcription, the key, its validation and the reading. WAINUT found the letter in the Estense collection (catalogue lead 2159, PR #242). Merged here in pull request #277.

The duke is Ercole II d’Este of Ferrara (1508–1559), and the letter is headed Hercules Dux Ferrarie . It is written to Claudio Ariosto, his secretary, on 23 April 1559, with a postscript on cc. 40–41. The duke’s clear sentences give the frame; the cipher is set into them where the matter is delicate. A countess has claimed arrears of rents from the duke and wants them used for her debts. The duke tells Ariosto what to say to her, and asks him about two other matters. Runs of cipher stand on cc. 39r, 39v, 40r, 40v and 41r. No decipherment is kept with them. The leaf belongs to the Autografoteca Campori, a collection of autograph letters, and the Estense records it only as “Lettera cifrata” with its postscript. Ercole II’s letter of 28 May 1559 (Lettera E, cc. 50–51) is in a different cipher with its own target ( targets/ercole1559 , not yet written up), and a letter of 15 July 1559 in Ariosto’s own hand has a sign that is not in this one; this key does not read it. C. 39r, lines 4–7, in the clear quanto ai ordinassimo in materia and then the cipher. The first run, q·3 &·4 Q i·1 a e Q q·4 k·3 u·8 y &·5 8·3 , decodes to diqueisunoidebitiaquali , read di quei suoi debiti a quali . The lowest line begins with the code number 22. Every group is a sign and, mostly, a small digit written above it. The sign is a consonant and the digit is the vowel that follows it, so one sign with its digit makes a syllable. The signs look Greek or Latin (alpha, omega, lambda, theta, kappa, upsilon, sigma, pi, tau, chi, phi), a few figures are used as signs (8 and 1 for l , 3 for a ), and most vowels have two digits. part what it stands for examples consonant signs one consonant alpha = n, omega = c, lambda = s, theta = d, kappa = b, upsilon = t, sigma = r, pi = m, tau = h, chi = p, phi = g, the double loop = f raised digits the vowel that follows 2 and 9 = o, 3 and 8 = i, 4 and 7 = e, 5 and 6 = a, 1 = u raised ring doubles the consonant upsilon with a ring = tt dot null — ampersand qu & with 4 = que numbers under a bar words 23 = Sua Maestà Catolica (Philip II); 22, 24 and 25–27 not resolved From targets/ariosto1559/key.tsv (Brice Dudout, CC BY 4.0), reading values. The vowel follows its sign and the letters are run together without word division, so the reader must cut the words. The key is not that of Ercole II’s letter of 28 May 1559 ( targets/ercole1559 ), nor Francesco d’Este 1546, Bresegno 1548 or Alfonso II 1576. Each was applied once to the training lines before any learning and none reads this letter.

The best of 200 keys made by permuting the key’s values scored 0.155, the median 0.038, a gap of 0.451. The thresholds fixed in advance (0.60, and 0.30 above the best control) were met. There is no contemporary decipherment, so there is no character score. A change after the test. The measured key read the double loop as n . Reading by sense showed it is f ( satisfare , far , prefata , fosse , favore , figliolo , Farnesi , and some ten more places). That change is outside the test, which held with the wrong value, and it is the only difference between the measured key and the reading key. It does not read it; that letter is another table, and nothing is claimed for it. Words written in cipher only, counted by script: of 402, 262 are certain, 95 probable, 6 restored from the sense and 39 unresolved. Certain and probable together give 357 words, 88.8%; with the restored words, 90.3%. The 95% bar is not reached. One of the certain words, satisfare (39r:05), begins with a sign read as t in both passes; it is kept certain as pre-registered and flagged. The cipher words construe as Italian sentences inside the clear letter, with gaps; one AI reader graded it B (coherent but raw), and no human palaeographer has checked the transcription or the reading. Et perché ci scrivete che detta […] la contessa, doppo d’essersi doluta de’ infiniti mali portamenti usateli dal suo consorte, né solo verso lei ma anco del figliolo […] And because you write to us that the said […] the countess, after complaining of her husband’s countless ill-treatments of her, and not of her alone but of their son […] […] a causa della sua ribellione non s’ha da haver nulla; si ché no accade che facia fondamento su li censi passati in pagar […] i debiti, ma si trovi maniera su li futuri […] because of her husband’s rebellion nothing is to be had; so she need not build on the past rents to pay the debts, but let a way be found on the future ones The countess’s debts. She wants the duke to have her debts paid out of her husband’s goods, and asks that they be paid from the arrears of the censi , not the future rents. The duke says he does not know which she means; he owes her no censo , only to restore what is hers. He had asked that the rents be held back so they could be disposed of as she wished, but if they were to pay her debts, after her husband had so many false complaints made against him at the court of Philip II, there is no appearance of honesty in it. The rebellion. She may think he owes the rents that fell due during her husband’s rebellion; Ariosto is to undeceive her, because of the rebellion nothing is owed. A way may be found on the future rents, which he would pay far more willingly for her than for her husband. The husband. She fears she must soon go to law against him, as she would have done before but for her honour and the harm to their son; the duke did not dissuade her. With this peace, in which he will be less needed, her husband will also have less favour if the suit begins. A favourite of his, Iacomo, is to have 4,000 ducats; the duke asks whether it is true. The count, her son-in-law, is to intercede, but the countess hopes little from it. Other news. The duke wants word of the rivalry between […] and Don Cesare, the marquis, and what will be done in their academies; and asks Ariosto to see whether a friend would act as of himself, since he has no commission from his masters, with a closing remark about the Farnese. The peace is presumably Cateau-Cambrésis (April 1559). The countess, her husband and the count are not identified. “Don Cesare” may be Cesare Gonzaga, count of Guastalla, and the unresolved dastalla of 41r:01 may be Guastalla ; “il marchese” may be the marquis of Pescara. These are hypotheses, not counted and not checked.

Translation translation.md # ariosto1559 - English translation (working translation of reading.md) Read in part: 88.8% of the cipher words without restorations. `[…]` = unresolved; `{nn}` = code number not resolved. The censi are annual rents (here owed by the duke to the countess's family). As to what we ordered about her debts, which she would like us to have paid out of her husband's goods: the answer His Holiness gave you {22} […], knowing she would not be satisfied unless she spoke with her husband. She asks us to have those debts paid, not the future rents (censi) but the arrears. Tell her that, wishing to please her, we had her told what we thought: that she could act to get what she wanted without her husband being able, with justice, to complain of us to His Catholic Majesty; since she will not, let her show us another way to satisfy her. As for past censi, we do not know which she means: she is owed no census by us, only that we restore what is hers. We wrote the other day that the censi should be held back so that they could be disposed of as she wished; if they were to pay Her Ladyship's debts, she can well see that, after he had so many false complaints made against us at the court of {23}, there is no appearance of honesty in it. (Postscript) She complained of her husband's countless ill-treatments of her and of their son, and fears she must soon go to law against him, as she would have done before but for her honour {24} and the harm to her son: we did not dissuade her. Show her that with this peace, in which he will be less needed, he will also have less favour if the suit begins. She perhaps thinks we owe her the censi that fell due during her husband's rebellion: undeceive her; because of the rebellion nothing is owed. Let her not build on the past censi to pay the debts; let a way be found on the future ones, which we will pay far more willingly for her than for her husband. Tell us whether it is true that Iacomo, her husband's favourite, is to have the 4,000 ducats he wrote of. As to the good office of the count her son-in-law with her husband, the countess hopes little from it: do not speak of it to the count otherwise. Tell us about the rivalry between […] and Don Cesare […] the marquis, and what will be done in their academies. As to […], see whether the friend would do anything as of himself, since he has no commission from his masters […] of the Farnese. Key: key.tsv

An unsigned Polish letter written wholly in a substitution of 23 composite sign groups, with no key and no contemporary decipherment (Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, Archiwum Sanguszków 134/8; DECODE R7513). Brice Dudout broke it from the ciphertext of the front, froze the key, tested it on the held-out reverse, and read all 71 words: the Swedes are arming and have ordered prayers and a fast for the third time. Brice Dudout · posted 30 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letter An unsigned letter in Polish, dated “Ultima Julij A° 1662” in clear at the head, two pages, to a lord addressed as “MM Pan”. The writer is in a region “towards the sea” where the Elector of Brandenburg is expected. Where Kraków, Archiwum Narodowe, Archiwum Sanguszków, teka 134/8; DECODE R7513. Catalogue no. 443 here. The cipher A simple substitution: each letter is one composite group of three or four strokes (digits, letters, squares, triangles). 23 groups, no word division, the writer’s own stops and commas kept; a cross over a group makes ą . How it was deciphered Annealing on a Polish letter model recovered the key from the front (254 groups); the key was frozen and the held-out reverse (66 groups) decoded afterwards: 97% of its groups have a value and 86% of its letters fall in words of the Polish lexicon, against at most 58% for 200 permuted keys and 70% for 200 shuffled texts. What it says The Swedes are arming and have ordered prayers and a fast for the third time, which the writer takes for a sure sign of war; he advises against leaving “this side towards the sea” bare, since it is far from Lwów back to Gdańsk, and expects the Elector in August. Still open Nothing in the cipher text. Three words are probable and one letter is restored from the sense. A few clear words before “zdrowie” were left in clear by the writer and are not transcribed in full. Credit Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée ), working with Claude Opus 5.5: the atlas of the 23 groups, the break, the held-out test, the reading and the English translation, by email of 29 October 2026. To our knowledge the first published decipherment.

The letter is in the archive of the Sanguszko family at Kraków. It is unsigned; a few clear words near the end, “… MM Pan”, are a form of address, and neither sender nor recipient is named. The place of writing is not stated either. The contents point to the Baltic coast, and Prussia is a hypothesis, not a finding. The date is given in clear at the head, “Ultima Julij A° 1662”, the last day of July. DECODE holds two images, the front of 21 lines and the reverse of six, with no decipherment and no key. The date in clear ( Ultima Julij A° 1662 ) and the first six lines of the front, the start of te nas wiesci dochodza z Rygiy y z Hamburku . Each group of three or four strokes is one letter; there is no word division. Image: Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, Archiwum Sanguszków teka 134/8, front, via DECODE R7513.

The system is a simple substitution with a very unusual alphabet. Each plain letter is written as a composite group made of a digit pair, a letter, a square, a triangle or a loop: ☐78O is t , 15☐c is e , 50lF is i , 83yΔ is o . There are 23 shapes, one for each letter the writer needs, with no homophones, no nulls and no nomenclator. The cipher has no signs for the Polish diacritics except a crossed group for ą , so the text is given in the spelling of the cipher. The shapes are in targets/asang1662/signs.md and the key in key.tsv (key K443).

The protocol. The atlas of the 23 groups was frozen before any computation, and a protocol was written and hashed. The front (21 lines, 254 groups) was kept for learning; the reverse (six lines, 66 groups) was held out and not decoded before the key was frozen. The break. The substitution was solved by simulated annealing on a Polish letter model. Latin, French, German and Italian models scored clearly lower, and the Polish text read at once. Two values were corrected from the reading of the front alone (g and k). The held-out reverse. One measurement was made on the reverse: 97% of its groups have a value and 86% of its letters fall in words of the Polish lexicon, with the segmentation fixed in advance. The 200 keys with permuted values reach at most 58%, and 200 shuffled texts at most 70%. The reverse is short; Brice Dudout says so. Two groups occur only there (Ꝑt33, a variant of the u group, and Mig4, f from the sense). The statistical check here. The project’s validator ( docs/_validate.py ) scores the reading of 320 groups (24 types) with a four-gram model of Polish of about 1790, as mean log-probability per letter. The reading scores −2.575; random keys of the same shape −5.447 on average (z 10.1); a key annealed onto the shuffled ciphertext −3.785 at best; and the same annealer, started from random keys on the real text, reaches −2.865. Verdict: pass.

Brice Dudout’s text in the spelling of the cipher. {x} probable; [x] restored from the sense. The clear words left by the writer between “Sam” and “zdrowie” are not counted. Te nas wiesci dochodza z Rygiy y z Hamburku, ze sie Szwedzi armuią y iusz to trzeci raz zapowiedzie[i]li modlitwy y post. Co nieomylnie iest znakiem, ze woyne meditantur, y ze {kogs} zagabną. Ia radze, zeby tey sciany ku morzu nie zostawowac ogoloconey, bo daleko z pod Lwowa bedzie do Gd. anska sie wracac. Sam [… MM Pan] zdrowie swoie miey na pieczy y nie kozdem{u} duchowi wierz. Cur{f}irst pewnie tu ma bydz in Augusto. These are the news that reach us from Riga and from Hamburg: the Swedes are arming, and this is already the third time they have ordered prayers and a fast. That is the unfailing sign that they are contemplating war and will attack someone. I advise that this side, towards the sea, should not be left bare: it would be a long way to come back from beneath Lwów to Gdańsk. You yourself, [… my Lord,] take care of your health, and do not believe every spirit. The Elector will surely be here in August. Brice Dudout’s notes place the letter in 1662. Sweden held Riga and Livonia under the Peace of Oliva (1660), and the writer reads the public prayers and fasts ordered there as the herald of a war. The Crown army was in the south-east, around Lwów, where the confederation of unpaid soldiers (1661–1663) held the country, hence the advice not to strip the side towards the sea (Royal Prussia, Gdańsk). “Kurfirst” is the Elector of Brandenburg, Frederick William, duke in Prussia, who came to Königsberg in the autumn of 1662 to bring the Prussian estates to heel. “Do not believe every spirit” is 1 John 4:1, nie każdemu duchowi wierzcie in the Wujek Bible (1599), a warning against false rumours. The full text and translation are under Full texts below.

{kogs}: the letters are certain; it is taken as kogoś (someone), written short. A proper name is not excluded (probable). kozdem{u} and Cur{f}irst, on the reverse: two groups occur only there and were not in the key drawn from the front. Ꝑt33, a variant of the u group, gives u ; Mig4 gives f from the sense, Curfirst = Kurfürst (probable). zapowiedzie[i]li: one group is partly covered by an ink blot; place and sense give i (restored from the sense). The clear words between Sam and zdrowie (“… MM Pan”) were not transcribed in full (uncertain reading) and are not counted. Where the writer was, and who wrote and received the letter, remain unknown; the place is Prussia only as a hypothesis.

Reading reading.md # Established text (Polish, spelling of the cipher) Conventions: {x} probable; [x] restored from the sense. The cipher has no signs for the Polish diacritics except a crossed a (ą); they are not added. Te nas wiesci dochodza z Rygiy y z Hamburku, ze sie Szwedzi armuią y iusz to trzeci raz zapowiedzie[i]li modlitwy y post. Co nieomylnie iest znakiem, ze woyne meditantur, y ze {kogs} zagabną. Ia radze, zeby tey sciany ku morzu nie zostawowac ogoloconey, bo daleko z pod Lwowa bedzie do Gd. anska sie wracac. Sam [… MM Pan] zdrowie swoie miey na pieczy y nie kozdem{u} duchowi wierz. Cur{f}irst pewnie tu ma bydz in Augusto. ## Modern Polish reading (for reading only) Te nas wieści dochodzą z Rygi i z Hamburga, że się Szwedzi zbroją i już to trzeci raz zapowiedzieli modlitwy i post. Co nieomylnie jest znakiem, że wojnę meditantur [rozważają], i że kogoś zagabną. Ja radzę, żeby tej ściany ku morzu nie zostawiać ogołoconej, bo daleko z pod Lwowa będzie do Gdańska się wracać. Sam [… MM Pan] zdrowie swoje miej na pieczy i nie każdemu duchowi wierz. Kurfirst pewnie tu ma być in Augusto [w sierpniu]. ## State of the reading First published decipherment, to our knowledge. 320 groups, 71 words. Published under Daniel Bourdeau’s rule: 95% of words read as sense, counted on the enciphered part only. Here: 71 of 71 words read as sense (100%): 67 certain (94.4%), 3 probable (4.2%), 1 restored from the sense (1.4%), 0 unresolved. Reasons in the notes. Translation translation.md # English translation These are the news that reach us from Riga and from Hamburg: the Swedes are arming, and this is already the third time they have ordered prayers and a fast. That is the unfailing sign that they are contemplating war and will attack someone. I advise that this side, towards the sea, should not be left bare: it would be a long way to come back from beneath Lwów to Gdańsk. You yourself, [… my Lord,] take care of your health, and do not believe every spirit. The Elector will surely be here in August. Key: key.tsv

Fourteen ciphered letters from Spain’s plenipotentiary at the Nijmegen congress to its envoy in Denmark. Ten carry a contemporary decipherment in the margin, four carry none, and no key survives. The syllabic nomenclator was recovered by aligning the ten margins with their cipher, and it decrypts the four letters without one, down to the loss of Ghent in March 1678. 58 28 10 65 y uf 22 16 lo s b ru n su i c — “los Brunsuic” y = n · 28 = s · 46 = de · xo = co · ef = se · ad = pa · d+ = que · H = V.S. Nijmegen → Copenhagen · syllabic nomenclator · June 1677 – March 1678 The marqués de los Balbases to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, 1677–78 Go to the full text ↓ Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. nr. 2559 · DECODE R985–R998, fourteen letters, 47 pages · ten with a contemporary decipherment in the margin, four with none No key survives. It was recovered from the ten margin decipherments and decodes all fourteen letters; the ten with a margin read from it (nine at 95% or more; R986, 28 August, builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.6%, under the 95% bar), the four with no decipherment decode only into syllable streams (decoded, not read) Daniel Bourdeau · posted 19 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: partial (70% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · partial (70% of the cipher) The letters Fourteen ciphered letters from the marqués de los Balbases, a Spanish plenipotentiary at Nijmegen, to Baltasar de Fuenmayor at Copenhagen, 1677–78. Where Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559. DECODE calls them “partially decrypted”, with the solution in the margin. The cipher Single letters and consonant-vowel syllables in numbers, disguised and reversed letter pairs, about twenty word codes and nulls. How it was read No key survives and none of the eight Brussels keys fits. An alignment program, started from cribs, rebuilt the table from the ten margin decipherments and applied it to the four letters without one. What it says The Imperial protest over the dissolution of the Bremen assembly, and the fear after the fall of Ghent: “con la pérdida de Gante…” Still open A handful of rare name codes, and homophones blurred by 4/9-type transcription slips. R985, 3 August 1677: the cipher block, with its contemporary decipherment in the left margin (“Alegrome de la buena esperança que Monsieur d'Amerong havia dado…”). The key was recovered from ten margins like this one. Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559, letter of 3 August 1677, via DECODE R985.

Fourteen letters, all from Nijmegen, dated from the clear parts: With a margin decipherment (ten): R988 (29 June 1677), R987 (18 June), R985 (3 August), R986 (28 August), R991 (5 October?), R990 (19 October), R989 (21 December), R993 (28 December 1677), R995 (26 January 1678), R994 (15 February). With no decipherment (four): R992 (19 September 1677), R996 (1 March 1678), R997 (8 March), R998 (22 March). Each letter opens with courtesies in clear, then gives a cipher block. Two letters (R985, R986) enclose a French clear paper on the Lorraine propositions.

This is a syllabic nomenclator with homophones. Groups are separated by spaces. Letters. Vowels: a 21, 3+; e 2+; i 22, 67; o 18. Consonants: b 10, n; c 9; d e ; f x ; g 16; j u+; l 8, 19; n y , 24, 20; p 26; r 23, 31; s 28, B; t 27; y 25; z h. The closing consonants s, n and r are the three commonest groups. Syllables in numbers. de 46, la 55, en 76, ra 65, re 66, te 71, do 48, ta 70, lo 58, no 63, to 73, da 45, ti 72, di 47 le 56, ni 62, vi 42, ne 61, in 77, ve 41, va 40, na 60, on 78, an 75, li 57, ga 50, go 53, tu 74 vo 43, ar 80, gu 54, un 79, er 81, du 49, nu 64, ro 68, tr 188 Letter pairs: a syllable with the vowel kept and the consonant disguised. c is written x , d or l : xo , do and lo all stand for co; the same holds for ci, ca, ce and cu. f is written n : no fo, ni fi, ne fe, na fa, nu fu. y is written r : ro yo, ra ya. Vowel-first pairs: the syllable reversed, with the consonant disguised. s is written f : ef se, if si, af sa, of so, uf su. Also ye es, ya as, yo os. p is written d : ad pa, ed pe, od po, ud pu. m is written c : ac ma, ec me, ic mi, oc mo, uc mu. h is written q or g : aq / ag ha, eq / eg he, og ho. Others: en em, ot ch, as za. Word codes. que: d+ (struck d), b+. de: p+, g+. V.S.: H. para: 05. por: 15, is . sobre: 184. quando: 148. alguno: 100. congreso: 120. ministro: des . materia: dus . duque: ep . embax[ador]: §. -mente: dan . nuestro: fe . Flandes: ban . Francia: bef . franceses: bin . Suecia: 163. Dinamarca: or . -bourg: 105. Nulls. 13+ and most 13s, 300, 200, 700, 07, 01, 18+, 16+, 35. Many of these mark the start or end of a cipher block. A few examples: 26 67 y di ed 28 = pr·i·n·ci·pe·s xo y no 23 ic 45 e = co·n·fo·r·mi·da·d xo 20 41 62 76 = co·n·ve·ni·en[te]

R998, 22 March 1678: the end of the clear text and the start of the cipher. The margin is empty. This letter and the three before it have no contemporary decipherment. Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559, letter of 22 March 1678, via DECODE R998. Decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026): the key decodes these letters group by group into syllable streams that do not yet build sentences throughout. On 22 October each stream was divided into Spanish words token by token ( read/R992_reading.md and the others); these partial readings have unread groups ([...]), unidentified codes ([85], [189]) and words only partly carried by the figures ([?word]) in most sentences. What follows is a summary of what can be made out, not a reading; the quotations are from the partial readings, holes kept. The group-by-group text is in targets/balbases1677/read/ . 19 September 1677 (R992). Balbases has seen the protest the Imperial ministers published over the dissolution of the Bremen assembly. “pues de nuestra parte no nos [85] que hacer, sino es [...] por nuestra desgracia [...] temer” a violent resolution of the confederates. After Charleroi they may insist at the union that the conquests be shared out before anything positive is settled. A rumour about the Danish chancellor and the Duke of Celle. He gives it no credit, “pues V.S. no lo ha penetrado ni me lo avisa[ra]”. The claim that the duke would take his share of his father’s conquests, the duchies of Bremen and Verden. 1 March 1678 (R996). Nothing in Sweden could undo “la desconfianza que arguimos hacia nuestros aliados”. What causes it is “la miserable postura en que [182] permanecen nuestras cosas”. The Brunswicks’ proceedings rest on solid suspicions. The ministers of the northern princes had thought of writing a protest about treaties of peace that would leave out their participation. He praises Fuenmayor’s diligence in avoiding that step. Strasbourg’s lack of constancy. A French gentleman has come back from France “satisfecho del Re[y] [...]ísimo”. 8 March 1678 (R997). In the business of the Brunswicks’ claim to the treatment of ambassadors, the Danes have conceded nothing. No formal act was made in writing at the first step. He comments on the Duke of [?Hannover] and his brothers: “Todo me parece muy bien pesado en la gran prudencia de V.S.; pero yo creo que nada de estas [?intrigas] [?llegará] a fin”. “los incesantes riesgos de Flandes, en que excuso discurrir por no crecerme la melancolía”. 22 March 1678 (R998). The dependencies between the princes of the north, “de suficiente calibre para tenernos embarazados”. The evils “que nosotros estamos padeciendo”. The loss in Flanders: “la pérdida de Gante estamos temiendo la de Ipre[s] [...] otras importantes plazas”. Ghent had fallen to Louis XIV on 9 March. They are still waiting on the others’ long delays while “la enfermedad” advances.

These were deciphered at the time. The key reproduces their margins, which recover illegible margin words and confirm the doubtful ones. Nine of the ten reach the 95% bar; R986 (28 August) builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.6%, under it. Their subjects: Amerongen’s hopes for a guarantee to the town of Bremen, 3 August. The dissolution of the Bremen conference, 18 June. Villahermosa, Temple’s recall and the Danish setback at Malmö. The Bishop of Strasbourg’s minister and Orange’s journey to England, 19 October. The loss of Saint-Ghislain, December. The Brunswick claim to ambassadorial rank, which runs through the winter letters of 1678. The margin text is transcribed in targets/balbases1677/tx/ and written out as running Spanish, spelling kept, in read/R985_reading.md and the others; the key decryption carries it group by group. In R991 a margin word left unread was filled from the figures (“de estos discursos”; 23 October 2026).

The images were fetched from DECODE. Two agents transcribed every cipher line and margin line by page into tx/ . They corrected DECODE’s transcriptions, which drop lines, confuse 46/96 and 48/98, and garble the margins. Repeated n-grams across letters were set against the margin text at the same relative position to find cribs: Brunsuic , principes , conformidad , novedad , conveniente . An alignment program ( align2.py ; hard expectation-maximisation that keeps the order of the text) was started from those cribs and run over the ten letters with margins. Each group emits a substring of the margin text, with nulls and skips allowed. Two rounds brought out the table. A frozen key then decoded all fourteen letters.

3% of groups (243 of 8,150) are unassigned. They are mostly rare 3-digit name codes: 82, 83, 150, 161, 182, 187, 189, 800. Several homophones carry a second value. The cause is transcription slips (4/9, in/ot), not the key: 41 gives di beside ve, 77 in beside ot, 61 ne beside ri. The four letters without a margin are decoded, not read: their partial readings have holes in most sentences, from rare codes with no value (fol, 85, 150, 182, 187, 17, 189, bon, i8 and others, once or twice in all fourteen letters, none in a margined letter) and from stretches whose homophones do not divide into Spanish. The doubtful (struck, overwritten) figures cannot be settled on the 1616-pixel greyscale DECODE scans; the originals are at the AGR in Brussels. None of the four has a check text. R992 is the least certain transcription. Its pages are heavily marked up.

Entretanto passamos esta residencia sin novedad alguna, con que estoy sin materia que añadir a V.S. mas de haver llegado hoy nuevas de que la plaza de Stetin estava para capitular, y que Suedeses pensavan a abandonar de todo el resto de la Pomerania; que si acaso llegare cierto, trocarà tambien muchas medidas V.S. en esas partes. Translation R993_en.md <!-- English translation of read/R993_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026), with the same holes. --> # R993, Balbases to Fuenmayor, 28 Dec 1677 (cipher): English translation I am informed by the contents of Your Lordship's first letter of the state in which, in other more recent ones, you told me those affairs stood, and of the purpose with which Monsieur de [?Ponctuo], Councillor of State of Denmark, had arrived in that town, to settle some treaties with the House of Brunswick; on which point Your Lordship reasons with all the sound considerations of your great understanding. I truly find it most delicate and very problematic whether it suits us to take an interest in its being carried out or to hinder it, for on both sides objections of the greatest consequence will arise; and so I would not know what else to tell Your Lordship, except that if it cannot properly be prevented, indifference will be necessary, and it will be advisable to keep gaining ground by always going in uniformity with the Imperial ministers; because the present state of things, and the turn that those of England are beginning to take — that King having decided to assemble his Parliament for the 25th of next month — might oblige them to change their appearance, and consequently their measures for the future. Meanwhile we pass our time at this post without any news, so I have nothing to add for Your Lordship, except that news arrived today that the town of Stettin was about to capitulate, and that the Swedes were thinking of abandoning the whole of the rest of Pomerania; which, if it proves true, will also change many of Your Lordship's measures in those parts. "el de [69]n" stays [?Nugen]; the Count's first name stays [?]. --> # R994, Balbases to Fuenmayor, 15 Feb 1678 (cipher) ## Reading Todo lo que V.S. ha ydo insinuando en orden a la pretension de los Brunswiques para el grado de Embaxadores que desean en sus ministros es muy correspondiente al govierno y genero en que aqui considerabamos acertada la forma de guiar esta materia; pero no me espanto ver ahora en la citada de V.S. de 8 que Daneses ayan cedido en esse punto, prostituyendose a la declaracion que insinua V.S. han hecho en favor de los Brunswiques, pues como son de tan pusilanime natural, en qualquier contrario suceso les havra ya parecido que el de [?Nugen], en que verdaderamente tenemos harto que sentir, los abate mucho si no se conforman a contemporizar mucho la casa de Brunswick. Aqui se ha procurado con destreza saver de essos Embaxadores Daneses lo que havia en el particular, pero ellos no solo se dan por innoticiosos de tal cosa, sino es que mas presto lo niegan, pareciendoles ser imposible que su Rey aya hecho semejante acto; y assi estimara yo que si a V.S. le fuesse facil obtener una copia de el, se sirviesse remitirmela, para que su contenido nos sirviesse de luz y de advertencia en lo que por aca se ofreciesse, siendo cierto que cada dia vamos hallando nuevos motivos hazia poder recelar que el intrinseco animo de los Brunswiques se ha revestido de menos buena intencion hazia nuestra alianza que la que conviniera. Estimo a V.S. la copia que me embia de la carta que el Embaxador de Suecia en Paris escrivio al conde [?] de Brahe, senador en Stockholm, insinuandole ser el intento del Rey Christianissimo compensar nuestras perdidas de Flandes con las de Suecia en Alemania; y no se si la indiferencia que en esse particular ha mostrado a V.S. el ministro Danes que le remitio esse papel sea artificiosa, pues oygo que tambien en Viena se ha esparcido esse genero de voces por el ministro de Brandebourg, quando en realidad no pueden de nuestra parte tener los aliados la menor sospecha, respeto no haverse llegado a terminos de estos discursos, quando ha querido la fatalidad que en todo y por todo dependamos en estas paces de lo que Inglaterra hiziere y Holanda apoyare; esto hasta aora esta todavia ignoto, y assi no podemos hablar con fundamento alguno, necessitandose ir en contemplaciones con todos hasta arrivar a la claridad de lo que ha de ser. Aqui corre voz de que el parlamento de Londres se abrio a los 7, empezando su primer discurso en esforzar el rompimiento contra Francia, y que el Rey Christianissimo salio en aquel mismo dia a las fronteras; pero yo no tengo cartas que me obliguen a dar seguro credito en nada de ambas cosas, por lo qual me remito a lo que por otras partes sabra V.S. Translation R994_en.md <!-- English translation of read/R994_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026), with the same holes. --> # R994, Balbases to Fuenmayor, 15 Feb 1678 (cipher): English translation Everything Your Lordship has been suggesting about the Brunswickers' claim to the rank of ambassadors that they want for their ministers is very much in keeping with the policy and the manner in which we here considered the way of handling this matter to be right; but I am not surprised to see now in Your Lordship's letter of the 8th that the Danes have given way on that point, prostituting themselves to the declaration that Your Lordship suggests they have made in favour of the Brunswickers; for since they are of so faint-hearted a nature, at any adverse event it will already have seemed to them that that of [?Nugen], over which we truly have much to regret, brings them very low if they do not bring themselves to humour the House of Brunswick a great deal. Here we have tried skilfully to learn from those Danish ambassadors what there was in the matter, but they not only profess to know nothing of such a thing, but rather deny it, thinking it impossible that their King should have done such an act; and so I would be grateful if, should it be easy for Your Lordship to obtain a copy of it, you would be pleased to send it to me, so that its contents might serve us as light and warning in whatever may arise here; for it is certain that every day we find new reasons to suspect that the inner mind of the Brunswickers has put on less good intention towards our alliance than would be fitting. I thank Your Lordship for the copy you send me of the letter that the Swedish ambassador in Paris wrote to Count [?] Brahe, senator in Stockholm, suggesting to him that the Most Christian King's intention is to offset our losses in Flanders with those of Sweden in Germany; and I do not know whether the indifference that the Danish minister who sent Your Lordship that paper has shown on this point is artful, for I hear that in Vienna too this kind of talk has been spread by the minister of Brandenburg, whereas in reality the allies cannot have the least suspicion of our side, since matters have not come to the point of such discussions, when ill fortune has willed that in everything and for everything we depend, in these peace talks, on what England may do and Holland support. This is still unknown up to now, and so we cannot speak with any foundation, it being necessary to go on humouring everyone until we reach clarity about what is to happen. Here the rumour runs that the London Parliament opened on the 7th, beginning its first speech by pressing for the break with France, and that the Most Christian King set out that same day for the frontiers; but I have no letters that oblige me to give sure credit to either of these things, so I refer to what Your Lordship will learn from other quarters. V.S. anduvo muy como de su prudencia en las prevenciones que hizo sobre este punto a los ministros Daneses, pues la positiva declaracion de una corona podra ser de grande inconveniente para las otras, demas de que traheria exemplares perniciosos para con tantos otros principes del Imperio de mayor y menor esfera que los de Brunswick, que querian el mismo tratamiento; siendo assi que los Duques de Lorena y Neoburg, que preceden a los Brunswiques, uno cuñado y otro suegro del mismo Emperador, no han instado en tal pretension, ni podrian sufrir se concediesse a los de Brunswick. Y es verdad que la decision de las materias de los Principes del Imperio tocan derechamente al concierto de la Dieta imperial; en el caso presente es punto privativo para solo los concurrientes ministros del congreso, donde se ajusta de conformidad entre todos la forma de tratamiento que deven observarse; con que los Brunswiques devian acudir aqui para este punto, que es en la conformidad que yo he respondido al señor Duque de Villahermosa: podia satisfacer las instancias que hazian a su [?] para librarse dellas, y no arrojarse a [?] que tenga la imposibilidad de cumplirse, ni a estado de [?] con mayor desconfianza los Principes de Brunswick, pues [?] se puede asegurarles que los ministros del Rey nuestro señor no seran los que menos se señalen en solicitar toda la satisfaccion que desean sus altezas; de que me ha parecido informar distintamente a V.S. para que se halle enterado de la respuesta que yo he dado, en caso que ahi se ofreciesse hablar en el particular. Los avisos que llegan estos dias parece que anublan algo las esperanzas en que los passados haviamos entrado hazia la paz, pues la obstinacion de Francia persiste en negar lo que visiblemente era gloria y ventaja suya; pero todavia quedamos pendientes de lo que el Rey Britanico acabara de resolver para el contrapeso de estas dudas, en que no nos dexara poco que recelar la Francia si atropella con querer tambien la guerra de Inglaterra. Translation R995_en.md <!-- English translation of read/R995_reading.md (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026), with the same holes. --> # R995, Balbases to Fuenmayor, 26 Jan 1678 (cipher): English translation I confess to Your Lordship that for some days now the way the Dukes of Brunswick behave in all their negotiations has obliged me to enter into some suspicions, and that what they did in the matter of the winter quarters, and what they now press for in having their ministers treated here as ambassadors, make me suspect that they have formed some concealed cabal of agreement with the French; for were it not so, the arrogance and effrontery with which they press for things without foundation and without precedent would seem excessive — seeking to get this declaration from the Danes there in advance of their agreements, and pressing the Duke of Villahermosa in Flanders so that we, the ambassadors of the King our lord, should make a positive commitment to give them this treatment. Your Lordship acted entirely in keeping with your prudence in the cautions you gave the Danish ministers on this point, for the positive declaration of one crown could be of great inconvenience to the others, besides which it would bring pernicious precedents with regard to so many other princes of the Empire, of greater and lesser rank than those of Brunswick, who would want the same treatment; the more so as the Dukes of Lorraine and Neuburg, who take precedence over the Brunswickers — one the brother-in-law and the other the father-in-law of the Emperor himself — have not pressed such a claim, nor could they bear its being granted to those of Brunswick. And it is true that the decision of matters concerning the princes of the Empire belongs properly to the deliberation of the Imperial Diet; in the present case it is a point reserved solely to the ministers attending the congress, where the form of treatment to be observed is settled by agreement among all; so the Brunswickers ought to apply here on this point. This is in line with what I answered the Lord Duke of Villahermosa: he could meet the requests they were making to His [?] so as to free himself of them, and not throw himself into [?] that would be impossible to fulfil, nor into a state of [?] the Princes of Brunswick with greater distrust; for [?] they can be assured that the ministers of the King our lord will not be the least forward in seeking all the satisfaction their Highnesses desire. I thought I should inform Your Lordship of this in detail, so that you may know the answer I have given, in case there should be occasion to speak of the matter there. The reports arriving these days seem to cloud somewhat the hopes towards peace that we had entered into in past days, for France's obstinacy persists in denying what was visibly its own glory and advantage; but we still remain waiting on what the British King will finally resolve to counterbalance these doubts, in which France will leave us not a little to fear if it rushes into wanting war with England as well. A copy of an intercepted field letter from Banér at Hof, days before his winter march on Regensburg, kept in Kircher’s correspondence (APUG 568 f. 239); posted on Cipherbrain in 2019, where the attempts failed. No Swedish key on DECODE fits; the key of the homophonic cipher in two-digit figures was recovered from cribs in the adjacent clear German ( durch , und ). 246 of 275 cipher figures decrypt (89.5%); a courier’s name, one corrupt stretch of the copy and fourteen code groups remain open. 92 39 73 43 · 30 27 69 · 24 78 27 69 66 50 39 21 71 37 n a c h · d e r · O b e r p f a l t z a = 18 39 46 74 85 · e = 19 27 41 62 75 86 · n = 11 26 49 64 92 98 Hof → Silesia · homophonic cipher in two-digit figures with code groups, inside clear German · 29 December 1640 Johan Banér to Torsten Stålhandske, Hof, 29 December 1640 from Johan Banér → to Torsten Stålhandske Go to the full text ↓ Pontificia Università Gregoriana, APUG 568 f. 239r–v, among Athanasius Kircher’s letters · a copy of an intercepted field letter, written at Hof days before Banér’s winter march on Regensburg · posted on Cipherbrain in June 2019, where the attempts failed; no decipherment found since The key was recovered from cribs in the adjacent clear German, with a language model of 1630s German · 246 of 275 cipher figures decrypted; a courier’s name, one corrupt stretch and nine of the fourteen code groups remain open (the other five read as letters) Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (90% of the cipher) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (90% of the cipher) The letter Copy of an intercepted letter from Swedish field marshal Johan Banér to Torsten Stålhandske, Hof, 29 December 1640. Where Kircher’s correspondence, Gregoriana APUG 568 f. 239. Posted on Cipherbrain in 2019 with Philip Neal’s transcription. The cipher Mostly clear German; seven passages in two-digit figures, with fourteen three-digit code groups. No Swedish key on DECODE fits. How it was read Two cribs from the adjacent clear text ( durch , und ) led the solver to nach der Oberpfaltz und , and the rest of the key followed. 246 of 275 figures decrypt (89.5%). What it says Banér means to march “nach der Oberpfaltz”; Stålhandske is to watch the enemy and report by spies. Still open The second courier’s name, a corrupt stretch in the fifth passage, and nine of the fourteen code groups (the other five read as letters).

The heading reads Copia Intercipirtes Schreibens General Baners an General Major Stallhausen : Stålhandske, who commanded the Swedish troops in Silesia. The letter is dated Hoff den 29 Decem. A. 1640 and signed with a flourished B. Kircher’s file calls it Copia litterarum interceptarum Generalis Baners Hoff in Silesia . The copy reached Rome, presumably so that Kircher could try the cipher; there is no decipherment on the two pages posted. The first page, upper half: the heading, the first two cipher passages (the routes of an earlier letter), and the third, which decrypts as nach der Oberpfaltz und gegen die [442] . Image: Pontificia Università Gregoriana, APUG 568 f. 239r, via the Museo Galileo Kircher Correspondence Project. The cipher passages (S1–S7 here) hold 275 two-digit numbers with 74 distinct values from 2 to 98, and fourteen three-digit numbers: 361, 442, 464, 508, 513 and 568, which stand for names or nouns, and a cluster 766–783 in the fifth and sixth passages. The work started from Neal’s transcription and the blog’s small images; it was then checked figure by figure against the Museo Galileo’s scans of f. 239r–v (1469 × 2304 px, served openly), which correct four figures: the first figure of S4 is 86 (Neal 66), a figure in Schlesien is 86 (Neal 36), one in guten is 47 (Neal 57), and the figure Neal could not read in S7 is 92.

The Swedish keys. DECODE holds the Riksarkivet’s box of Swedish chancery keys ( Chifferklaver , låda II, records R4103–R4329). Their archivists’ covers name the correspondents and give the values of a . Banér’s keys there, the Horn–Banér cipher (R4122), the code in use with Oxenstierna from late 1634 (R4123, copied in R4325 as Generalis Campi Marschalli Johan Banneris Cyffer ), and the other alphabets of the 1640 chancery register (R4325, R4266), were transcribed and tried, as they stand and at every offset from −30 to +30. None fits. Why a solver alone fails. Unconstrained homophonic annealing finds keys that score better than real German would. A control settled this: 1630s German from the Theatrum Europaeum , cut to the same segment lengths and enciphered with Banér’s 1634 key, scores −279 under the model built here ( de-1640s ), and the solver’s optima sit at −390 to −430. With eight known values the same solver, restricted to a few homophones per letter, lands on the true key. So the letter needed cribs. The cribs. The sixth passage follows mich aber von zeit zu zeit and opens 40 16 23 28 29: durch . The pair 28 29 ( ch ) comes seven times. 16 64 40 is und . With those fixed, the solver wrote nach der … pfaltz und in the third passage, the one that ends [442] loszugehen . Banér did march from Hof into the Upper Palatinate in the first days of January 1641, and surprised the Reichstag at Regensburg (this background is not from the sources and was not checked here): … Continance erleiden will, 92 39 73 43 30 27 69 24 78 27 69 66 50 39 21 71 37 16 64 40 33 62 51 75 98 63 77 27 442 loszugehen : nach der Oberpfaltz und gegen die [442] loszugehen. Image: Pontificia Università Gregoriana, APUG 568 f. 239r, via the Museo Galileo Kircher Correspondence Project. That phrase fixes twenty values, each consistent with durch and und . From there the key was extended word by word, and no value was kept unless it gave sense in at least two words: Schlesien agirende , dazu ziehen , gute acht geben , sobaldt , ehender , solche , Fürsichtigkeit nachvolgen , wohin er seine Marche zu richten , entgegen . The key has 70 values, one to six per letter, in no alphabetical or banded order.

Clear text in roman, the decrypted passages in italics, code groups in brackets, letters not recovered as ? . The transcription of the clear text is Neal’s. … welches ich im Duplo, als ein Exemplar Jobs [508], das andere aber in [513] n Johann ??????????? über [568] abgehen lassen … … undt gesonnen, wofern es nimmer die Ratio Belli undt des feinds … Continance erleiden will, nach der Oberpfaltz und gegen die [442] loszugehen, undt meinen aeussersten fleis anzuwenden. … es werde der feindt seine aeusserste macht von allen oertern her colligiren, undt so starck als es ihm muglig mir entgegen leitten, etwa auch die in Schlesien agirende [361] dazu ziehen. So wollt der herr General Major darau [f] gute acht geben und sobaldt (e)ich sein gegen [773] ehender [464] auf solche W ?????????????? zu [775] dem [767] ?? ein guten Fürsichtigkeit nachvolgen, mich aber von zeit zu zeit durch E(sp)ionen sie ko [m] en, dass sie mö [g] en, wie sein undt des feindes gelegenheit sey, eigentlich undt unschwierig berichten, damit ich ihm inmittelst mit seiner andeutung wohin er seine(n) Marche zu richte(n), entgegen wolten komme … In sense. Banér sent his letter of the 16th in duplicate, one copy by [508] , the other by a Johann by way of [568] . He has come to Hof and means, if the reason of war and the enemy’s bearing allow, to march through the Upper Palatinate and against [442] , most likely Regensburg or the Bavarians. He expects the enemy to gather every force against him, “and perhaps also draw in the [troops] acting in Silesia”. Stålhandske is therefore to keep good watch, and as soon as the enemy moves off, to follow with good caution. He is to report from time to time through spies on his own and the enemy’s situation, so that Banér, told where he means to direct his march, can come to meet him. The seventh passage, after mit seiner andeutung : 38 24 29 77 92 27 23 13 41 44 98 86 … wohin er seine(n) Marche zu richte(n), entgegen wolten . Re-measured 5 October 2026. measure_sense.py counts only figures inside words that read: 246 of 275 (89.5%). The old count (246 of 274) also credited a stray n after code 513. Every unread stretch was re-read at 2× from the Museo Galileo scan: the copy has 13. 12. 32 where Neal dropped the 12, so 12 = p and Espionen is whole. The S5 stretch ( …eise n o u i r e c h t e zu ) was scored against movirte , nachrichte and others with a model of 1640s German: none fits the confirmed figures. The 29 open tokens are the corrupt name, the S5 stretch and one stray letter, all with confirmed figures and fixed values. The second courier’s name (S2, eleven tokens after Johann , which decipher as ohrspacbuet ). The figures are confirmed on the manuscript and every value is fixed by other words, so the copy itself is corrupt here. The first courier’s name decrypts as Jobs [508], probably Jobst and a surname in code (graded M). A stretch of the fifth passage ( eisen o vi rechte , fourteen tokens), two tokens before ein guten , and a stray e in sobaldt e ich (probably er sich ). The manuscript confirms every figure and every value is fixed by other words, so this copy, the only one known, is corrupt here; the sent original or a Swedish register copy would be needed. Slips of the copy (graded C): d e i n for die in ; 93 (i) for n in Schlesien ; one letter missing from Marche ; the copy also drops a 12 from Espionen , restored from the scan (12 = p). The fourteen code groups. 442 is what Banér marches against; 361 is the force acting in Silesia; 508 and 568 are how the two copies went. The 7xx codes fall where letters are missing ( darau [778] for darauff , au [772] for auss , ko [770] en ), and five of them are letters: freed of fixed values, the solver itself returns au [772] solche [766] eise = auf solche Weise , and darau [778] = darauf , ko [770] en = kommen , dass sie mo [783] en = dass sie mögen (graded C). The other nine (361, 442, 464, 508, 513, 568, 767, 773, 775) stay open: no key survives and each occurs once. The copy is the only witness known. The sent original, or a register copy in Banér’s papers in Stockholm, would settle the corrupt stretches; neither is digitised.

Clairambault 325 f. 84r, lines 16–19: “…celuy de Ferrare a Calatheu”, the cipher, then “comme j’espere vous dire dimenche”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Clairambault 325 f. 84r, via DECODE R2285. The copy is headed “Lettre de M. Bayard a M. le Mal de Montmorency”, dated “5 Janvier 1526”, with the source reference “V. 41. f. 4” in the margin. It is signed “Gilbert Bayard”, “A Tollede le v e jo. de Janvier”. It reports Bayard’s talks with the viceroy Lannoy, with Lallemant and with Don Hugo de Moncada on the four points still open before the treaty of Madrid: the hostages, Fuenterrabía, and the sovereignty of the Constable of Bourbon. (This background is not from the sources and was not checked here.) The cipher comes where Bayard tells how the Imperial side had asked whether he had spoken to any Italian ambassador: “…et qu’il y avoit neuf moys que je n’avoye salué celuy de Ferrare a Calatheu [ cipher ] comme j’espere vous dire dimenche.”

There are 56 signs of 29 kinds (measured on signs.txt ): Greek-like letters (Φ, θ, ξ, φ, γ, ω, ∂), figures (7), Latin letters (n, o, R, b, x, k, e), triangles filled and open, a barred I, a circled m, and an m with a superscript m. With 29 kinds in 56 signs there must be homophones, nulls or code signs. Several of the shapes (7, R, n, θ, x, Δ, ε, ω, and the “ny” and K signs that are nulls in Raince’s key) belong to the pool used by French ciphers of 1525–26. The copyist drew them by imitation, so small differences between shapes may not be meaningful.

Print. Champollion-Figeac, Captivité du roi François Ier (Paris 1847), no. CCXVIII, pp. 462–463, prints the letter from “copie de Bréquigny, vol. 91”. His text has “…que j’avoye salué celui de Ferrare. A ce soir…”, with no mention of a cipher. Calvimont’s key (same volume, f. 67, key recovered by Norbert Biermann). Its signs were matched by shape (7 = m, 8/∂ = a, 5 = e, 6/b = t, barred I = d, ω = l) and fixed in a solver (simulated annealing). The result scores worse than with no values fixed and gives no French. Raince’s 1526 key (Tomokiyo, as re-measured for the Raince write-up), with the nulls removed. It gives −3.5 per sign under the 1530s French model, against −1.4 for the free solution, and the output is gibberish. The shapes are shared, but the values are not. Ciphertext only. Two homophonic annealing runs against a 5-gram model of 1530s French despatches: one free, and one allowing homophones only for common letters, with 24 restarts. The best restarts share no text. At 56 signs the problem is underdetermined.

The original letter (“V. 41 f. 4”, probably a Béthune or Brienne volume). Its signs would be clean, and a decipherment may be written on it. Another cipher letter of Bayard’s from the 1525–26 embassy in Spain, or a key for Montmorency’s correspondence with him.

Catalogue item 160 grouped five letters of Beatrice d’Aragona, Queen of Hungary, to Ferrara; since 14 October 2026 each cipher, and the plain letter, has its own page: the 1482 letters , 8 March 1486 , 2 May 1486 and the plain letter of 1505 .

R1154 is ordinary Italian chancery writing. Beatrice asks Ippolito to send a trusted messenger with letters for the cardinal of Esztergom, giving the journey the appearance of Ippolito’s own business. She then explains why she will not write more: Et per non esser certa che le littere pervengano secure, et per non havere cifra: non ce extendemo altramente per questa “Because we are not certain the letters will arrive safely, and because we have no cipher, we do not go into further detail in this letter.” Berzeviczy prints it as no. CCCII. The manuscript’s final dating clause, M° quingentesimo quinto , agrees with its docket and photograph label: 1505, not 1504 .

The despatch belongs to the quarrel over the bull of 1586 that let Henri III raise money by selling church property. The nuncio reports what the Duke of Guise has sent to tell him, what a well-placed informant heard, and the mood of the clergy’s assembly. The reading, the clerk’s single consonants kept, nomenclator words in full: Hogi il Duca di Guisa mi ha mandato a dire per questi Ambasciatore di Duca di Ferrara che egli hora tiene per fermo che il Re Christianissimo deba fare la pace con gli Heretici come prima havera riscoso quanti si deve vendere per la bola, ma che eso Duca di Guisa non vi aconsentira mai … Mi viene apreso hora riferito da personagio di molta autorita havere inteso da un gentilhuomo che, ragionando eso gentilhuomo ultimamente con eso Duca di Guisa di questi guerra, e venuto a dir ad eso Duca di Guisa che egli si potrebe contentar che la pace si facese quando se gli dese Metz et una buona soma di denari, et che eso Duca di Guisa rispose che piacese a Dio che cosi si facese. … Et di nuovo ho inteso che deta congreg. inclina ad apelarsi ad [?futurum] concilium, se vedera di non potere otenere quelli che hora tenta … “Today the Duke of Guise sent word to me through the ambassador of the Duke of Ferrara that he now holds it for certain that the Most Christian King must make peace with the heretics as soon as he has collected what is to be sold under the bull, but that the Duke of Guise will never consent to it … I am now told by a person of great authority that he heard from a gentleman that, when this gentleman lately talked with the Duke of Guise about this war, he came to say to him that he might be content for the peace to be made if he were given Metz and a good sum of money, and the Duke of Guise answered: would to God it were done so. … And I hear again that the congregation is inclined to appeal to a [?future] council if it sees it cannot obtain what it now attempts …” The King shows Guise every sign of confidence, but his heart is thought not to match; Guise is about to leave Paris; the city’s churchmen resent the bull for the alienation as it stands. The nuncio offers to send the clergy’s letters in his own cipher.

DECODE’s transcription D1610 (volunteer TimB) was decoded with Lasry’s key file as it stands, reading pairs and treating 8 as the null. That left 66 unknown groups, most of them marked nomenclator codes. Meister p. 324 no. 2 prints Ragazzoni’s key of 1583 for the Paris nunciature: the same letter alphabet, with a table of names and of marked words. In the OCR the names sit in a clean two-column list; the marked words are in one run with each code after its word, an alignment checked against R16 (26¸ che , 36¸ per , 28+ questi , 98+ essere , 20− non , 0̇ con ). Unknowns fell to 18, but the decode was still a run-on block with a hole in nearly every clause, and the reading audit of 22 October 2026 classed it decoded, not read. On 23 October 2026 the record’s attachment D3195 turned out to be Meister pp. 324–325 with the whole Ragazzoni nomenclator: names; the mark families x4+ ( Cardinale … denari ), stroked x4 ( Sua Santità , Sua Maestà ), hooked x6 ( che , per , come ), x8+ ( quanti , questi ), struck x0 ( non , lettere , mente , pace ) and dotted x4 ( Religione Cattolica , Heretici , Guerra ). The first decoder had also taken the 8 of 84+, 86 and 80− as a null. A new beam decoder scored with the it-cinquecento model was run on TimB’s transcription with 16 labels corrected on the images ( R16_corrections.tsv ); 29 is et (Meister), not che . Every one of the 428 words is carried by the figures, apart from the places listed below.

R16, [?futurum] : “futu” and a dotted 3 and 9, an abbreviation Meister’s table does not list; and the last eleven digits of f. 206v, before the signature flourish, which give no word. R16, five letters on look-alike digits (the writer’s 5 closes like an 8 and his 7 takes a hook): si [?e], [?ocorendo], [?l'aleenatione], [?fata], [?vedo]. The alternative gives no word in each case. The codes 18 and 48, earlier taken for open dukes’ names, were decoder misparses: 70 + 18 is “Ambasciatore di Duca di Ferrara”, and “uers·48” is uerso .

Seven lines in Giuliano Caprile’s 1519 two-tier cipher (DECODE R1128), the only one of his 1519 letters without a decipherment; the others were deciphered in 1882. Tables of values rebuilt from two of those decipherments give no Italian on it against random-key controls. Attempted, not solved; the key can still be rebuilt from the 1882 copies. L/7 · -/n · u/7 · x/7 · c/7 · m/n · -/a o · r · a · t · o · r · e a small sign over a base stroke; bracket signs stand for whole words ldquo;oratore a small sign over a base stroke; bracket signs stand for whole words rdquo; in the sibling letter R1133, from its 1882 decipherment Eger → Ferrara · two-tier cipher of graphic signs with code words · 9 March 1519 Giuliano Caprile, Eger, 9 March 1519 to Bonaventura Pistofilo Nine lines in Caprile’s 1519 cipher about his own lawsuit at Rome; values rebuilt from his letters deciphered in 1882 give no Italian on it, so it stays unread. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map Credits · Michael Brackx (pointer to a source) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter Giuliano Caprile, canon of Eger and secretary of Cardinal Ippolito d’Este, to the ducal secretary Bonaventura Pistofilo (the offices are not stated in the notes and were not checked here), Eger, 9 March 1519: nine lines of cipher and a clear postscript. Where Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, Caprili 1519–20 no. 1; DECODE R1128 (catalogue item 157), Vestigia 1853. The cipher Two tiers: a small sign written over a base stroke (7, m, n, a, t, 4), and bracket-shaped signs that stand for whole words. 183 columns of 78 kinds, 39 of them code words. How it was tried Caprile’s other 1519 letters in the same cipher were deciphered in 1882. Two of them were paired with those decipherments to rebuild tables of values, and the tables were run on R1128 against random-key controls. Why it resists The two pairings disagree on how the cipher works (one letter per column, or a syllable per column), and only about nine letter values are secure. None of the tables gives Italian on R1128. What would finish it A careful transcription of another 1882-paired letter (R1132 against its copy 6b, R1131 against 5b) to fill the table and the code list. The key material exists; the work is not done. Other ciphers Caprile’s 1520–21 letters use a different cipher, with its own page , where most of them are deciphered; Alfonso Cistarelli’s numerical cipher of 1520 has its own page . R1128, 9 March 1519: the cipher block at the head of the letter, above the clear text to Bonaventura Pistofilo. Each column is a small sign over a base stroke; the bracket-shaped signs are code words. Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, Caprili 1519–20 no. 1, p. 1, via Vestigia 1853.

DECODE ASMo b. 4 Vestigia Date What was found R1128 1519–20 no. 1 1853 9 Mar 1519 Nine lines in the 1519 two-tier cipher, no decipherment. Not deciphered. R1129–R1133 nos. 3a–7a 1855–1867 Apr–May 1519 Decipherments of 1882 filed as 3b/3c … 7b/7c. R1134 no. 8a 1870 12 Jun 1519 8b, 8c, covering pp. 1–3. R1135 no. 10a 1874 1519 Interlinear gloss on the leaf and 10b. The ASMo inventory notes that the decipherments of almost all the 1519 despatches are missing and were made only in 1882; those are the “b” and “c” items filed after the originals. No. 1 (R1128) has none. Its clear part and Caprile’s next letter (“In un’altra mia ve mandai in zifra…”) say it concerned his own lawsuit at Rome (“le ragioni mie … l’adversario”). The other 1519 letters are copies of reports to the King of France on the imperial election.

Each column is a small sign over a base stroke. Paired with its 1882 decipherment 7c, R1133 (1,327 columns, 16% illegible in a faded band) reads as one plaintext letter per column, with homophones: “oratore” = L/7 -/n u/7 x/7 c/7 m/n -/a, and c/7 = o, m/n = r, x/7 = t hold across the page. Bracket-L signs with an inner sign are code words: the run [d][s][&] recurs where the decipherment has “de vostra maesta”. A fifth of R1133’s columns are such codes. R1130 paired with its decipherment 4c points the other way: the upper sign gives a consonant and the base a vowel (7 none, m e, n o), and the brackets are syllables; about twenty values predict 16 of 18 held-out columns, against 8 for a shuffled table. The two readings conflict, and neither is settled.

A language-model search (simulated annealing) over R1133, R1134 and R1128 with the nine secure values fixed gives only scattered words. The known tables (2 October 2026): the R1130/4c syllabary covers 32% of R1128’s columns and scores like a random key with the same values (−3.22 against −3.24 per character); the R1133/7c values cover 13%. A factorised syllabary (consonant from the upper sign, vowel from the base) trained on both pairings learns the base tier cleanly but not the upper; decoded with it, R1128 scores worse than the same tables permuted (−2.92 against −2.41). Benedetto Fantini’s letters of 1517–18 from the same household use a cipher of the same family, and the 1519 values do not fit them either ( Fantini 1517–18 ).

The key material is in the file: R1131 and R1132 (eight pages) have their 1882 decipherments 5b and 6b. A line-by-line transcription of one of them against its decipherment would fill the letter table and the code list, and then R1128 can be tried again. Until then R1128 is attempted, not solved. A shorter route may exist. The Modena archivists reconstructed this key in the nineteenth century (ASMo, Cancelleria, Cifrario b. 8 fasc. 4), and Patrizia Cremonini printed its sheets, too small to transcribe sign by sign, in the Rivista di Studi Ungheresi XVI (2017), figs. 17.1–17.3. Michael Brackx found the reference ( issue #121 ), and pointed out that some small upper signs in our transcription of R1128 may be attached to the wrong base (not yet checked here). A photograph of the archive’s sheets is the next step.
