Among King Carlos’s clear French letters to Queen Amélie (ANTT, CAM maço 12) are three code telegrams of spring 1903. A Hotel Bristol card in the same unit is the decode of the 12 May telegram to Paris, and the undated one carries its decode in ink on the form. The two repeats of the May telegram fix 38564 = ter and 58215 = com; the code is not alphabetical. The telegram of 4 March to the Queen’s yacht at Oran, 47 items, has no decode. 38564 29955 58215 · 18111 91518 34678 · 38564 49452 58215 ter combinado com · Ros-a e ella · ter fallado com the two repeats fix 38564 = ter and 58215 = com Lisbon → Queen Amélie (Paris, Oran) · five-figure code · March–May 1903 · two of three telegrams decoded at the time King Carlos to Queen Amélie, 1903: three code telegrams from Carlos I of Portugal → to Amélie of Orléans Go to the full text ↓ Among King Carlos’s clear letters to the Queen are three code telegrams of spring 1903; two are deciphered by decodes made on receipt, and the third, sent to her yacht at Oran, has none. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 Method · m0054 and m0058 (decodes of the time on m0060 and on m0058): read from existing decipherment (complete) · m0056, Lisbon -> Tlemcen, 4 Mar 1903: not solved (none) · On the map Contributed by WAINUT (solution, transcription, identification, verification) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · partial · 2 of 3 telegrams (27 of 74 code items) The telegrams King Carlos I of Portugal to Queen Amélie, spring 1903: Lisbon to Paris (Hotel Bristol), 12 May; Lisbon to Tlemcen for the yacht Amélie at Oran, 4 March; and one undated. French clear text with five-figure code groups. Where Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Documentos de D. Carlos, D. Amélia e D. Manuel II , maço 12 (PT/TT/CAM/M12), images m0054–m0060 of 61. Catalogue entry 401. The code A code of five-figure groups, the same in all three telegrams (they share groups). It is not alphabetical: 38564 = ter stands below 58215 = com . How it was deciphered From the decodes of the time. A Hotel Bristol card (m0060) repeats the clear words of the 12 May telegram and puts a Portuguese sentence where its 14 groups stand; the undated telegram has its decode in ink on the form. What it says All are well at home; the Queen “may give” something, “but only after having arranged it with Rosa” and after the French Government has been spoken to; he has written to her at Malta. Still open The Tlemcen telegram of 4 March (47 items): no decode and no codebook. Which group carries which word in seven groups of the May telegram and in the undated one. Credit Transcriptions, dates and directions, the link between the May telegram and the card m0060, and the controls by WAINUT (27 October 2026), done with AI language-model agents; the transcriptions were made with a vision-capable language model and checked against the DigitArq images. The decodes are those made on receipt in 1903.

Maço 12 of the papers of King Carlos, Queen Amélie and Manuel II holds 61 images. Images m0001–m0053 are the King’s letters to “Ma chère Amélie”, in French and in clear, of 1904–1905. Only three telegrams are in code. The DigitArq record calls the unit not accessible; its images download all the same through DigitArq’s own JSON service. image route and date items decode of the time m0054 (cover m0055) Lisbon → Paris, Hotel Bristol, 12 May 1903 14 groups among clear French words the card m0060 m0056 (back m0057) Lisbon → Tlemcen, 4 March 1903, to the Queen “bord yacht Amélie, Oran” 47 (44 groups and three “03”) none found m0058 (back m0059) undated (spring 1903?) 13 (12 groups and “03”) in ink on the same form The May telegram is on printed strips. Its header, SS PARIS LISBOA 3428 33 12 12/40- HS , follows the rule printed on the form: the first number after the place of origin is the serial number and the second the taxed words. So it left Lisbon as no. 3428, 33 words, on the 12th at 12:40, and the Paris stamp reads 12 MAI 03. The first pass had it as Paris to Lisbon, 1903/04. The March telegram is written by hand on a French form: “Pour Tlemcen de Lisbonne No 1728 Mots 86 Dépôt le 4/3 1903 à 8h30”, stamped TLEMCEN 5 3 03 ORAN. Its sender is not named; it is filed with the King’s papers. The undated telegram is written on a blank form with no office data.

The telegram of 12 May 1903 as received in Paris: clear French words and 14 code groups on printed strips. A receiver marked one figure in most groups with a short stroke. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, PT/TT/CAM/M12, image m0054, via DigitArq. The French words are in clear. The 14 groups carry a Portuguese sentence, which the card m0060, printed “Hotel Bristol, Paris”, writes out in its place. The card repeats the telegram’s clear words in order and puts the Portuguese where the groups stand, so it is the decode of this telegram, made on receipt. The card m0060: the clear French of the telegram with the decoded Portuguese sentence in its place. The hyphens in “Po-des” and “Ros-a” are the decoder’s. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, PT/TT/CAM/M12, image m0060, via DigitArq. Merci dépêche. Ici tout et tous très bien. Podes dar, mas só depois de ter combinado com Rosa e ella ter fallado com Governo francez. Petits baisent main. T’embrasse. Carlos. “Thanks for your telegram. Here everything and everyone very well. You may give [it], but only after having arranged it with Rosa and after she has spoken with the French Government. The little ones kiss your hand. I embrace you. Carlos.” What is to be given is not said, and “ella” has no clear antecedent. Rosa is probably Tomás de Sousa Rosa, then Portuguese minister in Paris (an identification made here, not checked). Edward VII had visited Paris on 1–4 May 1903; whether the telegram has to do with that is not known. The two repeated groups fix part of the alignment. 38564 (groups 5 and 11) and 58215 (groups 7 and 13) stand two places apart, as “ter … com” does twice in the decode (“ter combinado com”, “ter fallado com”). So 38564 = ter , 58215 = com , and the groups between them are 29955 = combinado and 49452 = fallado . The last group, 82042, is left for “Governo francez”. The 19 Portuguese words stand on 14 groups, so some groups carry more than one word, and groups 1–4 and 8–10 cannot be split word by word. The decoder’s hyphens suggest that the code has syllables as well as words.

The undated telegram m0058: 12 groups and “03”, with the decode written in ink below them. The writer makes 5 like a long s. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, PT/TT/CAM/M12, image m0058, via DigitArq. Ici tous et tout bien. T’ai écrit à Malte. T’embrasse, et les petits salue tous. Carlos. “Here everyone and everything well. [I] have written to you at Malta. [I] embrace you, and the little ones greet everyone. Carlos.” “salue” is singular as written; “[I] embrace you and the little ones; greet everyone [from me]” is also possible. Malta fits the Queen’s Mediterranean cruise of spring 1903. The 12 groups and “03” do not map one to one onto the 15 words, so which group carries which word is not known.

The telegram of 4 March 1903 reached the Queen on board the yacht Amélie at Oran: 44 five-figure groups and three “03”, 86 taxed words. No decode was found in the maço. 17582 92270 19652 10734 92270 43554 76138 78341 76342? 93434 94057 33725 52162 55820 03 68564 90387 59338? 91518 38965 03 57174 43554 78341 85328 57944 14492 95268 58215 46864 56994 26722 85387 39965 03 42618 23014 82927 81037 73374 17582 84437 32937 56484 57218 93057 61742 It shares 58215 and 91518 with the May telegram, and 10734, 43554 and 78341 with the undated one. Of these only 58215 ( com ) has a value. The fourth group of line 3 was taken as 19338 in one transcription and 59338 in the other.

Two controls ( groups.py ). Random telegrams of 12 and 44 five-figure groups share two or more groups in 0 of 20,000 trials, so the shared groups show that the three telegrams use one code. In the undated telegram the decode has 60 letters and the 12 groups have 60 figures; taken letter for figure, the mapping has 37 conflicts, against 38.1 on average (minimum 32) for 1,000 shuffled orders of the figures. That is no better than chance: the 60 = 60 is a coincidence and the system is a code, not a letter cipher. The code is not alphabetical ( com has the higher number), unlike the code of Sabugosa’s telegrams of the same weeks ( targets/sabugosa1910 ), so the four values from the May telegram predict nothing about the rest of the book.

The Tlemcen telegram, all 47 items: no decode in the maço and no codebook. Only 58215 ( com ) has a value, and alone it gives nothing. May telegram, groups 1–4 (28548 40710 86415 23274 = “Po-des dar mas só depois de”) and 8–10 (18111 91518 34678 = “Ros-a e ella”): the words are given by the decode (grade H), but not which group carries which. May telegram: 38564 ter , 58215 com , 29955 combinado and 49452 fallado are fixed by the repeats; 82042 “Governo francez” is what is left over (grade I). The undated telegram: the words are given by the decode (grade H); the split over the 12 groups and “03” is not known, and the date is not on the form. Rosa as Tomás de Sousa Rosa, and the object of “Podes dar”, are not checked. Other units of the same collection and the Arquivo da Casa Real were not searched; they may hold a decode of the March telegram or the codebook.

An undated letter to the French ambassador in Scotland, wholly in a nomenclator of graphic symbols. George Lasry deciphered it; his plaintext overlays, published on Cryptiana in 2022, were compared with the manuscript and transcribed. It gives instructions on James VI’s upbringing and marriage and on English encroachment; the catalogue date of 1550 is an error. MON NEPVEV · LA PAIX DV DICT PAIS · LE CUEVR DES ESCOSSOIS LES ANGLOIS N’EMPIETENT AVCVNE CHOSE EN ESCOSSE French court → Scotland · homophonic nomenclator · 1565–67 or 1572 Charles IX to Philibert du Croc from Charles IX Go to the full text ↓ Archives départementales de la Nièvre, fonds du Bourg de Bozas, exact cote unreported · two pages, French, wholly ciphered · DECODE R2789, no decipherment on the record · catalogue item 34 George Lasry deciphered the letter, and his full-page plaintext overlays were published on Satoshi Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana in 2022. They were compared with the DECODE images and Destray’s facsimile and transcribed; no key was rebuilt here. Measured on the words of the transcription, the letter builds coherent sentences but reads at 92.8%, under the 95% bar. Paul Destray printed the address as “A monsr du Croq, mon conseiller et me d’hostel ordinaire et mon ambassadeur en Escosse” and catalogued the item as document XLIII, S. l. n. d. : without place or date. He noted that the letter, its addition, and the King’s second signature were in cipher; Pinart countersigned it. The two following facsimile leaves are the same images now served by DECODE. DECODE’s structured date spans 1550–1574 but supplies day and month as 1 January; the catalogue flattened that into “1 Jan 1550.” That cannot be a document date: Charles IX was born on 27 June 1550. Cryptiana’s cautious “1565–1567 or 1572” follows the periods in which du Croc served in Scotland and is retained here. The contents fit the minority of James VI, but they do not distinguish those missions securely. The recto: the main letter in graphic cipher, followed lower on the leaf by Charles’s signature and the beginning of the ciphered postscript. Image: Archives départementales de la Nièvre, letter of Charles IX to du Croc, recto, reproduced by Destray (1924), via Gallica and DECODE R2789.

Tomokiyo’s page George Lasry’s Solutions of Unsolved Ciphers has a section headed “Charles IX to Philibert du Croc (1565–1567 or 1572).” Beneath the manuscript it says “This is solved as follows” and reproduces Lasry’s plaintext in red directly over the signs on both pages. The overlay lies on the same two pages: page geometry, line breaks, signatures and the postscript agree throughout. The system is a French homophonic nomenclator: several graphic signs can represent letters, while other signs stand for whole words or names. Lasry’s displayed key includes values such as de , et , que , par , pour , je , vous , la Royne d’Angleterre , la Royne d’Escosse , and royaulme . It is not the symbol system used in Catherine de Médicis’s separate letter to du Croc of 27 April 1567. Lasry’s published overlay on the verso, continuing the postscript about English encroachment. It gives the sense of the whole document and leaves several groups as question marks. Image: Overlay by George Lasry on the verso, published by Satoshi Tomokiyo on Cryptiana, 25 May 2022.

The opening tells du Croc that he knows both the man and those with whom he must deal, and that his demonstrated devotion makes further advice unnecessary. He is to follow the instructions already given and those now sent, especially “le bien de la paix du dict pais.” Charles then turns from what can presently be done for “ma seur” to the young King: Je desire que mon nepveu aussy sur toutes choses soit bien nourri, qu’il ait tousjours, à l’imitation de ses predecesseurs, à moi et aux miens sa principalle affection. Du Croc is to attend closely to the settlement of Scotland’s peace, government, and council. Without revealing that the direction comes from Charles, he must ensure that James neither marries nor concludes a marriage before Charles has been informed and can send his intention. Above all, he is to retain the hearts of the Scots so that their accustomed affection for the French kings does not diminish. The postscript is blunter: Ce que vous avez principalement affaire par delà est de donner ordre que les Anglois n’empiètent aucune chose en Escosse… Du Croc must act prudently, make the Scots recognize that France seeks their preservation, and avoid occasions that could obstruct the friendship. The closing lines mention the English ambassadors and a possible treaty, but the gaps in the overlay are too large for a continuous translation. The repository preserves a line-by-line diplomatic transcription and a normalized summary.

The original has no surviving date or place; 1565–67 or 1572 is a range of possible dates. Destray names the Nièvre archive and the Bourg de Bozas collection but gives no exact cote. Lasry’s overlay has several explicit `????` groups. Other short phrases are partly obscured by the signs at the available resolution. No independent symbol-by-symbol transcription was made and no complete key was rebuilt here. The outcome is an existing decipherment, transcribed and checked against the images.

Normalized sense Charles says that du Croc knows the men with whom he must deal and needs no further advice. He should follow his earlier and current instructions, especially where the peace of Scotland is concerned. Because pressure cannot presently be applied on behalf of “my sister” without harming her, Charles turns to the welfare of “my nephew”: James VI is to be well brought up, retain the traditional affection of his predecessors for the French king and his house, and be surrounded by a peace, government, and council favorable to that end. Du Croc is to ensure discreetly that James neither marries nor concludes a marriage before Charles is informed and can communicate his wishes. He must retain the hearts of the Scots and prevent any diminution of their accustomed attachment to France. The postscript makes the strategic aim explicit: the English must not be allowed to encroach on Scotland. Du Croc is to act prudently so that the Scots recognize France's desire for their preservation, while avoiding incidents that could obstruct the friendship. Several final clauses—including part of the passage about the English ambassadors and a possible treaty—remain too incomplete in the published overlay for a responsible continuous translation. Français 3758 — Châtillon, 3 août 1635 f123r Lettre de Monsr le Mareschal de Chastillon à Mr Servien, escripte de Nimmeghen le 3e d’Aoust 1635. Monsieur, depuis le depart de Monsr de Charnacé les affaires ont changé de mal en pis, les ennemis ayant surpris une des plus importantes places de tout cet Estat. Icy Vous verrez par la carte que le fort de Seink est situé à la pointe d’une Isle où le Rhin se separe en deux grandes branches qui causent le meilleur pays que tiennent Mrs les Estats, car le long de ces deux rivieres sont assises les villes les plus considerables que nous ayons. Les ennemis ne pouvoient surprendre une place de plus grande importance que celle-là, laquelle à la vérité avoit esté fort negligée; Messieurs les Estats s’estant confiez à l’advantage de la situation, et comme les mauvais mesnagers sont bien souvent reculans tousjours de faire les reparations, le plus tard qu’ils peuvent. Il en arrive apres des ruines entieres, faute d’y avoir pourveu à temps. Le Gouverneur de ladite place a sollicité l’hyver passé à la Haye pour avoir quatre ou cinq mil livres pour faire les reparations qui estoient du tout necessaires, neantmoins n’en peut rien obtenir et fut contraint de s’en retourner à son gouvernement avec protestation qu’il feit f123v que s’il mesadvenoit de cette place, l’on ne s’en prist point à luy, et en ce lieu l’on ne luy avoit laissé que deux compagnies fort foibles dans ce fort qui est d’aussy grande garde que la citadelle de Calais. Ces deux fautes-là l’ont faict perdre. Cela donne un tel espouvantement à tout cet Estat que qui ne sçauroit à quoy se resoudre. Depuis trois jours j’ay veu Mr le P. d’Orange varier en ses propositions, sur quoy j’ay dict mes advis peut estre un peu trop librement. J’advoue ingenuement que Je ne cognois plus rien en son humeur et le trouve tellement changé et irresolu que cela me faict grand peine. Ses parens du costé de la maison de Nassau et les principaux officiers de son armée sont dans le mesme estonnement que moy, car ils advouent qu’ils ne l’ont jamais veu sy froid comme il a esté toute cette campagne cy. f124r J’advoue ingenuement que je ne cognois plus rien à son humeur et le trouve tellement changé et irresolu que cela me faict grand peine. Ses parens du costé de la maison de Nassau sont dans le mesme estonnement que moy, car ils advouent qu’ils ne l’ont jamais veu si froid comme il a esté toute cette campagne cy. Nous avons encor 25 mil hommes d’aussy bonne infanterie qu’il y en aye en l’Europe, et six mil chevaux d’aussy bonne cavallerie qu’on en puisse desirer, principalement les trois mil chevaux qui nous restent encor sont en bon estat. Cependant avec de telles forces on a faict difficulté de prendre un logement à deux lieues d’icy vis-à-vis du fort que nous avons perdu, où l’armée des ennemis se peult loger et par consequent maintiendront leur conqueste. Au lieu que sy nous les eussions prevenus, nous eussions bloqué ledit fort sy estroittement qu’ils ne le pourroient plus secourir ny y avoir aucune communication, et par ce seul moyen nous pourrions leur rendre inutile et esperer de regagner cette place dans peu de jours. Au contraire, sy nous donnons loisir aux ennemis de s’y affermir, cela causera un tel estonnement dans ce petit Estat qu’ils auront peine à s’en relever. Sy l’armée du Roy n’y estoit, Je ne sçay là où ils en seroient, puis que nos forces jointes aux leurs on a grand peine à les asseurer. Mr le prince d’Orange allegue qu’il ne pourroit prendre ces logemens sans hazarder une bataille, laquelle f124v n’estoit pas conseillable, les ennemis ayant douze mil chevaux et vingt mil hommes de pied effectifs, parce qu’en la perdant le pays estoit generalement perdu à cause de l’advantage de la place qu’ils ont gaignée. Apres avoir bien debattu les raisons de part et d’autre, Il s’est resolu de passer de l’autre costé du Rhin afin de ne rien hazarder. J’ay creu qu’il estoit à propos de Vous donner franchement advis de tout cela. Nous en conferasmes hier long temps, Monsr le Mareschal de Brezé et moy en particulier, et resolumes de Vous l’escrire. Au reste Je Vous puis asseurer que jamais nous n’avons mieux esté ensemble que nous sommes à present, avec ferme resolution l’un et l’autre de continuer cette estroitte intelligence. f125r La derniere despesche que nous avons receue du Roy nous a esté rendue par le Sr Boutard, dont nous avions eu le duplicata huict jours auparavant par la voye de Liege. Sa M. nous faisant l’honneur de respondre à une despesche que j’avois faicte du 14e de Juin, par laquelle Je Vous avois representé assez franchement l’estat où nous estions alors, prevoyant les inconveniens où nous sommes tombez depuis, Il Vous a pleu me faire cognoistre que j’avois hazardé en Vous escrivant sy librement sans chiffres, ce que Je ne pouvois faire par ce que Vous ne m’en avez point donné. Depuis Monsr le Mareschal de Brezé m’a donné celuy dont Vous Vous servez avec luy au voyage d’Allemagne, et auquel Je me serviray en quelques lignes de cette lettre. Touchant la proposition que Vous faictes à Monsr le Prince d’Orange de jetter un corps d’armée dans la Flandre pour essayer d’y faire quelque progrés, ou pour le moins essayer d’obliger les ennemis d’y envoyer des forces et ainsi les divertir, asseurant que Sa M. feroit faire une attaque du costé d’Artois (Monsr le Duc de Chaulnes ayant charge d’y entrer avec huict mil hommes de pied et deux mil chevaux). Maintenant que cette malheureuse surprise du fort de Seink est arrivée, nous n’oserions (Monsr le Mareschal de Brezé et moy) insister sur cette proposition-là, et mesmes n’avons pas jugé à propos de le presser de nous faire trouver des batteaux afin d’embarquer le regiment du Sr de Wardenburch pour l’envoyer à Calais, suivant l’ordre du Roy que nous avons receu par une lettre que nous a rendue le Sr Vincent commis duquel f125v le Roy veut que nous nous servions conjointement avec le Sr Royer à l’exclusion de tous les autres commis dont Sa M. croit estre mal servie. Nous ne manquerons de suivre l’ordre du Roy ponctuellement en toutes choses et de remettre le soin des monstres entre les mains de ces deux commis qui à la verité ont tesmoigné une grande fidelité et affection à l’exercice de leurs charges. Il y a une autre consideration qui nous oblige à retenir ledit regiment pour le present, nostre infanterie estant tellement affoiblie par les maladies que Je la crois diminuée de trois mil hommes depuis la derniere monstre que nous fismes faire le lendemain du depart des Srs de Charnacé et d’Espenan. Les grandes traictes que nous avons faictes pour venir icy, et le peu de pain qu’on leur f126r Du conseil que j’avois donné à Monsr le P. d’Orange lors que nous arrivasmes à Ruremonde, ayant faict tout ce que j’ay peu pour empescher le sejour de dix sept jours que nous y avons faict. Je veuille accuser la grande prevoyance [correction au-dessus: inexperience?] de Monsr le P. d’Orange, mais ayant soubz sa conduite deux armées d’humeurs differentes, et dans un pays qui n’avoit pas accoustumé d’avoir de sy grands fardeaux sur les bras, Il ne faut pas s’estonner s’il s’est trouvé embarrassé en cette conduite-là. f126v a baillé, qui encore estoit fort mauvais, ont achevé de les abattre, et a faict de sorte que de jour à autre nous voyons tomber quantité de malades. La cavallerie se tient maintenue jusques icy sans en avoir. Il n’y a maintenant capitaine de chevaux legers qui n’ait dix ou douze de ses compagnons malades. Il en meurt peu de ceux qui sont bien secourus parmy l’infanterie. Ils vont assez viste à cause de la mauvaise nourriture qu’ils ont receue. Nous esperons que le Roy trouvera nos raisons bonnes sy nous n’avons en ce point obey au commandement qu’il nous avoit faict d’envoyer ledit regiment en toute diligence à Calais, attendant un ordre nouveau sur la reussite des affaires presentes. Au reste Monsr, plusieurs sont tesmoins du conseil que j’avois donné à Monsr le P. d’Orange lorsque nous arrivasmes à Ruremonde, ayant faict tout ce que j’ay peu pour empescher le séjour de dix sept jours que nous y avons faicts, recevant de tres grandes incommoditez, car au lieu de nous raffraichir nostre cavallerie, elle s’est extremement fatiguée, et les vivres y ont esté tousjours fort rares et fort chers, ce qui me faisoit presser de quitter ces logemens pour s’aller camper vers Cleves ou Zanten sur le bord du Rhin. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained Credits · Brice Dudout (new cipher) not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter Alfonso Cistarelli, Cardinal Ippolito I d’Este’s agent at Eger, to the Cardinal, 25 July 1520: four pages, the cipher on the second, clear text before and after it. Where Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, Cistarelli no. 3 (b. 4/26); DECODE R1137 (catalogue item 158), Vestigia 1904. The cipher Two-digit figures written without spaces, most ending in 5 or 0, with a few letter signs (f, k, u, y): 584 figure groups and 83 other signs, set inside clear Italian. Homophonic on the evidence of the search. How it was tried A ciphertext-only solver (simulated annealing on a sixteenth-century Italian model), checked against the same figures shuffled; cribs from Caprile’s letters of the same months, checked against control words. Why it resists The solver finds more language than in the shuffled control, but only phrases. Two readings of the same lines disagree on one group in seven, and no key or decipherment exists in the file, on DECODE or in print. The October letter Cistarelli no. 7 (Kraków, 14 Oct 1520, to Duke Alfonso I; Vestigia 1908), in the same figures. Only one line of its cipher is legible in the surviving photocopy, and it does not decode. What would finish it A better photograph from the archive, to settle the digits, then the search again. Other ciphers Giuliano Caprile’s letters in the same box are in other ciphers, each with its own page: his 1520–21 sign cipher and his 1519 two-tier cipher . R1137, the second page: the clear opening line, then the figures run together without spaces, with clear words between some of the groups. Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, Cistarelli no. 3, p. 2, via Vestigia 1904.

Cistarelli was the Cardinal’s agent at Eger, the Hungarian see Ippolito d’Este held; Vestigia has twenty of his records. Two of them carry cipher, no. 3 of 25 July 1520 and no. 7 of 14 October 1520 (section 02), and neither has a decipherment, a clear copy or a gloss. Pages 1 and 3 are clear text and page 4 the address; the cipher is on page 2. DECODE’s “partially decrypted” probably reflects the clear passages (this is not from the sources and was not checked here).

Brice Dudout pointed out a second letter in the same figures (28 October 2026): Cistarelli no. 7, 14 October 1520, Vestigia 1908, not on DECODE. Vestigia names Duke Alfonso I as the addressee and Kraków as the place, and the clear text agrees. It answers the Duke’s letter about “la grave infirmità e disperata salute” of the writer’s lord and reports his death: Cardinal Ippolito died on 3 September 1520. It goes on about the Queen, the King of Hungary, and the bishopric and castle of Eger. The groups are the same as in July: two digits ending in 0 or 5, mixed with the letter signs f, k, u, y, x, h, g and m. The October letter, line 7: after “dala S.ma Regina”, 34 figure groups and letter signs, then the clear “e sino questo”. Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, Alfonso Cistarelli no. 7, via Vestigia 1908 (photograph of a photocopy). Line 7 can be transcribed (34 tokens), and so can seven groups at the end of line 27. The roughly six lines of cipher below them are mostly lost in the dark bands of the old photocopy that the online image shows. With the July letter’s search key, line 7 decodes as “adlmodegmo?racentogseti?tipodtare”. A new search over both letters gives “…framento…portare”. These are fragments, not a reading. Brice Dudout has asked the archive for the original.

Ciphertext-only search. Simulated annealing on the 667 tokens settles part of a key (e = 0, 25; a = 86; o = 70; i = 45; t = 95; r = 85; s = 90; n = 65) and phrases such as “lettere per”, “presto”, “saria meglio”, “non se poteria” and “dua milla” (grade M). On the same tokens shuffled the score is lower (−3.05 against −2.69 per token), so there is language in it; but the output does not run into sentences. Known keys. Every key of the series, the archive and the decade available here is an alphabet of signs, not of figures (Caprile’s 1519 and 1520–21 keys, Bonzagni 1512–14, Sadoleto 1482, Maffeo 1489); DECODE has no Este key of 1490–1550. None could be applied. Cribs. Words from Caprile’s letters of the same months (custode, Agria, Alfonso, debito, Buda, episcopato) were placed at every consistent position and re-annealed, against six control words that should not occur. The cribs gain no more than the controls. The transcription. A second reading of four lines against the image disagrees with the first on 13 of 92 groups (8 or 9, 4 or 9, 0, 5 or 6, 80 or 86, and where a group starts). The digits are about 25 pixels high on a faded page, so the image itself does not settle them.

Better photographs of Cistarelli no. 3, and of the original of no. 7 rather than a photocopy, from the Archivio di Stato di Modena, then a fresh transcription and the search again. Whether noise is really what stops the solve is a judgement, not a proof. Attempted, not solved.

Contribute · five ways in How to contribute The ledger records historical ciphers: what has been deciphered, by whom, and how. Anyone can add to it. A contribution is credited by name on the write-up it belongs to and on the contributors page , whether it arrives as a GitHub pull request, an issue or an email. Play from the start, with sound From the start, with sound The letter How it works The ledger How to contribute To the archive Five kinds How to send How credit works What happens next To the archive Contributors Daniel Bourdeau and contributors · posted 13 October 2026 · updated 29 October 2026

A solution to a cipher already in the ledger Any target in the catalogue , any write-up marked not solved , and any open item in the notes . Send: the target (catalogue number, write-up page or folder name) and the documents covered (shelfmark, folio, DECODE record); the key: the sign-to-value table, the code groups you have values for, and the nulls; the full texts of every document you claim as read, in full or in part: the complete transcription of the ciphertext and the complete decipherment, line by line against it, with the passages you are unsure of marked. They are shown on the write-up, inline or linked when long, so that the text can be used by historians and the reading judged by those who worked on it before you; the key, in full if you recovered, extended or corrected it, and if you can, a short summary of what each document says and its historical context; how the key was obtained: from the ciphertext alone, from plaintext beside it or elsewhere, from an existing key (whose), or from an existing decipherment. This sets the method shown on the write-up; whether the reading was already published anywhere, as far as you know. A fuller reading of one left partial Many write-ups are read only in part. Their notes list what is still open and why: code groups with no value yet, lines hard to read on the images, letters for which no key is known, pieces that need the original in the archive. The list of readings to take further shows each one with its open gaps, the most workable first. You do not need to finish a reading to help: one step is enough. Send: the write-up and the gap you worked on (the line in its notes, or the code group, folio and line); what you propose: a value for a code group, a corrected key value, a new reading of a passage, a key or a clear copy found elsewhere, a reading made from the original in the archive; the evidence: every place the value occurs and how it reads there, the image or source you worked from, and anything that still does not fit. Each step is credited on the write-up, and the reading’s extent is re-measured with it. A visit or a request to an archive. Some gaps can only be closed from the original or from a book the project cannot reach: a line lost in the binding, a leaf never photographed, a decipherment in a volume that was not digitised, an edition behind a login. They are listed by archive and city on To the archive . Take one on with the “I can do this” link (it opens the archive-request form with the request filled in), then send the photographs, the reproduction or the passage. A visit that finds nothing is reported and credited too. A new unsolved cipher A ciphered document with no known decipherment that is not in the ledger yet. Send: the archive, shelfmark and folio, and a link to the images (Gallica, DECODE, the archive’s viewer) or the images themselves if you may share them; date, sender and recipient if known, and the language you expect; what you know of its status: listed as undeciphered where, any key or decipherment you have looked for; a transcription, if you have one. It is not required. A new cipher with its solution Both of the above: the document, then the key, the full transcription and decipherment, and how you obtained them. Results that have never been published are welcome; say whether they may be shown here in full or only noted. A verification of a reading already here The verification queue lists the readings whose key was recovered or matched here and that no one outside the project has checked. Take the images and the key from the write-up, decipher a passage yourself (a paragraph is enough), and report: which passage, and which images you worked from; where your reading agrees with the write-up, and every place it does not; any key value you would change, with the evidence. A check that finds errors is as useful as one that confirms. Both are credited.

On GitHub. Open an issue with one of the forms at github.com/dbourdeau/cyphersolver/issues/new/choose (solution, fuller reading, new cipher, new cipher with solution, verification), or send a pull request. The repository’s CONTRIBUTING.md explains the folder layout and the files a target keeps. By email. Not on GitHub? Write to with the same details and any files. The entry is made for you and credited the same way.

On the write-up. The page names every contributor under its outcome line, with what each did: solution, new cipher, verification, key correction, transcription, identification, a pointer to a source, or the key or decipherment the reading used. On the contributors page. Credits are added up by person and by kind, each count linking to the write-ups. The top contributors are listed on the front page. Your name, your way. Say how you want to be named (full name, initials, a handle) and where your name should link. Unpublished work. An earlier solution you never published is noted as unpublished, and shown in full only with your agreement. Earlier scholarship. Keys and decipherments taken from editions, archives and databases are credited to their makers too, in a separate list, so living contributors are not ranked against the nineteenth century.

The contribution is checked against the images: the key applied to the ciphertext, the decipherment read for sense. It is filed in the target’s folder with its key, transcription and notes, given a method and an extent, and written up or added to an existing write-up. Where the target is on DECODE , the corrections and the decipherment are queued for the DECODE record, credited to you. The ledger also feeds a study of how language models perform against historical ciphers. A result you contributed is marked as yours and is kept out of the model’s figures. Tools are your choice, including AI. Say what you used, and check the reading against the images before sending it.

Where Hessisches Staatsarchiv Darmstadt, D 4 Nr. 248/3, a file of 39 letters from Erbach to Ludwig (1654–1670) described as “partly ciphered”. Only these three of the 39 contain cipher. The cipher Number pairs written inline, such as “3,14. 1,19.”: line and letter of an eight-line rhymed Lord's Prayer that begins “O Vatter aller frommen”. Any occurrence of a letter in the verse may be used. How it was deciphered A Latin outline of the long letter, in a hand of the time, was filmed beside it. Its phrases gave the first letters. The rows of the key then began to spell German words, and the verse filled in the rest. What it says Eight reasons why Erbach cannot leave his county, among them his wife's illness, his young brothers' government and disloyal councillors. Can a lord, he asks, “put his sheep under hirelings”? Still open 19 pairs are the writer's slips, read from context. Some words of the clear German around the cipher are illegible on the microfilm, and the long letter is undated (before 27 April 1666).

The file D 4 Nr. 248/3 of the Hessian house archive at Darmstadt holds 39 letters from Count Georg Ernst zu Erbach to his friend Landgrave Ludwig VI of Hesse-Darmstadt (1630–1678), dated 1654 to 1670. The finding aid notes alchemy (it mentions a Dr Johann Tack) and “z. T. chiffrierte Briefe”, letters partly in cipher. The archive's 78 microfilm images are online. Most of the letters are about alchemical work and court news, and are signed with an anagram (“J. Strenuus Segrego” = Georgius Ernestus). Ludwig answers as “Tuus Totus 666”: LUDOVICUS read as Roman numerals sums to 666. The cipher is in three letters only, all from a numbered series of 1666 addressed to Ludwig “à Stokholm”: No. 1 of 22 March, with two short runs; No. 2 of 27 April, with one; and an undated letter of two pages that is almost all cipher. Its points are headed in Latin, Primo to Octavo , and it ends with a question in Latin ( Hic quaeritur …). The scans are microfilm frames, with the leaves small and turned on their side. The undated letter, page 1, from just before Primo to per veniam aetatis : pairs such as “1,1. 5,3. 7,9.” between Latin and German words in clear. Image: Hessisches Staatsarchiv Darmstadt, D 4 Nr. 248/3, image 004, via Arcinsys Hessen.

Each pair a,b is the b -th letter of line a of a short verse, counting letters only. The verse is a rhymed German version of the Lord's Prayer, in eight lines: line text (as rebuilt) letters 1 O vatter aller frommen 19 2 geheiligt werd dein nahm 21 3 las dein reich zu uns kommen 23 4 dein will der mach uns zahm 22 5 gib brod vergib die sund 20 6 kein args das hertz entzunde 24 7 los uns aus aller nott 18 8 p ? x … (only 8,1 and 8,3 used) So 1,1 is o , 7,18 is t , and the e of a word can be 1,6, 2,2, 3,5, 4,2, 6,2 and many more. Erbach usually ran forward along one line, so stretches of plaintext come out as rising numbers (1,10 1,11 1,12; 3,20 3,22 3,23). The 610 pairs use 123 different cells. Letters of the verse that no pair uses are filled in from the wording of the rhyme. Line 8 is known only from two cells ( p and x ). No printed source for this version of the verse was found. About one pair in thirty is a slip, where Erbach miscounted by a letter or two: 5,14 ( d ) three times for t or u , consrliis for consiliis , beschafmenheit . Every slip lands on a neighbouring letter of the right line, and the context corrects all of them. They are listed in the reading file.

The undated letter answers a question Ludwig must have put: whether Erbach would leave his county, presumably to join him. The two had agreed that “inter nos conventum sit” each should speak “secundum conscientiam”. Erbach then sets out his reasons for refusing. Deciphered text is plain; the Latin headings and German connecting words in clear are in italics. Primo; obstat turbulentus statu[s] publicus. Secundo; pericula ex bello electorum mihi proximo … Tertio; morbus uxoris quotidie crescens. Quarto et praecipue; fratris regimen partim per conniventiam, partim per veniam aetatis jam jam suscipientes. Quinto; ex ipsorum consiliis iuvenilibus pericula jamdum apparentia, jam quoad salutem subditorum quam meam domesticam. Sexto: subditorum proinde praecipua et bona in me fiducia. Septimo; divisio bonorum cum fratribus… Octavo; et quod maximum est, defectus fidelitatis consiliariorum. First, the troubled state of the Empire. Second, the war of the electors close by. Third, his wife's illness, worse every day. Fourth and chiefly, his brothers taking up the government, partly by connivance and partly by a dispensation of age. Fifth, the dangers already visible from their young counsels, to his subjects and his own household. Sixth, his subjects' trust in him. Seventh, the division of property with his brothers. Eighth and greatest, the disloyalty of the councillors. The letter then asks: Hic quaeritur; an rebus sic stantibus quidem dominus, cui deus salutem ecclesie, subditorum, domus et uxoris sue concredidit, sine lesione conscientie et offensione dei hec omnia possit deserere, mercenariorum directioni oves suas submittere, ac sic periculis jamdum praevisis exponere? Ego quidem non credo… “Whether a lord to whom God has entrusted the welfare of the church, of his subjects, his house and his wife can, without hurt to his conscience and offence to God, abandon all this, put his sheep under the direction of hirelings, and so expose them to dangers already foreseen? I for my part do not believe it.” The hireling who leaves the sheep is John 10:12. For Ludwig, he adds, it would be quite another matter, since he need fear none of points three, four, five, seven and eight. The short runs in the other two letters belong to the same business. No. 1 (22 March) speaks of “unsers vorhabens” (our plan) and promises news of the “mutationes” since. No. 2 (27 April) says that “im Majo oder Junio will Gott unsere bonorum divisio vorgehen”: God willing, the division of the property will go ahead in May or June. That is point seven of the long letter. No. 2 also says Erbach has already sent “meine rationes” by letter, hoping Ludwig will find them “relevant genug” and not accuse him of inconstancy: so the eight reasons were written before 27 April 1666. The cipher hides exactly the family and political matters, not the alchemy.

The 571 pairs of the long letter were transcribed from rotated, enlarged crops of the microfilm, and checked against a second filming of the same leaves. The numbers looked like coordinates: no row goes past 24, and stretches climb inside one row. A homophonic solver with a Latin language model could not settle 124 symbols on so short a text. The crib was on the same microfilm frame. A slip next to the letter carries a Latin outline in a hand of the time: Status turbulentus …, onerosa … quotidie crescens , subditorum fiducia , divisio bonorum , defectus fidelitatis . On its lower flap is an almost word-for-word gloss of the closing question, up to mercenariorum directioni oves suas submittere . The contemporary outline: the eight points (top) and the gloss of Hic quaeritur (lower left), with “ac sic periculis jamdum praevisis” (right). Image: Hessisches Staatsarchiv Darmstadt, D 4 Nr. 248/3, image 004, via Arcinsys Hessen. Laid against the cipher, turbulentus , defectus , dominus cui deus salutem , conscientie et offensione dei and oves suas fixed about eighty cells. Read row by row, those cells began to spell German: line 4 dein will … uns , line 3 las dein reich zu uns , line 7 los uns aus aller not , line 1 o vatter aller frommen . That is a rhymed Lord's Prayer, and its wording supplied the rest of each line. With the verse unchanged as the key, all three letters read. Checks: 591 of the 610 pairs give the intended letter exactly. The letter-model test ( docs/_validate.py ) scores the reading at −2.39 per letter, against −4.60 for random keys of the same shape and at most −2.59 for keys fitted to shuffled ciphertext; verdict: pass. Before this work, no edition, study or modern decipherment of the letters was found.

Nineteen pairs are slips (fifteen in the long letter, four in the short ones). Each reads from context and is listed with its correction. The least certain is zu b⟨r⟩ingen in the opening of the long letter. One pair in No. 2 and a short blotted clause in the long letter are under ink on both filmings. Some words of the clear German around the cipher are marked doubtful or unread. The text survives only on this microfilm, and the Kurrent is small. The long letter is undated. It must be the letter of “rationes” that No. 2 refers to, so it was written before 27 April 1666. Line 8 of the verse is known only as p ? x , and the source of this version of the rhymed prayer is not identified.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. Letter 004, undated [before 27 Apr 1666], two pages Erbach gives Ludwig VI eight reasons why he cannot leave his county: the troubled Empire, the electors' war nearby, his wife's illness, his brothers taking up government by connivance and a dispensation of age, their youthful counsels, his subjects' trust, the division of property, and disloyal councillors. He asks whether a lord may abandon church, subjects, house and wife and 'put his sheep under hirelings' (John 10:12). No. 2 (27 Apr 1666) refers to this letter of 'rationes', so it predates it. Translation en_004.md # Letter 004: English translation of the cipher passages and their frame [I have had to form] my thoughts about it, to disclose them obediently to Your Highness and to ask humbly for Your Highness's understanding opinion. Your Highness will graciously remember that it was agreed between us that in this matter each should speak and act according to his conscience. Accordingly I cannot refrain from saying it out, as I ought: for the following reasons, however hard it is for me to bring myself to it, I have had to change the resolution ... First: the troubled state of public affairs stands in the way. Second: the dangers from the electors' war, which is closest to me, and if armies and war parties pass over or through it, of devastation. Third: my wife's illness, growing daily. Fourth and chiefly: my brother's government, which they are about to take up, partly by connivance, partly by a dispensation of age. Fifth: from their youthful counsels dangers are already apparent, both for the welfare of the subjects and for my own household. Sixth: hence the subjects' particular and good trust in me. Seventh: the division of the property with my brothers, which is still to be made. Eighth, and the greatest: the want of loyalty in the councillors. If Your Highness will consider these eight points carefully, you will find them of no small weight, for in my judgement they could well confuse many a compass. The question is whether, things standing so, a lord to whom God has entrusted the welfare of the church, of his subjects, of his house and of his wife can, without hurt to his conscience and offence to God, leave all this, put his sheep under the direction of hirelings, and so expose them to dangers already foreseen. I for my part do not believe it; but I anxiously await Your Serene Highness's heartfelt opinion [by letter, for I fear writing may not be safe]. With Your Highness it would be quite another matter, since you need fear nothing of the third, fourth, fifth, seventh and eighth points above. I will not trouble Your Highness longer now, but commend it all faithfully to God's protection[?], and myself to your lasting grace ... The "hirelings" and "sheep" are John 10:12. Who the brothers are and what move Ludwig had proposed are not said in the cipher; the 1666 letters in the file (Nos. 1 and 2, below) speak of a planned undertaking ("unsers Vorhabens") and of the division of property due in May or June. It is in Italian, partly in cipher. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Espagnol 318 no. 5, ff. 5–6v (Gallica, canvases 32–35). It is one of five ciphered letters in the volume, catalogue item 9. The cipher The cipher issued to Joan Ram Escrivà, the Spanish ambassador at Naples: signs for letters and a nomenclator of letter groups beginning with p, q, r, s, t, v or x. How it was deciphered Ivan Parisi identified the cipher and printed the whole letter in 2020. His article was found here by searching the shelfmark. The nomenclator groups he lists were checked on the leaf and match. What it says Federico confirms the pre-agreement for the marriage of his nine-year-old son Ferrando, duke of Calabria, to one of the Spanish infantas. Other letters The other ciphered letters of the volume use other ciphers and have their own pages: no. 92 (the Cifra general ), no. 95 (Lasry’s alphabet) and nos. 93–94 (key not identified).

No. 5 of BnF Espagnol 318, the Ruffo di Scilla collection of letters to Ferdinand and Isabella, is a letter of Federico III of Naples, the last Aragonese king of Naples, written at San Germano on 11 January 1497. A later endorsement at the head names d. Fadrique Rey of Naples, en cifra . Its first clear line names the man whose cipher it uses: Da poi de havere resposto ad micer Joan Scrivà, oratore de le Maiestate Vostre . Until 14 October 2026 it shared a page with the volume’s four other ciphered letters, which are in other ciphers and now have their own pages. F. 5r: the endorsement naming d. Fadrique Rey , the clear opening naming micer Joan Scrivà , then the cipher. On the second line the first group after declarato , qix , is del in Parisi’s list. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Espagnol 318 f. 5r, via Gallica (btv1b52503046q).

The first check was for an existing decipherment. Searching for the shelfmark rather than the cipher turns up Ivan Parisi, Un cifrario in prestito per una lettera segretissima di Federico d’Aragona re di Napoli ai Re Cattolici nel BnF, Espagnol 318 , in Studi di storia medioevale e di diplomatica , n.s. IV (2020), pp. 157–177, open access, DOI 10.54103/2611-318X/14378. It prints the letter entire. The article’s point is an anomaly. Federico wrote to Ferdinand and Isabella to confirm a pre-agreement for the marriage of his nine-year-old son Ferrando, duke of Calabria, to one of the Spanish infantas. He had the secret part enciphered in the Spanish ambassador’s cipher , the key issued to Joan Ram Escrivà, who was standing in Naples at the time. Parisi pins the encipherer by a Spanish speaker’s mistake: whoever wrote the cryptogram failed to use the double- s sign in possano , obedientissimo and promesso , an error an Italian would not make and a Spaniard would. So the king of Naples handed his minute to the ambassador, and the ambassador made the fair copy and enciphered it. The nomenclator elements Parisi lists are legible on the Gallica image at 3000 px and match the image: qix del , qao duque , qav de , qae con , qed cosa , qie como , rae el , rof en , ru mensajero , saf Italia , sul la , tad no , tay parte , vee que , vet si , vog sobre , xer and xoq Vuestras Altezas , xit una , pam bien . The band of initials, p, q, r, s, t, v, x, is what rules this key out for the volume’s nos. 93 and 94 .

Only the search, and the check of Parisi’s nomenclator list on the leaf. No transcription was made and the key (printed by Parisi in 2004) was not applied; the text is Parisi’s. Nothing about it is new here.

À Versailles le 9 xbre 1678. Monsr le Marquis de Feuquières, vostre depesche du 11 du mois passé m’a fait voir le plan que le Roy de Suede vous a fait sur la manière dont il croyoit que je puisse faire la guerre pour son secours en faisant passer une flotte dans la mer Baltique . La depesche que je vous escrivis il y a huit jours vous aura fait connoistre combien j’envisageois de difficultez à pouvoir reduire entièrement les ennemis de la Suede par la force, que je crois important de profiter des dispositions où ils paroissent de s’accommoder avec cette couronne, mesme aux despens de quelque partie des Estats qu’ils ont occupé sur elle, et qu’elle ne peut guère refuser et donner au mauvais estat de ses affaires. Je vous ordonnois encore de vous expliquer adroitement de ces sentimens au Roy de Suede et à ses ministres, et de les accoustumer aux difficultez qui se rencontrent presque insurmontables à le restablir par mes armes lorsqu’il ne luy reste pas une seule place en Allemagne. Mais si vous estes servu auprès de luy des oppositions naturelles d’un trop grand esloignement et de la jalousie que le Pays de Cleves pourroit causer aux Estats Generaux, vous pourrez vous servir du plan mesme qu’il vous a fait f156v Pour luy faire toucher sensiblement l’extreme difficulté de cette entreprise. Tant qu’il a conservé quelques villes et quelques ports dans l’Empire l’on auroit pû fonder quelque esperance sur la mer, mais aujourd’huy que toutes les costes du Jutland, des Isles du Dannemarc et de la basse Allemagne luy seront contraires, il est difficile de se promettre un grand effet de la flotte qu’il demanderoit que j’envoiasse dans la mer Baltique. L’on sçait combien les descentes sont tousjours difficiles et combien les succez en est incertain dans un pays ennemy. Ce seroit entreprendre une conqueste sans aide et sans assistance aucune dans des provinces où l’on trouveroit des forces considerables à combattre. Tant que la Suede conservoit encore Stralsund, une ville de cette importance pouvoit assurer une entrée favorable dans l’Empire, des magazins et une retraite. Sa perte a fort changé la face des affaires; ainsy la confiance qu’il met en une armée navalle est combattue naturellement par de grands obstacles, et ce seroit sans doute le trop flatter que d’en attendre des effets si prompts et si avantageux qu’il s’en promet. Mais quand bien mesme il croiroit pouvoir surmonter ces difficultez, j’essaye de luy en faire envisager de grandes f157r du costé de lAngleterre. Vous pourrez luy faire connoistre que pour estre en liberté de faire passer des Vaisseaux dans la mer Baltique, jaurois besoin destre asseuré de cette Couronne, que dans lestat incertain et agité où elle se trouve on ne peut guères respondre des resolutions quelle pourra prendre. Que jaurois travaillé à la faire declarer en faveur de la Suede. Que lon my auroit fait paroistre de la disposition Mais que lon me tesmoigne à cet heure quavant que de sengager au secours de cette Couronne, on voudroit scavoir à quelles Conditions Elle voudroit faire la Paix. Je me suis expliqué en la maniere que jay tousjours fait sur ce sujet, que je demanderois quelle fust entiere. Jy ay trouvé une repugnance ouverte et lon sest declaré que lon croioit juste quelle abandonnast quelque partie des Provinces quelle a perdues pour en recouvrer le reste. Vous pourrez faire considerer en Suede ce quil y a à craindre de semblables dispositions, et sil ne seroit pas à apprehender que lAngleterre ne se declarast contre cette Couronne lorsquelle la verroit attachée à ne rien donner pour le bien de la Paix. A letter to the League general Gottfried Huyn von Geleen on the relief of Hildesheim and the army’s pay, with the sensitive words in two-digit numbers. Brice Dudout recovered the key from the numbers alone, tested it on five held-out lines (0.656 of letters in German words against at most 0.113 for shuffled keys) and read 186 of 221 cipher words. Nineteen words are lost in the binding of the microfilm, which caps the reading at 91.4%. 21 17 23 25 17 12 31 21 … angesehen der … Kniphausen mit Hessen sich coniungirt starck impegnirt Cologne → Geleen’s army · simple substitution of two-digit numbers in clear German · 22 October 1633 · key from ciphertext only The Electors of Mainz and Cologne to Geleen, 22 October 1633 from Ferdinand of Bavaria, Elector of Cologne Go to the full text ↓ A letter on the relief of Hildesheim and the army’s pay, with the key recovered from the numbers alone and 84.2% of the cipher words read. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 4 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (84% of the cipher) Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · WAINUT (pointer to a source) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (84% of the cipher) The letter Anselm Casimir, Archbishop-Elector of Mainz, and Ferdinand, Elector of Cologne, to Gottfried Huyn von Geleen, major-general of the League army, [Cologne], 22 October 1633, answering Geleen’s letter of the 11th from Rheinberg. Both Electors signed it. Where Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Munich, Clm 10406 no. 206 (Collectio Camerariana 56), fols. 184r–185v, digitised microfilm (MDZ bsb00116454, views 653–656). Not on DECODE and not in the project’s catalogue. The cipher A simple substitution: each letter is a two-digit number from 12 to 36, written run together without word division in the middle of the clear German text. About 1,180 numbers; 22 numbers have a value, two rare ones (33, 38) do not. How it was deciphered Three known keys of the period (Camerarius 1621, Rákóczi 1632, Kurz 1638–39) do not apply. The key was built by annealing with a model of 17th-century German on the letter minus five held-out lines, corrected from three clear contexts, and frozen. On the held-out lines 0.656 of the letters fall in German words of five letters or more, against at most 0.113 for 200 shuffled keys. What it says Everything must be done to relieve besieged Hildesheim; Bönninghausen has been advised although Kniphausen has joined the Hessians; at least a thousand horse are to be sent; the 3,000 reichsthalers paid at Cologne should have reached Geleen by bill of exchange; his services will be rewarded by the united Catholic Estates. Still open Of 221 cipher words, 27 are unresolved: 19 lost where the line ends of fol. 184v vanish into the gutter, 4 whose numbers contradict the expected word, 2 cut word ends and 2 runs with no recognisable word. The bound microfilm caps the reading at 91.4%. Credit Brice Dudout transcribed the numbers, recovered and tested the key and read the letter, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. WAINUT found the letter in the Camerariana volumes.

In the autumn of 1633 the Catholic League had almost no army left in the north. Hildesheim was besieged by the troops of Brunswick-Lüneburg, allies of the Swedes, and Kniphausen’s Hessians held the County of Mark. The Electors, Anselm Casimir of Mainz in exile at Cologne and Ferdinand of Cologne, answered Geleen on 22 October. The letter is signed in their own hands and is in clear, but nearly everything about troops, money and people is in cipher. No contemporary decipherment is on the piece or in the neighbouring items (nos. 205–207). Fol. 184r: the numbers are written run together without word division, with clear words such as angesehen der set between them. Image: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 10406 no. 206, fol. 184r (view 653), via MDZ, Public Domain Mark 1.0.

Numbers 12 to 36 stand for letters: e = 17, n = 31, s = 13, t = 35, i = 12, a = 30, d = 21, r = 22. One number serves u and v (15), and l has two (18 and a rare 28). The values of 34 = f and 23 = m come from the clear context vom Feind , 14 = p from Kniphausen , 28 = l from Geltmittel ; the rest came from the annealing. The protocol was hashed before transcription, with five lines of fol. 185r (186 cipher letters, up to the clear word Bedanken ) held out. One measurement on them gave 0.656 of letters covered by German words of five letters or more, against at best 0.113 for 200 shuffled keys (threshold fixed at 0.60), and a language-model score of −2.51 against at best −4.18. The held-out lines read: zum besten nichts erwinden lassen und euch hingegen vor gewiss versichern, das solche eure merita und getrewe dinsten von uns und den sambtlichen unirten catholischen bundsständen mit würcklichem Danck remunerirt werden sollen .

Of 221 cipher words, 151 are certain, 35 probable, 8 restored from the sense and 27 unresolved. Certain and probable together give 186 of 221 (84.2%); with the restored words, 87.8%. The 95% bar is not reached. Hildesheim. The Electors share Geleen’s view that everything must be done to relieve the town, still besieged, and keep it from further violence; they have advised General Bönninghausen, although Kniphausen has joined the Hessians, and ask for at least a thousand horse to be sent at once. Money. The 3,000 reichsthalers paid at Cologne should now have reached him by bill of exchange; a much larger sum is being raised and counted out to Lerchenfeld, Maximilian’s envoy, for the army. The League. Geleen is to spare nothing for the common good; his merits and faithful services will be rewarded by the Electors and the united Catholic Estates. Hamburg. The Electors thank him for passing on the report of the Hamburg correspondent Menselius, who complains bitterly about a Jew held in Geleen’s custody; Geleen is to see that this merchant and Menselius are satisfied.

19 words are cut or lost in the gutter of fol. 184v, where the volume was microfilmed bound; only the original or a new photograph would show them. Two more word ends are cut there ( le , non ). Four words read with the numbers as written do not give the expected Statt , Weg , Wachtmeister , richten : a blind re-reading of 14 words (4 Nov 2026) confirmed nine and left these four as the numbers stand. 25 and 23 may have a second value, or these are slips. Two runs give no recognisable word ( derdselfemlh , anewerder ); on the images the digits are not separable (2, 3 and 5 alike, one pair reads as 11, which is not a number of the key), so derselbe mehr is possible but cannot be shown. Eight restorations from the sense are marked in the reading, two of them where the key gives almost the word. No deciphered copy is known, so the key is checked on the letter itself, not on an independent text. The Munich edition, Briefe und Akten zur Geschichte des Dreißigjährigen Krieges , Neue Folge II/8 (Bierther, 1982), covers the episode but is not online; a summary of this letter from a clear copy cannot be ruled out.

Hildesheim. The two Electors share Geleen’s view: everything must be done to relieve Hildesheim, still besieged, and keep it from further violence. They have advised Major-General Bönninghausen — although the enemy is strong, Kniphausen having joined the Hessians — and will do all they can to send Geleen as soon as possible at least a thousand horse, to carry out the relief more conveniently. They ask him to weigh what the loss, for want of troops, of so considerable and so near a town would mean. Money. The three thousand reichsthalers paid in Cologne should by now have reached him by bill of exchange; a much larger sum (“zehnere”, tenfold?) is being raised, counted out to Lerchenfeld (Maximilian of Bavaria’s envoy at Cologne) and meant for the army. Any indispensable expenses Geleen advances will be repaid without fail once he names them. This page has the most gaps: its line ends are in the binding. The League. Meanwhile he is to spare nothing for the common good, with the valour he has shown so far: his merits and faithful services will be rewarded by the Electors and by “all the united Catholic Estates” (den sambtlichen unirten catholischen bundsstanden), that is the League, with real gratitude. Hamburg. In clear, the Electors thank Geleen for passing on what the Hamburg correspondent Menselius (in cipher) sent him; and since Menselius complains bitterly about a Jew held by Geleen (in cipher), Geleen is to see that this merchant and Menselius himself are fully satisfied. Menselius may be the imperial commissioner resident in Hamburg mentioned by Aitzema (not checked). Key: key.tsv

Sixteen Latin-letter strings stamped on seven bars said to certify $300,000,000. They contain almost exactly ten of every letter: chi-squared 1.25 against uniform where random sampling predicts 25, a flatness no encryption of a natural-language text can produce. Not a cipher: the letters were counted out by hand and there is no message. MQOLCSJTLGAJOKBSSBOMUPCE FEWGDRHDDEEUMFFTEEMJXZR ZUQUPNZN · VIOHIKNNGUAB Shanghai · 1933 · Latin letters stamped on gold bars · Schmeh Top 50 no. 49 The Chinese gold bar cryptograms Seven bars said to certify a deposit of $300,000,000, stamped with sixteen strings of Latin letters for which no decipherment has been proposed in ninety years The strings contain almost exactly ten of every letter, a distribution flatter than any encryption can produce. The letters were counted out and arranged by hand, so there is no ciphertext and no message. The flat count had been noticed before (a commenter on Schmeh’s blog, Nick Pelling, Bret Bowen); this page checks the transcription against the photographs and measures how improbable the pattern is. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not applicable closed At a glance Not applicable · not a cipher The document Sixteen inscriptions of 263 letters on seven gold bars said to have been issued to a “General Wang” in Shanghai in 1933. Where Photographs and transcription by Kevin McCurley, IACR (1996); the item has long been on Elonka Dunin’s list of famous unsolved codes. Why it resists Twenty-one of the 26 letters occur exactly ten times; chi-squared is 1.25 on 25 degrees of freedom where random sampling predicts 25. No encryption produces that. What it says There is no message: the letters were laid out ten of each to look like cryptograms. Still open The transcription gives 263 letters; checked against the photographs the true total is 261 or 262.

The story, as Kevin McCurley set it down for the IACR in 1996, is that seven gold bars were issued to a “General Wang” in Shanghai in 1933, functioning as metal certificates against a deposit with an American bank. The Chinese text on them describes a transaction of more than $300,000,000 and gives the bars’ combined weight as 1.8 kilograms. A dispute over the claim was live at the time, and McCurley published the photographs in the hope that reading the cryptograms would help settle it. One of the bars (IACR, 1996). The cryptograms are stamped around the portraits, above and below the figure 300000000. Image: Kevin McCurley, “Cryptograms on Gold bars from China”, IACR (1996), iacr.org/misc/china. Elonka Dunin has carried the item on her list of famous unsolved codes ever since. In 2020 she reached the attorney named on the IACR page, who confirmed he had seen the bars, described them as about the size of a remote control, and said the banks had not treated the claim as legitimate; his file was closed. Others have noted that the aircraft depicted on the bars is a model that did not fly until 1934 or 1935, after the date the bars claim for themselves.

The same strings recur across the bars, which is what first suggested they were meaningful. In full, longest first: SKCDKJCDJCYQSZKTZJPXPWIRN MQOLCSJTLGAJOKBSSBOMUPCE RHZVIYQIYSXVNQXQWIOVWPJO FEWGDRHDDEEUMFFTEEMJXZR XLYPISNANIRUSFTFWMIY HFXPCQYZVATXAWIZPVE YQHUDTABGALLOWLS UGMNCBXCFLDBEY ABRYCTUGVZXUPB JKGFIJPMCWSAEK KOWVRSRKWTMLDH HLMTAHGBGFNIV MVERZRLQDBHQ VIOHIKNNGUAB GKJFHYXODIE ZUQUPNZN 263 letters in all as McCurley transcribed them. He noted at the time that “some of the letters are hard to read so there may be inaccuracies”. The transcription was checked against his fifteen photographs for this write-up: fourteen strings are confirmed letter for letter on at least one clear bar, UGMNCBXCFLDBEY is thirteen letters on every bar that carries it (the glyph before the final Y reads E on the clearest cast, possibly B on another), and the second K of KOWVRSRKWTMLDH is not visible on any bar. Details in the notes.

Counting the letters shows the pattern. Gold is the observed count for each letter; the pale red behind it is what 263 letters of English would give. English towers at E and falls away to nothing at Z. The bars do neither. Twenty-one of the twenty-six letters occur exactly ten times, and the five that do not are off by one, except I which is off by three: letter count letter count E 11 O 9 I 13 T 9 S 11 all other 21 letters 10 Ten of each would be 260 letters exactly; the transcription gives 263. Checking the photographs removes one letter (the fourteen-letter string is thirteen on the bars) and leaves one more in doubt, so the true total is 261 or 262. It does not remove the deviations: I is thirteen on every reading, and depending on how the two doubtful glyphs are transcribed the letters off by one are three to seven. The bars themselves carry about ten of each letter; the deviations are not transcription noise. Under every defensible reading the chi-squared stays between 1.2 and 1.5 and the probability near one in a trillion. A person counting out ten of each letter and losing count by one or two gives this pattern.

test value index of coincidence 0.0350 (English 0.0667, random 0.0385) chi-squared against uniform, 25 df 1.251 (random sampling predicts 25) P(chi-squared ≤ 1.251) 9.3 × 10 −13 about 1 in a trillion chi-squared against English letter frequencies 1488 random 263-letter strings at least this uniform, out of 200,000 0 The argument rests on the distribution being flat beyond what randomness allows . The candidate ciphers in turn: Simple substitution renames letters but cannot change how often they occur, so it preserves the plaintext’s skew. Index of coincidence stays near 0.066. Any transposition reorders letters and leaves the counts completely untouched. A short-key Vigenère flattens partway, to roughly 0.045, and leaves periodic structure behind. A long key, or a one-time pad , reaches a flat expectation, but by random sampling, and random sampling is noisy. Draw 263 letters uniformly and the counts scatter with a standard deviation near 3.1, so you expect a spread from about 4 to 16 and a chi-squared near 25. Twenty-one letters landing on exactly ten is not what randomness looks like. Only deliberate construction produces it. The arrangement of the letters into the sixteen strings looks random. There are 71 places where a letter repeats inside a string, against 65.6 expected when the same pool of letters is shuffled at random into the same lengths. Somebody counted out ten of each letter and distributed them.

The inscriptions are decorative filler, made to look like cryptography on an object whose purpose was to look like a security. That sits with everything else known about the bars: an aircraft that had not yet been built on a bar dated 1933, banks that declined the claim, and a legal file closed without resolution. The item should be reclassified on the lists of famous ciphers as a construction with no message in it. The statistics explain why ninety years of attempts produced no decipherment. On the transcription: the argument was first made on the IACR’s 1996 transcription alone, with its author’s warning that some letters were hard to read. The letters have since been re-transcribed from the fifteen IACR photographs, enlarged and contrast-stretched. Fourteen of the sixteen strings are confirmed; one is a letter shorter than published and one letter in another is unresolved at the resolution available. The statistics were recomputed for every reading, and the result does not move.
