Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) key matched At a glance External key matched · none (key obtained, text not read) The letter Dr Nicholas Wotton, Mary I’s ambassador in France, to the Queen, Soissons, 13 June 1554, about 118 lines of cipher. Where British Library, Harley MS 1582 ff. 8r–10v; DECODE R8499, listed as “N. Wottoy ?” to an unknown recipient with no decryption. The cipher A homophonic alphabet, a row of nulls and some 140 code signs for Carew, the rebels, the Constable, the French king and others, in graphic signs. How it was read The key is DECODE R354 (TNA SP 106/2 f. 162, “France 1554”), filed in another series. After eight passes, 75.0% of 2,801 non-null signs decrypt firmly and 89.4% counting tentative values. What it says Carew is at Compiègne with the French king; the king has raised the rebels’ pensions; a repentant rebel met secretly in Paris asks the Queen’s pardon. Still open About forty rare code signs absent from the only surviving key; a contemporary deciphered copy at ff. 5r–7v is not digitised. Harley MS 1582 f. 8r, first lines: “Pleasing it your highness to understand that” in clear, then the cipher: “Carew was at Compiegne and spake of … with the French king, the rebels, with the Constable …”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 1582 f. 8r, via DECODE R8499.

R8499 has six images: ff. 8r, 8v, 9r and 10v of Harley MS 1582 and two binding views. The hand is Wotton’s, the address is to the Queen, and the close reads “And thus I beseech Jesu long to preserve your highness”. The body is cipher, about 3,200 signs, with clear-text pieces between the runs (“the king being then in his journey … the Court resting as yet nowhere”, “declaredde unto him your highness pleasure”). The letter is not in the Calendar of State Papers Foreign, Mary , which gives only Wotton to Petre, Soissons, 14 June, and later letters to the Queen from SP 69. The key is DECODE R354, a single sheet in TNA SP 106/2 f. 162 headed “France 1554”. It gives three to six homophones for each letter, a row of nulls (“Nihil significantia”), and a nomenclator whose entries fit Wotton’s embassy that spring: the Emperor, the Queen’s Highness, the French king, the Constable, Peter Carew, the rebels, my Lady Elizabeth, the Earl of Devonshire, the Prince of Spain, Strozzi, Siena, Guisnes, Calais, the Low Countries, “fair words”, and short words ( and, the, of, to, was, shall, have, hath, it, is ). The signs and nulls of R8499 are those of R354. The key, TNA SP 106/2 f. 162 (DECODE R354): the alphabet a–z with its homophones in columns, and below them the nulls, “Nihil significantia”. The nomenclator fills the rest of the sheet. Image: The National Archives, SP 106/2 f. 162, via DECODE R354.

The phrases below are taken in order from the reading column of the line-by-line decryption, final_v9.txt , with modern punctuation and the spelling as decrypted; … marks the stretches between them that do not give English. Square brackets with a number mark signs not decrypted; words in italics are tentative (grade C or M). They are not a reading: only about one sentence in ten of the decryption holds as English (10 of 98, 23 October 2026). f. 8r: Carew at Compiègne Pleasing it your highness to understand that Carew was at Compiegne and spake of with the French king, the rebels, with the Constable, and Carew. I am enformid Carew saith [1] he have had meny gentle and fair words … the Constable tooke it [4] that the French king had gyven him … and where Carew requyred that the band of the rebels should have the Emperor’s wagis … the Constable comenid with him how the ysle of Wight might be taken [13] most, and how it might be kept. The rebels finallye, Carew [also] advertisith me, they have concludid that … to attempt against your highness … the Prince of Spain’s coming … in the Low Countries … He the French king hath encreasidde the pensions of dyvers of the rebels … of the Cardinal Farnese , who shewing him much favour … two hundred … crownes and nothing other, likewise … offerid fowre hundrid and the leading of a band, yf him list, as he saithe. f. 8v: the rebels’ plans The rebels may dwel in France where they be, and the Emperor’s pensions to continew til the time the French king may restowr them to the Emperor’s countre … the Emperor’s ambassador sent me word that whereunto cam of late a servant of Carew to him out of the Low Countries, who shall that certein gentlemen home send him word that … in the west partis they … to take part with them … and that they [1] take Plymtown [5] and keep it rady … The king being then in his journey, the Court resting as yet nowhere, so as I could … I wold first make a step to Paris ere I went, to talk secretly with … and to advertys him of your highness’ mind … I found the meanes to talk with him in a [2] place and declaredde unto him your highness’ pleasure concerning him … he must first speak with Carew ere he could take [1] to him. The effect of his answer was these: first … the resolucion taken betwen the Constable and Carew [6] … the Constable, being enformedde that Carew was departid [from] Compiegne , satisfied , had sent the lord [16] to him to … meny fair words, and to shewe him that the rebels’ band shulde have theyr wagis. f. 9r: the repentant rebel … for lack of money … charges offred, and he would not entre in service to the French king … he did receve money of him, he could not find in his heart that they be untrew to him; and besides that, he doubting lest it be known that he gyveth me advertsmentes … would be gladde to depart this shortly; and although he sayde he took me to be an honest manne, and therfore did not mistrust my wordes … what kind of effect your highness wolde requyre of him to be done … that it were perceived that he wente abrode to attempt the Emperor against the French king … he came not fynde in his herte to return into England. He thinkith that your highness can not forget this offence … and in case your highness could forget it, yet he reckening assuredly that the French king will [not] forget it … so that, being persuadedde that he can not lyve in England without [pardon] of this, he entendeth not to return … that it would please your highness to give him … and suffer him to have a gentlemanes lyving in [2] countrey … He entendith not to open the circumstances of this fawte … if he must detect meny gentelmen, who, remaining unknown, may live honestly at home. f. 10v: Cornwel, the lantzknechtes, Saint-Quentin This is th’effect of … He shewed me that one Cornwel is rover to late and … I have not yet spoken with him … the said Cornwel … For he doutith whether he may trust him, for he was longing to the lord [4] … There is one who calling him self Greneberye , who hath been twyse offred … the first tyme they toke him for a spye … and besides that, this felaw who cam with him the first declared to Carew what he was and where … the Emperor’s sisters; Carew namid to be twenty enseignes, and lye abowte Laon, of new lantzknechtes … not the third part … passid within a myle of this towne fifty and nine canone. It is told me that … Paris, and it semith to take the way towardes Saint Quintin … what the Emperor’s intent is, is kept [2]. It is thought that the French king will be in the camp him[self] … whether the Emperor be strong to meete them. The Constable hath ben sike and is not yet [1] strong. The Duke of Gwyse [7] … And thus I beseech Jesu long to preserve your highness …

Identification. The opening and close in clear name the Queen; the hand and the signature fix Wotton; the BL catalogue record and the Harleian catalogue of 1808 give Soissons, 13 June 1554. Transcription. A first sign transcription (3,212 signs, 158 types) was made before the key was found. A homophonic annealer on the en-1640s model, validated on synthetic controls, failed blind: the nulls and word codes defeat it. Key. The key sheet R354 was found on DECODE among the SP 106 keys and transcribed ( key_R354.md ). With its nulls removed and its letter and code values fixed, the text began to give sense (“Compiegne and spake of … the rebels with the Constable”). Re-transcription. Several first-pass tokens merged distinct key signs (ω d and ꬯ and ; the French king and “your highness”; the barred and plain x). They were split sign by sign on the images (v2), then every page was re-transcribed at full resolution (v5). Unified key and nomenclator. Page-by-page keys were merged into one (v6), all ~140 nomenclator entries were transcribed and tested against every unread stretch (v7), and a shape pass separated the upright and arched triangles and the barred and plain C (v8). Measure. Each pass was counted on non-null signs: 47%, 65%, 72%, 75%, 75% firm. The last two passes added no firm values. page non-null signs firm incl. tentative f. 8r 734 66.6% 86.1% f. 8v 683 75.1% 90.0% f. 9r 709 81.8% 90.6% f. 10v 683 76.9% 91.4% all (v8) 2,801 75.0% 89.4% (The page rows are the v7 count on 2,809 signs; v8 removed two doubly transcribed signs and relabelled others without changing the totals.)

Checked again 23 October 2026. Every DECODE record of Harley MS 1582 was opened (R8009, R8010, R8498–R8505); none holds ff. 5r–7v, the contemporary deciphered copy (R8010 is a duplicate of R8505, ff. 263r–264v). The British Library’s catalogue now records the volume as digitised (ark:/81055/vdc_100162940894.0x000001), but its images have been unavailable since the 2023 cyber-attack; when they return, ff. 5r–7v can be fetched without an imaging order. A further pass on the same images and key cannot close the open stretches, so the letter stays decoded, not read. Re-measured 5 October 2026. The figures above count signs that have a value. A sense measure ( measure_sense.py ) subtracts readings that make no English (160 signs on 52 lines): 68.9% of the non-null signs on the final transcription v9 (p. 1 56.5, p. 2 73.3, p. 3 75.5, p. 6 71.0; the value count is 74.7%). Open and nonsense stretches are about 31% of the signs (p. 1 l. 13, l. 24 (fy)ve hundrid , p. 2 l. 25, p. 6 ll. 13–14, p. 3 l. 14). The contemporary decipherment, Harley MS 1582 ff. 5r–7v, is not digitised. About a quarter of the non-null signs are not decrypted or are tentative: short runs on f. 8r (lines 13–15, 18, 24), the name after “the lord” on f. 8v (16 signs; perhaps “Brymstane”, Crichton of Brunstane, a Scot: M), the name after “the Duke of Gwyse” on f. 10v (“Gaspard”?: I), “Greneberye” (M), and the code Ie , taken once as “the Emperor’s ambassador” (M). Blocker: the contemporary deciphered copy, Harley MS 1582 ff. 5r–7v, is not digitised by the BL or on DECODE and needs an imaging order. About forty rare code signs ( .I .p .d .M N. R. , the C with cedilla, the tailed Q, the tall looped f, the large circle) match no legible cell of R354, the only surviving copy of the key. The dotted N and R codes are probably names added to Wotton’s copy and missing from this one. Tested against the nomenclator and rejected: .I Therouanne, .M Trent, -P , the script y as “either”. The Isle of Wight sentence, f. 8r lines 13–16, re-read on the image on 30 Sept 2026. “concludid” is firm (H): c o n c l u d i d from the key, with one extra sign (the looped d, i on the key) written after the n, a slip or a null. After “taken” thirteen signs stay unread before “most”: the c with a dot below ( u if it is the key’s c with a tail, M; the shape pass judged it a different sign, and key v6 reads it s), then s, an underlined x ( i on the key), a barred b, a second c-sign, and p, r, the hooked d, a sign under an ink stain, a, t, e, s. They give “us i? l/o u pr[i?][?]ates” or “ss i? l/o s pr…”, neither of which is a sentence; the best language-model fit for the end is “privates” (I, not adopted). The sign before “advertisith” ( Ie ) is given as also , the connective that fits five of its seven places on ff. 8r–8v (I); it is not on the key sheet. Tentative code values: .Z = that, T. = me, L2 = Calais (C). Firm: 4 = that, B. = of, .B = not, dotted y = yet, small circle = hath. Grades of the connected passages: the Carew–Constable narrative of f. 8r, the rebels’ wages and pensions, and the repentant rebel on f. 9r are H; the Isle of Wight and Plymouth are H for the place names, C for the verbs; the Farnese and Greneberye names are M.

The last line of Livingston’s letter, six pairs of code numbers, is printed in the Selected Papers of John Jay as undecipherable and explained as six syllables ending in r. Livingston’s draft writes a syllable under each pair, and Jay’s own copy of the Thomson code lists the same additions: be, ce, de, fe, ge, he as 600 to 605. Each pair spells its syllable, with 226 as e, not r. 69.226 — 600 · 538.226 — 601 · 346.226 — 602 · 216.226 — 603 · 209.226 — 604 · 259.226 — 605 be — 600 · ce — 601 · de — 602 · fe — 603 · ge — 604 · he — 605 b 69 · c 538 · d 346 · e 226 · f 216 · g 209 · h 259 Philadelphia → John Jay at Madrid · Thomson’s printed syllable code · 28 November 1781 · read from the draft’s glosses and Jay’s key sheet Livingston to Jay, 28 November 1781: the “undecipherable” addition to the cypher from Robert R. Livingston → to John Jay Go to the transcriptions ↓ The one line of this letter that the modern edition could not read is a key change. It adds six syllables, be to he, as 600 to 605, and Livingston’s draft and Jay’s key sheet both give its meaning. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Brice Dudout (verification) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter Robert R. Livingston, the new Secretary for Foreign Affairs, to John Jay at Madrid, Philadelphia, 28 November 1781, carried by Lafayette. The body is printed in full; the open item was its last line, an instruction to add six groups to the cipher. Where Sent original (ALS), New-York Historical Society, Jay Papers (EJ 598); draft, NHi, R. R. Livingston Papers (EJ 1537). Both are imaged as photostats in Columbia University’s Jay Papers (ldpd:6328, ldpd:11572), with Jay’s copy of the Thomson code (ldpd:50144). Unsolved Catalogue no. 636. Not on DECODE. The cipher Charles Thomson’s printed list of about 600 words and syllables, with numbers written in by hand. The sent original uses a copy numbered differently from Jay’s: the copy that was lost at sea with William Palfrey. How it was deciphered Livingston’s draft writes a syllable under each pair. Jay’s copy of the code lists the same six syllables against 600–605. Each pair spells its syllable letter by letter, with 226 as e every time. What it says “Make this addition to your cypher: be, 600; ce, 601; de, 602; fe, 603; ge, 604; he, 605.” Still open Nothing in the line. How the three groups of “cypher” (23.473.370) divide into syllables is not settled.

Livingston took office as Secretary for Foreign Affairs on 20 October 1781. This was his first official letter to Jay, then minister at Madrid. It reports the winter after Yorktown, Congress’s anger at the Spanish court, and whether Jay would rather go to Paris. It ends with one line: Make this addition to your cypher: 69. 226–600; 538. 226–601; 346. 226–602; 216. 226–603; 209. 226–604; 259. 226–605. The Selected Papers of John Jay (vol. 2, 2012, pp. 644–46; Founders Online ) decode the cipher passages of the body from the draft. They print this line as figures, and note 7 explains it as “an attempt to simplify the Thomson code … adding six symbols for syllables ending in r”, calling the passage undecipherable on the authority of Richard B. Morris’s John Jay: The Making of a Revolutionary (1975), p. 664. The line on the sent original. A later hand has written “to your cypher” over 398, 264, 23.473.370. The second 226 of the fifth pair is squeezed in above 209. Image: New-York Historical Society, John Jay Papers (EJ 598), ALS of 28 Nov 1781, last page; photostat in Columbia University RBML, Jay Papers, ldpd:6328 (image ldpd:6321), via Columbia Digital Library Collections.

Charles Thomson, secretary of Congress, made nomenclators on a printed form: about 600 words and syllables in alphabetical order, with the numbers written in by hand (Weber’s WE007). Each copy could be numbered differently. Major Franks carried one copy to Jay, and it survives at Columbia. Thomson gave Livingston a second copy, numbered differently, which was meant to go to Jay with the consul William Palfrey. Palfrey was lost at sea. Livingston explained the muddle to Jay on 9 May 1782 ( Founders ). His letter of 28 November went by Lafayette “in a cypher delivered to me by mistake, by Mr. Thompson, and lost with Colonel Palfrey”. The original is endorsed “Recd. 24 Feb. 1782 … not decd.”. The duplicate and triplicate were re-encoded in Jay’s copy, and they stop at the signature, without the line. In the same letter Livingston says his letters “only notes a slight alteration in Mr. Thompson’s cypher”. That is this line. Looking up the six pairs in Jay’s copy gives nonsense (69 twelve, 538 into, 346 el, 216 en, 209 sha, 259 their; 226 edge). The figures are in the lost copy. A nineteenth-century copy of the coded passage of Livingston’s 20 October letter, with the figures written under the words (Columbia ldpd:32488), confirms that the lost copy is the same form renumbered: there not is 203, his 139 and will 175, where Jay’s copy has 281, 88 and 279.

Two witnesses give the line’s meaning, and they agree pair by pair. Livingston’s draft writes “Make this addition to your cypher” in clear, then the six pairs in a column, with a syllable written under each: Be, Ce, De, Fe, Ge, he . The first two are clear; the lower four are smudged in the photostat but can be read in that order. Jay’s copy of the Thomson code , headed “Thomson cypher, 11 July 81, as modified by Livingston 6 July 1782”, has a handwritten list at the foot of its second page: be 600, ce 601, de 602, fe 603, ge 604, he 605. A first “he 604” is written over. Later additions follow: le 608, me 652, ne 656, pe 651, and Washington 640, Greene 641, Morris 642. The draft. Under 69.226 – 600 stands Be , under 538.226 – 601 Ce , and so on down to he under 259.226 – 605. Image: New-York Historical Society, R. R. Livingston Papers (EJ 1537), draft of 28 Nov 1781; photostat in Columbia University RBML, Jay Papers, ldpd:11572 (image ldpd:11561), via Columbia Digital Library Collections. Jay’s key sheet: be 600, ce 601, de 602, fe 603, ge 604, he 605, then the later additions. Image: Columbia University RBML, John Jay Papers, Thomson cypher of 11 July 1781 as modified 6 July 1782, p. 2 (ldpd:50144, image ldpd:50139), via Columbia Digital Library Collections. Read against them, the line on the sent original is: Cipher Reading 398 · 264 · 23.473.370 to your cypher 69.226 — 600 be — 600 538.226 — 601 ce — 601 346.226 — 602 de — 602 216.226 — 603 fe — 603 209.226 — 604 ge — 604 259.226 — 605 he — 605 Each new group is defined by spelling its syllable in two existing groups, the consonant and then e. In the lost copy, b is 69, c 538, d 346, f 216, g 209, h 259 and e 226. Jay’s printed form has no entry for any of these six bare syllables: it has bea, been, bes, ca, ch, den, dent, fel, fen, fer, ger, head, hear, her , but no be, ce, de, fe, ge or he . The addition fills that gap. The edition’s “syllables ending in r” came from reading 226 as r. It is e. The form already has the r-syllables (in Jay’s copy ar 76, er 86, ir 150, or 382, ur 331), so there was nothing to add there.

The Founders text located the line. All six imaged copies of the letter in Columbia’s Jay Papers were then stitched from their full-resolution IIIF tiles, with Jay’s copy of the Thomson code and the 20 October copy. Two leads failed first. Jay’s own numbering does not fit the line. A four-page word code catalogued at Columbia as the key to this letter (ldpd:50124) gives 69 = apparent and 226 = destroy, so it is a different code. The draft’s glosses and Jay’s list then gave the reading, and the printed form was checked for the gap it fills.

All 17 code groups of the line are deciphered, and every reading is graded H: two independent witnesses agree. “Cypher” is three groups, 23.473.370. The obvious division is cy·ph·er, but 473 also stands under thing in the nineteenth-century copy of 20 October. Either that copyist’s figures drift against the words, or the division differs. The word itself is certain. Where Jay got the addition is not proved. The duplicate he could read does not carry it, and his key sheet is headed with Livingston’s changes of 6 July 1782, so that letter (Columbia, EJ 90354) is the likely source. It was not checked. Morris’s explanation in John Jay: The Making of a Revolutionary , p. 664, was not consulted.

Read: 17 of 17. ## The line in clear > Make this addition to your cypher: be, 600; ce, 601; de, 602; fe, 603; ge, 604; he, 605. Each pair is spelled in the code letter by letter: b, c, d, f, g, h followed by e (226). It gives each consonant + e syllable a single new group. The printed Thomson form has no entry for any of these six syllables (it has *bea, been, bes, ca, ch, ci, den, dent, fel, fen, fer, ger, head, hear, hence, her*, but no bare *be, ce, de, fe, ge, he*). The addition fills that gap. So the edition's note 7, "six symbols for syllables ending in r", is wrong. The syllables end in *e*. The r-syllables *ar, er, ir, or, ur* already have their own entries in the printed form (76, 86, 150, 382, 331 in Jay's copy). ## Values of the lost code these give The ALS of 28 Nov is in the copy of the Thomson form that Thomson gave Livingston by mistake. The copy meant for Jay was lost at sea with William Palfrey. It is the same printed word list with different numbers. Eight letters catalogued as June 1523 ciphertexts to an unknown recipient are Hurtado’s letters of May 1523 to March 1524 to Charles V and the Grand Chancellor Gattinara, in the system of 1522 with a changed key. The key was recovered from adjacent plaintext, the clerk’s clear version of part of the letter of 5 February 1524. Two letters were calendared by Bergenroth from contemporary decipherments; the other six are partly deciphered, from a quarter to two thirds of each. xul · zar · xug · zil · ∂ ʇʇ ω ∂ φ f ω y 4 · ton lo · de · la · con- · t r i b u c i o n · que Rome → Charles V and Gattinara · three-letter code with a homophonic alphabet of cursive signs · May 1523 – March 1524 Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome to Charles V and Gattinara, 1523–24 to Charles V Go to the full text ↓ Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid, Colección Salazar y Castro 9/28 (A-28) and 9/30 (A-30); DECODE R9667, R9683, R9695, R9846, R9866, R9867, R9868, R9869. The catalogue listed them as eight ciphertexts of June 1523 to an unknown recipient, with no decipherment. They are six letters to the Emperor and two to the Grand Chancellor Gattinara, written from Rome between May 1523 and March 1524, in the system of Hurtado’s 1522 letters with a changed key. The key was recovered from adjacent plaintext, the clerk’s clear version of part of one letter; the part of that letter it covers is taken from the clear. After a sign-by-sign re-reading on the images, three letters of 1524 build sentences with it; the other four decode only into word pieces with unknown code groups in most clauses: they are decoded, not read. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method · R9866, R9868, R9869 (1524, clear with cipher runs): key recovered based on adjacent plaintext (partial) · R9846, ff. 130r-v (clerk's clear on f. 133r): read from existing decipherment (partial) · R9667, R9683, R9695, R9867 (decoded, not read): not solved (none) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) · Gustav Adolph Bergenroth (earlier solution) adjacent text At a glance Key recovered from adjacent plaintext · partial (about 66% of the cipher tokens, estimated) The letters Eight letters of Lope Hurtado de Mendoza, Charles V’s agent at the papal court, 1523–24. Where Salazar volume, DECODE R9667 and R9846 among eight records; Bergenroth calendared two of them ( CSP Spain ii nos. 548, 617). The cipher The 1522 system: three-letter code groups and an alphabet of cursive signs, with the key changed between 1522 and 1524. How it was read The clerk’s clear version of the first third of the February 1524 letter (f. 133r), aligned against 38 cipher lines, gives 105 values, 65 confirmed. What it says Beaurain’s mission to Clement VII, the Pope’s wish to see France ruined or a truce made, the Emperor’s want of money, Hurtado’s unpaid salary. Still open The six uncalendared letters are one quarter to two thirds deciphered; about thirty code groups and look-alike signs remain. R9846, f. 130r (5 Feb 1524). The letter opens in the clear, “El papa ha holgado con la nueva de la venida de mossiur de Beure…”, and goes into cipher at “para lo de con[tribucion]”: zil con- and the spelled letters t-r-i-b-u-c-i-o-n. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Colección Salazar y Castro A-30 (9/30) f. 130r, via DECODE R9846.

The dates come from the date lines, the dockets and, for R9867, from the date spelled out in cipher at the foot. DECODE’s dates, addressees and volume are wrong for several records; the corrections are in the last column. DECODE ff. date to state DECODE says R9667 9/28 ff. 6–9 Rome, 5 May 1523 Emperor clear with cipher runs; CSP ii 548 June 1523, unknown recipient R9683 9/28 f. 171 Rome, June 1523 (docket 10 June) Emperor clear with 8 cipher lines unknown recipient R9695 9/28 ff. 339–340 Rome, 8 July 1523 Emperor autograph draft, much struck through June 1523 R9846 9/30 ff. 130–133 Rome, 3 and 5 Feb 1524 Emperor almost all cipher; clear of the first third on f. 133r; CSP ii 617 1523, 9/28 R9866 9/30 ff. 285–286 Rome, 28 Feb 1524 Grand Chancellor Gattinara half cipher 1523, 9/28, unknown recipient R9867 9/30 f. 351 Rome, 4 Jan 1524 Emperor wholly cipher, 30 lines 1523, 9/28 R9868 9/30 ff. 430–431 Rome, 20 Mar 1524 Grand Chancellor Gattinara half cipher 1523, 9/28, unknown recipient R9869 9/30 ff. 444–445 Rome, 28 Mar 1524 Emperor half cipher 1523, 9/28 The Calendar check went through Bergenroth’s CSP Spain vol. 2, pp. 547–709, by the Salazar folio numbers he prints. Only ff. 6–9 of A-28 (no. 548) and ff. 130–133 of A-30 (no. 617) are calendared. The other six letters are not. R9667 has a leaf headed “Claro” bound beside it, which looks like a crib. It is not one. The leaf is imaged mirrored, and its docket reads “Del abbad de Najera a dos de mayo”: it is the clear of the Abbot of Nájera’s letter of 2 May 1523, not of Hurtado’s of 5 May. For R9667 the content comes from Bergenroth’s abstract, which he made from a contemporary deciphering that is not among the images.

R9846, f. 133r. The clerk’s clear, headed “Al Rey — de Lope hurtado de v de hebrero MDxxiiij”. Only this page is imaged; it breaks off at “y assegurar el buen animo”. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Colección Salazar y Castro A-30 (9/30) f. 133r, via DECODE R9846. The clear on f. 133r covers the cipher of ff. 130r–130v from “para lo de contribucion” to “el buen animo”, and every clause has its cipher counterpart. Most of the letter alphabet came out of spelled runs whose length matches the plaintext word exactly, with known code groups on both sides: contribucion , ayuda , menester , salida , pensar , determinacion . The alignment gave 105 values, 65 of them confirmed (grade C). It also corrected six words of the first transcription of the clear: señorear , poco daño , concierte , deudas , seguir , conservar . The 1522 key is the starting point, and 25 of its code groups and the signs for n, e, a and o hold in 1524. Some values changed. tef is paz in 1522 and nec- ( necesidad , necesario ) three times in 1524. The sign L is i in 1522 and r here. So the 1522 key cannot be applied unchanged.

Notation: […] marks a passage not yet deciphered. Coverage is the share of cipher tokens that have a value, which is an upper bound: many of them are single letters in runs that do not yet make words. The “reads as Spanish” column is the better measure. Gists are graded M unless stated. DECODE tokens with a value reads as Spanish gist R9667 fragments little benefices for the Pope’s servants (list on f. 7); CSP 548 has the content R9683 67/91 fragments the Pope well disposed since Volterra’s arrest; restore the benefices of the chamberlain and Francisco (clear) R9695 184/249 almost none rumoured poisoning; the Duke of Camerino’s men still in prison; naturalisations for the Pope’s intimates (clear) R9846 first third from the clear first third (C) Beaurain’s coming; the Pope wants France ruined, or else a truce R9867 418/467 about 60% Beaurain has left the Pope content; the Emperor must not show need of money R9866 561/649 a quarter to a third to Gattinara: the French mean to stay this side of the Alps; the writer’s unpaid salary R9868 328/353 f. 430r mostly to Gattinara: Capua gone, all business hangs on the Datary, who must be satisfied R9869 310/339 about two thirds the Pope’s money offer through Beaurain; Florence undecided; Capua to be well received 5 February 1524, to the Emperor (R9846, CSP 617) The clerk’s clear, which the cipher of ff. 130r–130v matches clause for clause (grade C), with spelling and punctuation normalised from the line-by-line transcription r9846_clear.txt : El papa ha holgado con la nueva de la venida de mossior de Beuvre; spera le con desseo, sera provechosa su venida aqui en esta coyuntura generalmente para todos los negocios y particular para lo de contribucion, que segun hay pocos dineros toda ayuda es menester, fasta ver si la salida del visorey haze retirar los franceses, que donde agora estan haze pensar lo que ha de ser, como quiera que la determinacion del papa es que bayan fuera de Italia. […] Dize me su Sd. que querria una de dos cosas: teniendo v. mad. aparejo, lo que mas dessea es que el Rey de Francia se destruya […]; no pudiendo ser esto, dessea que se tomasse assiento de tregua o paz antes que las cosas de v. mad. veniessen a necessidad. The Pope is glad of Beaurain’s coming, since money is short and every help is needed until the Viceroy’s march makes the French withdraw; he is resolved that they leave Italy. If the Emperor has the means, what he most wants is for the King of France to be destroyed; if not, a truce or peace before the Emperor’s affairs come to necessity. The rest of the cipher (ff. 131r–132v) is not deciphered here; Bergenroth’s abstract no. 617 gives its content. 4 January 1524, to the Emperor (R9867; decoded, not read) Wholly in cipher, with no clear. The date and signature are spelled at the foot, “de Roma a quatro de enero — Lope Hurtado”, eleven signs for l-o-p-e-h-u-r-t-a-d-o, all but one already in the key. About half its sentences hold; the rest break on open code groups (partial reading R9867_reading.md ): Mussiur de Beure [?dexa] al papa contento de lo que le ha dicho de parte de V. Mt. … No deve mostrar necessidad, porque […]emos […] que aqui son poco[s] para sacar dineros; y que estar sin [?dezir] aprovechara […] para que los buscasen los que […] dizen que no los tienen. … De Roma a quatro de enero. Lope Hurtado. On 22 October 2026 the three letters below were transcribed again sign by sign on the full-resolution DECODE images (look-alike signs resolved word by word, corrections in <record>_corrections.tsv ) and decoded with the key; their clear text with the cipher runs (in italics) now builds Spanish sentences, with holes at the open code groups. 28 February 1524, to Gattinara (R9866) The letter builds coherent sentences but reads at 91.4% of its words, under the 95% bar. Los franceses desean por maña o por fuerça quedar desta parte de los montes, segun el credito que [?an] [?allanado], en no los aver ofendido por esas partes los exercitos de su V. Mt., y el que sea perdido en no poder hazer nada. Beaurain’s coming was timely, and Hurtado has briefed him. The French want to stay this side of the Alps; the Emperor must not grant peace or truce while they hold a palm of ground, and must drive them out: “que si no son vencidos, quedan vencedores, y lo de aca esta perdido”. Naples should be made to pay the army. Hurtado asks Gattinara to read a chapter he wrote to Soria and to help him get paid what he is owed. 20 March 1524, to Gattinara (R9868) A copy of Hurtado’s letter of 11 March to the Emperor goes with it. The archbishop of Capua has left, and in his absence all business hangs on the Datary, Giberti: A Su Mt. tengo escrito por otras la necesidad que ay de [?gratificarle], porque de lo passado era mal contento, segun el lugar que tiene. Tengolo por inconveniente, y cada dia me parece mas necessario [?cunplir] con el. Naturalisations would help two or three of those closest to the Pope; the protectorship would be better with Colonna, whom Vespasiano “obedecele como al Prospero su padre”, and who could complain with cause if forgotten. 28 March 1524, to the Emperor (R9869) The letter builds coherent sentences but reads at 92.7% of its words, under the 95% bar. The Pope has sent Beaurain money proposals and told Hurtado he would fulfil the rest, pleading his need; Florence has not yet decided; Fuenterrabía is held lost by the French. If the archbishop of Capua finds the army ready to sustain the war, his report will match the Pope’s offer. “La voluntad y palabras del papa no pare[ce] que hera[n] mejores […] […]. Quiera Dios que tales sean las obras. ” Easter news, Hungary and the Turk are in the clear. June and July 1523 (R9683, R9695) Both letters are mostly in the clear, and little of their cipher lines is deciphered. R9683 says the Pope has been well disposed since the arrest of Cardinal Soderini of Volterra, and asks the Emperor to restore the benefices of the Pope’s chamberlain and of Francisco and to pay what is owed to the Pope. R9695, an autograph draft of 8 July, reports that the rumoured poisoning could not be verified, that the Duke of Camerino’s men are still in prison and that the Pope eats apart, served by old servants; it asks naturalisations for the Pope’s intimates.

About thirty code groups, among them rub , ʃug , zid , tol , tid , zib , xer , xir , xal , ʃal , yab , tas , toc , yic : they leave the holes in R9866, R9868 and R9869 and most of R9867 unread. There is no crib for them. R9667, R9683 and R9695 (1523): decoded, not read. The 1523 hand uses letter signs of the 1522 notation that are not in the 1524 key, and there is no 1523 crib; R9667’s contemporary decipherment, from which Bergenroth worked, is not imaged. Look-alike signs: ∂ and barred ∂, two- and three-bar crosses, and a barred m that is f in some places and c in others. Most were resolved word by word on the full-resolution crops on 22 October 2026; a few stay ambiguous. R9846 ff. 131r–132v: not deciphered here. The rest of the clerk’s clear is probably on f. 133v, which is not imaged; the RAH Biblioteca Digital copy of Salazar A-30 would give more of the key. R9667: no crib. Its content is known only through CSP 548. R9683: the docket’s sender reading and the date line (“[x]vi de junio” against the docket’s “diez de junio”) are not settled.

Sacred Catholic Caesarean Majesty, From the arrest of Volterra the greatest favour has come to Your Majesty's affairs and to all your servants, and it seems that Pope Leo has not been lacking to the Cardinal de' Medici. His Holiness is content with him and says he must treat and honour him greatly, and the Cardinal is satisfied with His Beatitude. The adversaries have received such a reverse that they do not know where they are. The Duke has handled this negotiation very well, and treats the Cardinal so that he holds himself not Your Majesty's servant but your slave. *[…] the Pope does not declare himself; but in […] nor in any other thing […] that […] Your Majesty,* and they are now without any hope of good for themselves. At present everything here is well on its way, as Your Majesty will understand at more length from the Duke's letters. In these matters *[…] in this […] [?French] that [?was thought] […],* because all are as glad of what the Pope has done as I am, and so is Theodoric, *who was the one most [?suspected].* It is reasonable that what the Pope has done and his good will should earn that Your Majesty do them the favour of having those closest to His Holiness made naturals of these kingdoms; the memorial of them goes with this. Likewise Your Majesty ought to have the benefices that the Pope gave in Flanders granted to the chamberlain and to Francisco, because Madame had offered them to them, commending the person of His Holiness, so that they should receive them from Your Majesty as patronage; for all are displeased to learn that in these kingdoms they would not give a benefice to Pedro de Roma, saying he was not a native, and that in Flanders *[…] them […] Your Majesty […]; Your Majesty what […] will [?give] them […]. […] that the Pope has said that Your Majesty […] that of benefices* to his servants. *No that […] in […] the […] in his […].* At present it seems to me that this provision would be necessary so that they may be better disposed in what they are bound to, the service of Your Majesty. The Pope was very glad to have been paid Bormediano and to know that the houses would be paid him. May Your Majesty have it provided, and also give him somewhat more of the bull of Saint Peter, since the things despatched have cost so little, being ordinary ones of good settlement. I wrote to Your Majesty some days ago that the Duke ought to have some credit here for the needs that might arise. Your Majesty answered me that you ordered the viceroy to see to it. The Duke says he knows of no such provision made by Your Majesty, except only that he be repaid what he had spent up to that provision of Your Majesty. It is a thing Your Majesty must order to be provided, for new things arise here every day and the Duke has no surplus of what he needs for his necessities, and has trouble enough keeping himself. Your Majesty ought to do him the favour of having him helped, for the ambassador's salary is little for his expense, which is great and very honourable. As for me, I have already written to Your Majesty that I have nothing here in which to serve. May Your Majesty remember to send me orders on what I am to do, and to have me provided with my salary from what is the Pope's, as I have begged in other letters to which I refer; and in this one I say no more. May Our Lord keep and increase Your Majesty's most royal person and estate. From Rome, 5 May 1523. Lope Hurtado [enclosed list:] Pedro the chamberlain. Francisco. The dean of […], his chamberlain. Uncertain readings of the clear keep their `(?)` as `[?…]`. Written 22 Oct 2026, batch b07. The Pope has been pleased by the news of the coming of Monsieur de Beaurain. He awaits him eagerly; his coming here at this juncture will be useful for all business in general, and in particular for the matter of the contribution, for, as there is little money, every help is needed, until we see whether the viceroy's going out makes the French withdraw, for where they now are makes one think what is to come. However, the Pope's resolve is that they should go out of Italy, and if he saw the means to humble the pride of the King of France and to aggrandise Your Majesty, His Holiness has told me he would like to help in it. And the archbishop of Capua has also told me this, [?and says] he has given his advice to the Pope that he ought to do so, saying that, to resist the Turk, to remedy the Lutheran matter, for the quiet of Italy and the memory of his house, the best remedy is to aggrandise Your Majesty. They are of this mind; but as they have seen the great [efforts] of Your Majesty, and the little harm that has been done in France from Flanders and from Spain, and the bad provision of money here, and the great cost of keeping the army, they fear that Your Majesty may have no means to keep it up, and that, the King of England slackening, he may tire or come to terms, and that the French may press on to make themselves masters of things here. His Holiness tells me that he would like one of two things. If Your Majesty had the means, what he most desires is that the King of France be destroyed; that for this Your Majesty should not rely on his money, for he says that [?for a long time] it can hardly be kept up, given the debts and how ruined the Church is; but I believe that if he saw a way for Your Majesty to be able to follow this, he would help with money, and likewise publicly. This being impossible, he wishes that a settlement of truce or peace be made before Your Majesty's affairs came to necessity, so that it might be made on the best terms and with more reputation. This is the Pope's aim. On this, let Your Majesty see what best suits his service, and let Your Majesty order that more despatches come, because the Pope holds it a very great drawback, in a time of such need, to hear so seldom from Your Majesty; and whether the war is to be pursued, to keep and secure the good disposition […] R9866, Rome, 28 Feb 1524, to Grand Chancellor Gattinara (9/30 ff. 285-286) read in part To Gattinara: Beaurain's coming was timely; the French mean, by craft or force, to stay on this side of the Alps, and the Emperor must not lose the world's respect while he spends so much on the war; Hurtado asks Gattinara's help to be paid what he is owed. Passages in cipher in the original are in *italics*. Most Illustrious Lord, The coming of Monsieur de Beaurain has been very timely. I have briefed him on matters here as best I understand them, as Your Lordship will see by his letters; and since the third party in everything is negotiating here, I shall be brief. The French want, by craft or by force, to stay on this side of the mountains, given the *credit that [?they have] [?levelled], by not having been harmed* in those parts by *the armies of Your Majesty,* and that it is *lost* by being unable to *do anything.* If *His Majesty can, in [?no other] way does it suit him [to grant], for few or […] days, peace or truce, if the French stay here with […] a foot of [?ground],* for it will be, fearing the *[?Swiss] and the [?reputation] they have gained, [?to be], when they [?wish], lords of Italy;* and that His Majesty should not be [lord] of the world, with them leaving it. Since so much is spent over there on the war, *and it profits as much as His Majesty […] to avoid the cost over there and [?to set] with the army that he has here,* for it is the best that any prince ever had, in captains and men by land and sea; and if His Majesty is to rely on *this, let him not [?think] that money from the [?contributions] [?will be] of [?help], […] that no […] army;* it is needed *to get it from them, the allies, so as to resist the enemies,* until the time comes that *the French do not hold […] Italy.* And in the opinion of all His Majesty's servants, although *[…] the […], and [?] the best that His Majesty has in his […], he must not fail [to] […] and [?drive] the French from here; for if they are not beaten, they remain the victors, and all here is lost. Let His Majesty provide money with […],* and if in Naples *[…] is to be sold,* let him give a commission to a private person so that *he sells and the army is paid;* for it seems that, if the *viceroy had done it,* and everyone knew that *he would not [?lack] money, the French would [?all] go;* and some who now *say they have none would have [?looked] and would [?look] for it, to fulfil what has been agreed.* But as they are *afraid that on His Majesty's part […], needs; and peace seems so profitable to them, [?as] [?I have] written, […] they would not be very harmful to His Majesty,* as Monsieur de Beaurain will bring. So I do not say it here, except to beg Your Lordship to look at a chapter he wrote to Soria, and to do me the favour of helping me so that His Majesty does not allow me to suffer so much harm and shame by not ordering that what is owed me be paid. May Our Lord keep and increase Your Lordship's most illustrious person and estate. From Rome, 28 February. Passages in cipher in the original are in *italics*. Most Illustrious Lord, By the letter that goes with this, which is a copy of the one I wrote to His Majesty on the 11th of this month, Your Lordship will have learnt of the departure of the lord archbishop of Capua. With his absence all business has come to hang on the Datary, and he stands as far forward with the Pope as can be. I have written to His Majesty in other letters of the need there is *to [?reward] him,* because *he was ill-content with the past,* given the place *he holds.* I hold it *to be inexpedient,* and every day it seems to me more *necessary to [?satisfy] him.* Let it not be in *the ten moneys that the Pope* held on the *[…] of […],* because he would *not take them from them,* for they have been shared out among the Cardinals like the other benefices; and he thinks His Majesty will approve, as the King of France has done with the benefices he held in France. Since the payment *of this one* is necessary, His Majesty should *consent to it* where he may be content. In my opinion the absence of the *[?archbishop]* from here will not help *Your Majesty's* affairs, because I am more *[?confident] of him than of those who are here,* and it is surer and better served. Since Your Lordship is there, have His Majesty *treat him* in such a way *that he comes back more [?obliged];* and the sooner *he returns,* the better he will think it. Bernaldino de la Barba has likewise gone there. It would be well to do him some favour, to encourage His Holiness's servants who stayed here, who *are […] very mistrustful.* Some are already speaking to the lord Duke about petitioning for naturalisations; if it could be done amicably in that kingdom I think it would be useful, at *least for two and three* of those who are *closest to His [?Beatitude].* I likewise wrote to His Majesty some days ago how many Cardinals wished to be protectors for His Majesty, and that as I understood it [?it would be] better with *Colonna.* In that or in anything else His Majesty should remember him, because he is the most valiant person *[?there is] in the College,* and in his house. Vespasiano *obeys him as he did Prospero his father when he was […].* He has many sons and nephews, who all *[…];* none of these is engaged in the war or in anything else, not one with His Majesty's pay. *The cardinal,* in the matter of the *[…],* Your Lordship will have seen what he did, and how he gave up the *[…] of [?Catania]* freely. If His Majesty did not remember *him, it seems he [?could] complain with cause;* and such a servant, *it is very useful [?to keep him] here, if they understand that His Majesty has them taken as […];* and in this time, goods; *[?avoid] all things they could complain of.* I believe the lord Duke has written at greater length on all these matters; so I say no more here. May Our Lord keep and increase Your Lordship's most illustrious person and estate. From Rome, 20 March. Mt. *[…] de los dineros que ofrecio el papa a mussiur de [?Beure] ha [?enviado] […] los [?quatro] destos tomaron […].* A me dicho Su Sd. que *cunplira el resto; […] pero dize su necessidad.* De Florencia hasta agora no se a *tomado resolucion;* todavia *[?se] escusan.* La semana que viene dizen que partira el Cardenal Quartona con Ypolito, sobrino de Su Sd., alla, y que llegado [alla] *[…] [?bueno].* Las nuevas que destas partes tenian y de Ingalaterra avian *mudado de proposito a todos.* Agora con tener por cierto que los franceses an perdido a Fuenterrabia, que aviendo la nueva por avisos de mussiur de Borbon y de Leon, aunque son diferentes: unos dizen por conbate y otros por partido. Los franceses conocen que se a perdida, pero dizen que por traycion. A faborecido mucho las cosas de V. Mt. Y si el arçobispo, llegado a V. Mt., halla *el exercito de V. Mt. en […] para [?poder] en Francia, o a V. Mt. con aparejo para sostener la guerra aca,* siendo *su relacion [?buena], no [?tengo] por […] que aca* seran sus obras conformes a lo que el *papa envio a ofrecer a V. Mt. quando fue elegido.* V. Mt. deve mandar mirar alla que el *arçobispo* sea *tomado de manera que sus […] [?aprovechen] […];* y si el viniese y *[?assiento]* de lo que dicho seria muy mejor, porque de quien aca *que […] toda […] se tiene la confiança que del.* Y segun ay *necessidad de dineros,* y quan malos *son […] [?sacar],* qual[qui]era *ayuda es buena, […] mas la del arçobispo,* que en parecer aca no tiene V. Mt. *[…] […] [?tomador].* La voluntad y palabras del *papa* no pare[ce] que hera[n] mejores *[…] […].* Quiera Dios que tales *sean las obras.* Esta pascua a venido dos nuevas al papa: una de Alemaña que dize en que los ungaros se acordavan con el Turco dandole tributo en cierta [?suma]; y la otra por Venecia, que con el Cairo y la mayor parte de Soria se avia alçado al Turco un vasallo. Hasta agora ninguna de las dos se tiene por averiguada. El Legado llego en Norimberga a xiiij deste; scrive a xix que fue muy bien recebido y tratado del S. Infante, y que ya avia hecho su proposicion, pero que no pensavan que en aquella dieta se pudiese hazer nada. Y assi lo scrive Salamanca a uno que solicita aqui las cosas del S. Infante. Gran daño haze a las cosas de aca, a lo que todos dizen y parece, venir tan pocas cartas de V. Mt. Pues ya es verano, que se podra navegar mejor, creo que seria muy provechoso que V. Mt. mandase scrivir mas vezes. Agora no se ofrece otra cosa de que avisar a V. Mt., cuya muy Real persona y estado guarde Nuestro Señor y acreciente. De Roma a xxviij de março. Passages that are in cipher in the original are in *italics*. S[acred] C[atholic] C[aesarean] M[ajes]ty *[…] of the money that the Pope offered to Monsieur de [?Beaurain], he has [?sent] […]; the [?four] of these took […].* His Holiness has told me that *he will fulfil the rest; […] but he speaks of his need.* From Florence no *resolution has been taken* so far; they still *[?make] excuses.* They say that next week Cardinal Cortona will leave for there with Ippolito, His Holiness's nephew, and that once [there] *[…] [?good].* The news that they had from these parts and from England had *changed everyone's purpose.* Now, holding it for certain that the French have lost Fuenterrabía, having the news by reports from Monsieur de Bourbon and from Lyon, although they differ: some say by assault and others by terms. The French acknowledge that it is lost, but say it was by treason. It has greatly favoured Your Majesty's affairs. And if the archbishop, having reached Your Majesty, finds *Your Majesty's army in […] to [?be able] [to go] into France, or Your Majesty with the means to sustain the war here,* his *report* being *[?good], I do not [?hold] for […] that here* his deeds will be in keeping with what the *Pope sent to offer Your Majesty when he was elected.* Your Majesty should have it seen to there that the *archbishop* is *taken in such a way that his […] [?profit] […];* and if he came, and *[?settlement]* of what was said would be much better, because of whom here *[…] all […] has the confidence that of him.* And given the *need of money* here, and how bad *they are […] [?to raise],* any *help is good, […] the more so the archbishop's,* for in the judgement here Your Majesty has not *[…] [?taker].* The goodwill and words of the *Pope* could not seem better *[…].* God grant that *the deeds* be such. This Easter two pieces of news have come to the Pope: one from Germany, saying that the Hungarians were coming to terms with the Turk, giving him tribute in a certain [?sum]; and the other by way of Venice, that a vassal had risen against the Turk with Cairo and the greater part of Syria. So far neither of the two is held as confirmed. The Legate reached Nuremberg on the 14th of this month; he writes on the 19th that he was very well received and treated by the Lord Infante, and that he had already made his proposition, but that they did not think anything could be done at that diet. Salamanca writes the same to someone who looks after the Lord Infante's affairs here. It does great harm to affairs here, as everyone says and as it seems, that so few letters come from Your Majesty. Since it is now summer, when sailing will be easier, I believe it would be very useful for Your Majesty to have letters written more often. Nothing else offers at present to report to Your Majesty, whose most royal person and estate may Our Lord keep and increase. From Rome, 28 March. M.” that a “worthy lord” has allowed him to write and that, if something comes about, this lord means next January, with help, to pursue the enemy to the utmost. Still open Two unglossed runs (13.32 and 27.13.65), and any measurement of the key: there is no held-out part. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée) transcribed the runs, rebuilt the key and read the unglossed runs by sense, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. The decipherment is the clerk’s. The lead (2181) is from Daniel Bourdeau’s sweep.

Halm’s catalogue of 1874 (p. 123) lists the piece as “Schreiben an den Kaiser s. d. zum Theil in Chiffern”, between letters of Gabriel Bethlen to the Emperor (Kassa, 29 May 1624). The text, however, addresses “E. M.” and speaks of the Emperor as a third party (“von dem Kayser erlangt”), so it is written to another king. The Palatine papers of the collection make Frederick V, King of Bohemia, the likely recipient, but the writer is not named either.

The letters are two-digit homophones (a 6, 9, 15; c 8; d 12, 36, 60; e 13, 19; f 14, 20; n 42, 45, 51; r 49; s 50, 56, 59; t 63, 69 …); 27, 32 and 65 occur once each and have no value. Every value comes from a word glossed over the cipher at the time, so the key is taken from the page, not tested against it. No part of the cipher was held out: it is one page, most of it glossed, and no other piece of Clm 10403 uses the same code. The key is therefore not validated.

Six runs carry no gloss. Three are certain (deciphered from their context): -olgen (the end of verfolgen , split across the line), -liche in der löbliche Herr (c = 8 rests on this context alone) and kü- (the start of künftigen ). One is probable, an s ( auffs ). Two stay unresolved, 13.32 and 27.13.65, because 27, 32 and 65 each occur once. Of the 18 letters of the unglossed runs, 15 are deciphered, 83%, below the 95% bar. The run 62.61.42.36.19.45 decodes wünden (or sünden if 62 is s), probable but of unclear meaning. The normalised German and an English summary are under Full texts.

Two unglossed runs are unresolved, and 8, 36 and 45 rest on one occurrence each. The key is not measured: no held-out part exists, and no other piece shares the code. Several glosses are hard to read on the microfilm (412.01, 412.07, 412.08, 1492, 2999). The four-digit code groups and the clear German text were glossed at the time and are not transcribed here. One reader (an agent) on a microfilm scan; no human palaeographic check. The writer and the addressee are not identified. No printed text was found (Halm 1874 and Szilágyi 1879 checked; Tadra, Briefe und Akten and the other editions are not available as full text).

Fifteen ciphered pages of the Duke of Mayenne’s Guyenne campaign, his and Forget de Fresnes’s despatches to Henri III and Villeroy (BnF fr. 15572, fr. 15571 f. 177), for which Tomokiyo knew no decipherment of the time. Michael Brackx re-transcribed every leaf and found contemporary clear copies of three letters; his eleven per-leaf keys were merged here into one Cipher-1 key. 10,616 of 16,677 cipher tokens decode into runs of French, measured, and the decode agrees with the copies on 85–93% of letters. ʓ yy c ʓ x dd m α v Ze n Δ o yy t h ff m t 6 w L h 49 12 … 76 s’estant laissé entendre comme il se vouloit départir du roi de Navarre 49 = comme · 76 = le roi de Navarre · 59 = argent Guyenne → Henri III and Villeroy · homophonic figures with a numbered nomenclator · 1585–1586 · 14 of 16 documents deciphered into sentences and translated, two pages decoded, not read Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-1, 1585–86 from Charles de Lorraine, duc de Mayenne → to Henri III Go to the full text ↓ The ciphered despatches of Mayenne’s campaign in Guyenne, on Pons and Taillebourg, credit, an unpaid army, Castets and the siege of Monségur. Michael Brackx re-transcribed them; here each leaf was deciphered sentence by sentence against the images, his figure labels corrected where the image disagrees, and translated. Four letters also have clear copies made at the time. Sixteen ciphered pages or page groups in all, 17,913 cipher tokens. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15572 ff. 110, 123–124, 143, 150, 154, 173, 196r–v, 201 and fr. 15571 f. 177, on Gallica. Catalogue item 12 here; Satoshi Tomokiyo knew of no contemporary decipherment for them. The cipher Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-1: several figures and invented signs for each letter, and numbers for common words and names (12 il , 14 que , 49 comme , 76 le roi de Navarre ). Some figures look so alike that a reader can only narrow them to two or three letters. How it was deciphered Tomokiyo’s table, checked here on two letters deciphered at the time, and Michael Brackx’s eleven per-leaf keys merged into one, decode every leaf. A decode with holes in most sentences is not a reading (George Lasry, 22 October 2026). So each leaf was then built into sentences against the full-resolution images: every break looked at, about 400 of Brackx’s figure labels corrected where the image disagrees, a few letter values added per leaf, and the result translated into English. Four letters also have clear copies made at the time (ff. 155–157, found by Brackx; fr. 15571 f. 176, found here), and the decode matches them. What it says A plan on Pons and Taillebourg dropped when Turenne took the field; Mayenne telling Villeroy that the King may end the war but not by ruining his reputation; no money at Marmande and the march on Sainte-Bazeille; the captain of Castets bought away from the King of Navarre; lenders who will lend only on Forget’s word; the siege of Monségur in May 1586, with Mayenne in a fever and a battery of fifteen cannon. Still open ff. 123r and 124r give only 41% and 56% of their sentences clean after three passes each: decoded, not read. ff. 177, 110, 123v, 124v and 173 build sentences but read at 94.1–94.9% of their words, under 95%. Holes remain in some lines of f. 110, fourteen code numbers have no value, and the label corrections have had one reader. Credit The transcriptions, the per-leaf keys and most code values are Michael Brackx’s (issues 64–83, October 2026, with Claude Code). He also found the clear copies on ff. 155–157. The key tables are Tomokiyo’s. The label corrections, the sentence-by-sentence decipherment, the translations, f. 196v and the copy on f. 176 are this project’s (22 October 2026).

In 1585–86 Charles de Lorraine, Duke of Mayenne, led a royal army against the Protestants in Guyenne, with Marshal Matignon at Bordeaux and Pierre Forget de Fresnes in his camp. Their despatches to the King and to Villeroy are bound in BnF fr. 15572 and fr. 15571. Tomokiyo (cryptiana, Henry III’s Cipher with Ambassadors ) sorts their ciphers into three. This entry holds the one he calls Mayenne–Forget’s Cipher-1. Cipher-2 and Matignon’s Cipher-3 are different ciphers, each with its own page. “Clean sentences” below is the share of sentences with at most one hole in ten words ( docs/_check_reading.py ), before and after the leaf was worked on the images on 22 October 2026. Measured word by word on 24 October 2026, five leaves (fr. 15571 f. 177, ff. 110, 123v, 124v and 173) build coherent sentences but read at 94.1–94.9% of their words, just under the 95% a complete reading needs, so their extent is partial. Tomokiyo publishes partial tables for Cipher-1. The project checked and completed them in September 2026 against two letters in the same volume deciphered at the time: the postscript of f. 14v, written out in clear on f. 15r, and the long despatch of f. 18, deciphered on f. 19. The figures do not separate cleanly. Three shapes of “6” stand for i , n and s , and on the scans their correlation is above 0.9. So the key is kept as letter sets, not single letters, and a program scores the possible letters with a model of period French and keeps the likeliest. In October 2026 Michael Brackx re-transcribed every Cipher-1 leaf from full-size line crops. He used a label set that keeps apart figures the earlier transcriptions had merged, and he fitted a key to each leaf. His eleven keys differ in a few letter sets, mainly whether θ is m or m/s and how e and ε divide. Here they were merged by union: each figure keeps every letter any leaf gives it. The merged key decodes every leaf at least as well as the leaf’s own key (9,855 against 9,609 tokens in runs of French). Agreement with the clear copies does not move by more than a point. The differences were in the reading of the hands, not in the cipher. Trimming rarely used letters from the merged key lowered the score, so it was not done. Code values come from the crib leaves, the clear copies and context: 12 il , 13 qui , 14 que , 15 quoy , 17 car , 24 mais , 25 nous , 26 vous , 27 nostre , 33 vostre , 34 ainsi , 35 parce que , 36 toutesfois , 40 bien , 43 point , 46 rien , 47 tous/tout , 49 comme , 51 pas , 52 plustost , 53 affin , 54 aussi , 61 beaucoup , 62 peut , 63 après , 64 quelque , 73 the syllable oi on f. 18 and le Roy on f. 177, 76 and 78 le roi de Navarre , 82 le gouverneur de Coul[…] , 84 le vicomte de Turenne , 88 Monsieur du Mayne , 104 mil . 44 is a stop. 59 is argent , added here: on f. 154r the cipher has “nous prester icy de l’[59] a rendre a Paris” where the clear copy f. 157r has “de l’argent”, and the word fits its four other places. On 22 October 2026 each leaf was taken again on the full-resolution images, sentence by sentence (section 04). The merged key stays the key; what a single hand needs beyond it is kept in a small key per leaf ( key_cipher1_<leaf>.json ): on f. 110 a looped tilde for s and a large C for l or r ; on f. 196v four figures not seen before (a small double cross for t , a barred figure for r / rr , a looped x for x , a looped y for z ); on f. 177 three figures that are nulls, which the clear copy leaves out.

Quotations are from the decipherments in texts/reading_*.md , in the spelling the figures give. A word in brackets with a question mark is carried only in part by its figures; […] is a run of figures that does not form a word. Each leaf has an English translation beside it in the Full texts below. Pons and Taillebourg, 31 December 1585 (fr. 15571 f. 177). Forget tells Villeroy of a plan to besiege Pons and Taillebourg together: taking Taillebourg would deprive the enemy of the toll on the Charente, oster un grand revenu qu’ils tirent du passaige de la Charante , and the country offered thirty thousand écus for the siege. Then Matignon had word from Bordeaux that the vicomte de Turenne estoit paru en campaigne avec forces et canons , and the despatch was rewritten. Forget comments: Voila comment noz opinions sont erantes. A clear copy of the whole cipher, made at the time, is on the preceding leaf, f. 176r–v; it agrees with the decipherment and settles the few words the figures carry only in part. Villeneuve-d’Agenais, March 1586 (f. 110). Mayenne to Villeroy, wholly in cipher. The dateline, earlier transcribed “De Bellebourg”, reads on the image De Villeneufve d’Agenoys . He asks Villeroy for advice as a friend and states his case: Si le roi est ennuié de la guerre, et qu’il la veuile finir, il ce peult faire plus [?honnestement] que par la ruine de ma reputation . Left without the promised money, the army périra toute entière avant qu’il soit [?six] sepmaines , and Sa Maiesté en perdra plus que moi. Lines 1–4, 8, 10, 14–16, 24–25 and 36 keep holes. Marmande, March 1586 (ff. 123–124). Mayenne to the King, opening in clear. On f. 123v he answers those who would have him live off the province as he once did in the Dauphiné: here the enemy are si meslés parmi ce qui vous reste de bons subiects que persone n’habite la campaigne , and contributions could be raised only by garrisons. He sends Forget, with the sieur de Gourgues, to borrow et argent et draps (f. 124v), and resolves d’aller attacquer Saincte Basille sitost qu’il m’aura envoié cinq canons et la pouldre et les balles ; Turenne has come to Nérac. ff. 123r and 124r are decoded, not read : the gist given here for them is pieced together from fragments and may be wrong in detail. On f. 123r more than a hundred thousand écus would be needed, there are not twelve thousand in the treasurer’s hands, and Matignon has borrowed twenty thousand; on f. 124r Mayenne proposes putting the army into garrison, or taking it into the Rouergue or the Quercy. Castets, April 1586 (f. 143). The clear half of f. 143r reports on Marmande, Sainte-Bazeille and the capitulation of Castets. The cipher half explains a private bargain with the captain of Castets. The clear copy on f. 155r opens: s’estant laissé entendre comme il se vouloit départir du Roy de Navarre, duquel je sçay qu’il est tres mal contant Mayenne judged him the best soldier on Navarre’s side and treated with him: twelve thousand écus over three months, leave to sell his property, a pardon to be registered by the Parlement, and a promise not to bear arms for his party for six months. The last ten lines of the cipher, after the foot of f. 155r, were deciphered on the image: C’est se qui m’a meu d’entrer plus volontiers en ce traicté . The copy goes on at the head of f. 155v and agrees with them word for word. F. 155r, the contemporary clear copy of the f. 143 cipher, beginning S’estant laissé entendre comme il se vouloit départir du Roy de Nav[arre] . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15572 f. 155r (canvas 162), via Gallica. Forget to Villeroy (ff. 149v–150, 154). Forget, writing in cipher under Mayenne’s clear letters, reviews the Castets bargain (“if there was a fault in the substance, there was more in the form”). He complains that the two commanders listen too readily to their own people. After Easter he reports the pay crisis: two musters owed, the captains’ complaints, and lenders who had promised money to be repaid in Paris backing away. Villeroy’s advice to raise money on exchange is answered on f. 154v. Clear copies of all three exist (ff. 155v–157r). Credit (f. 173). To the King, 1586, from the man Mayenne sent back to the town a second time to raise money. The town will not contribute, trusting the King’s letters that it is held to nothing for this army, and il ne s’est peu trouver un seul escu soubs [?les] obligations de Monsieur du Mayne . Only some merchants of Paris and elsewhere, with money to recover in Paris, would lend sur ma foy . The page ends in mid-sentence. Before Monségur, May 1586 (ff. 196, 201, 196v). One despatch survives twice, ff. 196r and 201r, fair copies of one enciphered draft, with different homophones and more of it in clear on f. 201. Mayenne has worked so hard at the siege qu’il y a gaigné un reume qui luy a causé la fièvre ; Marshal Matignon is pressed to come; Sainct-Chamarand is ill, la Barge and Montberault carry the siege, la Binault is dead. f. 196v, which was not among the transcriptions and was transcribed here, carries the despatch on: a battery of fifteen cannon to open the day after tomorrow, and the defenders resolved to hold pour ne recevoir la honte que le roi de Navarre a faict recevoir à celui qui commandoit dans Saincte Bazeille . Navarre is leaving for Saintonge to meet his reiters, Turenne holds the province from Nérac, and the army’s wants sont quasi arrivées à l’extremité . It is dated in clear Du camp devant Monségur ce […] jour de May 1586 .

Sentences, not tokens. George Lasry reviewed this page on 22 October 2026: the decryptions of the leaves without a copy could not be built into coherent French sentences, and he was right (5–24% of their sentences were clean). Each leaf was then taken sentence by sentence: where a sentence would not form, the figures were cropped from the full-resolution image (openapi.bnf.fr) and looked at, the label or the key value corrected, the leaf decoded again and the sentence rebuilt. The per-leaf result is in the table above. A leaf counts only when its sentences hold (0.66–0.79 clean, with the holes marked) and it has an English translation; ff. 123r and 124r do not reach that and are not counted. Label corrections. About 400 of Brackx’s figure labels were changed where the image disagrees, each listed with its line, the old and new label and the word it gives ( brackx2026/corrections/*.tsv ): f. 110 131 in three passes, the second against a set of exemplars cut from this hand; ff. 123r–v 138; ff. 124r–v 75; ff. 196/201 46; f. 173 14; f. 177 12; f. 143v 10. Two untranscribed lines were added (f. 123r l. 37, f. 143v l. 35). The letter values a hand needs beyond the merged key are kept per leaf ( key_cipher1_<leaf>.json ). The copies. Where a copy of the time exists, the key’s decode agrees with it on 85–93% of letters: f. 143r 0.93, f. 150r 0.85, f. 150v 0.90, f. 154r 0.89, f. 154v 0.89 and 0.93. With shuffled keys it is 0.25–0.38. Two more copies were found on 22 October 2026 and transcribed. fr. 15571 f. 176r–v is the clear copy of f. 177: compared word by word with the decipherment, it confirms 73 le Roy , 64 quelque and the null figures, and the cipher has one word ( dicte ) that the copy leaves out. The f. 143 copy does not stop at the foot of f. 155r: it runs on over seven lines of f. 155v, which agree with the decipherment of the last ten lines of f. 143v (the cipher has one word more, si ). The twin. ff. 196 and 201 carry the same figures at most positions: they are two fair copies of one enciphered draft. They were aligned figure by figure and deciphered together, and f. 201’s clear foot lines up with the first seven lines of f. 196v and gives 63 après . Shuffled keys. With the key’s letter sets permuted among its figures (set sizes kept, three seeds), the decode falls to 12.1% of tokens in runs of French, against 63.7% with the key. That token figure counted short corpus words strung together (“la que le estoit”) and is kept as evidence that the key is right, not as a measure of the decipherment. Leaves with no outside text (23 October 2026). ff. 173, 196v and 124v have no clear copy, no decipherment of the time and no print: each rests on the key, a figure transcription corrected by one reader, a few letter values for that leaf alone, and a reading chosen from the figures’ letter sets. Re-scored on the running text alone (an earlier sweep had counted line markers as holes), they hold 0.72, 0.885 and 0.667 of sentences with no more than one hole in ten words. Because the key gives many figures two to four letters, the readings were also aligned with their figures: they are carried on 96–97% of letters, against 45–49% for the same figures read as shuffled or unrelated French, and they use a second or third value of a set about as often as f. 143v does where the clear copy decides. They stay deciphered, with a lower confidence grade (B) than the leaves a copy checks. One reader. The label corrections and the sentence-by-sentence decipherments were made by one reader (Claude) on the images. No second reader has checked them yet.

ff. 123r and 124r, decoded, not read: 0.41 and 0.56 clean sentences after three passes each. The third pass re-cut the labels figure by figure and built an atlas of the hand’s 5,111 figures with classifiers across the leaves, and tried code values from the other leaves. The remaining breaks fall on legible figures of their ordinary shapes: they are the writer’s omissions or slips, and codes with no value. They need a clear copy or another letter in the same hand. Holes inside f. 110 (ll. 1–4, the corner of l. 1 being damaged, 8, 10, 14–16, 24–25, 36), where no single key change fixes the letters. Code numbers 16, 19, 23, 45, 47, 60, 65, 66, 67, 99, 101, 102, 103, 9 and the name code 98 have no value; each occurs one to three times and no copy covers them. 9 matches “Comme il” in one copy and “Mais s’il” in the other, so it is not one word. 103 falls where the f. 19 decipherment itself has an unreadable word. f. 20r, the end of the f. 18 despatch, now has its clear copy of the time: the end of f. 19v, posted as written by Michael Brackx (issue #87, 23 October 2026). It is taken as the reading of f. 20r, in part (86% of its words read as sense, the expansions of abbreviations counted as holes): two of the four regiment names are unread, and the day ( vj , the 6th) is doubtful. The copy has q[ue] ce fust honte at l. 5, which confirms code 14 = que ; there is no wording difference between copy and cipher. It tells of the remains of four regiments and Colonel Heid’s Swiss meeting again on the 6th of next month, and of letters of Turenne to the King of Navarre, intercepted, showing that Tulle was about to compound for four or five thousand écus. A second reader for the label corrections.

[I did so] in consideration of a promise he has made me not to bear arms for his party for six months, and of some particular service he has promised to do you in that time; and also because in truth he agreed to almost everything we wanted for the surrender of his place, which was still strong enough to hold us at this siege had they chosen to hold out obstinately a while longer. That would have cost a great deal of expense, and still more of time, which is very dear to us, because I would have had to cross the river to get there and then cross back to come here. For all these considerations, and for the first more than the others, I have verbally promised him ## f. 143v to have him paid the sum of twelve thousand écus within three months; to obtain for him Your Majesty's permission to enjoy his property, or permission to sell it; and moreover to intercede with Your Majesty to have him granted a pardon for all his past offences. I most humbly beg Your Majesty to confirm this, and to believe that I have settled none of it except subject to your good pleasure. Yet I would not have gone so far in this treaty had I not known that it was enough to come near(?) a great gain, with the risk of little loss(?). M.té de pouvoir jouir de son bien, ou avoir permission de le vendre, oultre d'intercéder envers Vostre Majesté pour luy faire accorder un pardon de toutes les faultes passées. That will be taken for pure folly by anyone who considers the times we live in, in which there may ## f. 154v befall such a mishap as would ruin me from top to bottom. But the fear of a still greater misfortune makes it count for less with me. I have been obliged to draw bills of exchange for all these sums on Monsieur Castille. I beg you, Monsieur, to give orders that they be paid, and I can assure you I would not have done it so readily but for what is in one of your despatches, where you tell us we should try to raise as much money on exchange as we can. Monsieur, it is no longer a matter of making predictions, but I cannot hide from you that unless this army is otherwise provided for, by the end of next month there will not be two thousand men left together. For they say openly that the army of Dauphiné is paid every month and that this one is the out-of-favour army, with talk so ugly that I cannot repeat it to you. And I can tell you that those held to be the wisest are, in this, almost less so than the others. f. 154v The same letter continued in two cipher blocks: Villeroy's advice to raise money on exchange, and the difficulty of doing it at Bordeaux. Cg.13 is the general cipher Devos dates 1587 and Tomokiyo found in use by Philip II, Parma and Mendoza in 1588–89; Viète broke it in France and Phelippes in England, and the copies in this volume are Phelippes’s file. Its letters are single figures or letters ( n = a, b = u, m and 9 = e, 1 = o, 7 = y, g = el), its syllables two-figure groups in rows of five in the order a e i o u (ta–tu 10–14, sa–su 20–24, na–nu 40–44, ra– 50–, va–vo 55–58, ma–mu 60–64, pa–pu 65–69, ca–cu 70–74, ga–gu 75–79, ha 80, la–lo 85–88), some rows reversed (bu–ba 95–99, fu–fa 90–94, du–de 36–39), with the qu-row at 45–49 so that 46 is simply que . Three marks after a group add a letter: a colon adds n (10: = tan, 73: = con, 9: = en), a point adds s (85. = las, 37. = dos, 7. = ys), a cross adds r (68+ = por, 56+ = ver); a stroke above inserts r after the consonant (30ʹ = dra) and a bar doubles an l . Words of the nomenclator are two- or three-letter groups ( na carta, yu cosa, quer Rey, quor Reyno, Zan para, he aviso), with the same marks for plural and changed endings ( na. cartas, he+ avisar, yenc otra).
