Dos papeles que se han escapado de [Inglaterra*] refieren que salieron de alli en compañia de Manuel de Andrada, [portugués*], que segun les dixo, pasados a [Francia*], y va a llevar dos cartas, una al Reyno de [Francia*] y otra al principe de Bearne; de [quien] entendieron juntamente que las copias desta carta vernian a parar a vuestras manos; y que Antonio de Goda, [portugués*], que es castellano y governador de un castillo y ysleta que esta a la boca del puerto de Premua, seria [fru] que quisiesse hazerme algun servicio con entregarme lo que tiene a su cargo si yo hiziesse alguna negociacion con el. Y pues el Manuel Andrada va con pensamiento de veros, ya avreys entendido el [tum] que esto puede tener, y a haver alguno para encaminar el negocio, que seria tan a proposito, no dudo que avreys procurado ponerlo en [cor], porque por todo buen respeto me ha parescido avisaros desta particularidad que se me ha dado, y encargaros que me aviseys si aveys entendido algo del [tum] que tuviere. Two papers smuggled out of England report that their writers left in company with Manuel de Andrada, a Portuguese (Dom António’s agent, Walsingham’s informant “David”), who said he had crossed to France carrying letters for the French court and for Navarre, and who expected copies of the present letter to reach Mendoza; and that a Portuguese castellan of an island fort at a harbour mouth might hand it over if the King dealt with him. Andrada means to see Mendoza; the King wants the matter followed and reported. Letter B (f. 12, copy f. 76). Receipt of Mendoza’s letters of 27 July, 2 and 8 August; the death of el Rey mi hermano (Henry III, 2 August) ha sido cosa de gran lastima ... por todos los respetos que se pueden considerar ; with France in such confusion Mendoza is to suspend the leave he has to quit the kingdom, porque siendo tan importante vuestra [gu] en el [bu] para el buen assiento de las cosas , and in no way absent himself without a new order, but attend to los negocios con el cuydado que soleys , steering towards el bien publico, que es solo el fin que yo tengo ; news of England is badly wanted, en lo que toca a sus [designios*] y lo que traman y traçan , since the route by which their fleet came home is known from prisoners; Mendoza is to keep his sources going and write often, y de creer es que entre ellos y el de Bearne se deven andar urdiendo malas cosas ... todo importa entenderlo, y en particular sus armaçones .

Decoded from the other letter. pur = respeto ( por todos los respetos que se pueden considerar ; the copyist of A wrote “puerto” for por todo buen respeto ). bor , which the copyist of A rendered “porque”, is not: Phelippes’s decipherment on f. 5 has dur for porque , and pero fits both letters. mes = vuestro (A: a vuestras manos ; B: glossed vro ). san = negocio: B has a la forma que el negocio pidiere and, where the copyist wrote “a lo necessario”, the cipher has a los with a plural mark before san ; in A it gives para encaminar el negocio, que seria tan a proposito . A miscopy. The copyist’s tur in A does not exist; the cipher has tum in both places ( el tum que esto puede tener ... algo del tum que tuviere ): one word, perhaps fundamento . Two wrong readings. The copyist wrote francia for dun in A and glossed tam as francia in the same letter; two groups cannot both be France. In B, dun is the power whose fleet came back by a route known from prisoners, whose plots run entre ellos y el de Bearne , and whose armaçones matter: England, in the summer the Drake–Norris expedition returned. So dun = Inglaterra* and tam = Francia*, which is where Andrada went and where Mendoza was. The copyist’s struck Inglaterra on f. 14 shows him weighing exactly this. And si se hiziesse alguna negociacion con el stands where the cipher has 18 = yo : the King wrote si yo hiziesse . From Phelippes’s own hand. His interlinear decipherment of Parma’s letter of 30 December 1588 (f. 5, same cipher) confirms the syllable values at every overlap and supplies bur persona, dom dicho, dur porque, pen mucho, mis V. M., and the x-row at 25–29. From Viète’s papers. fer , qualifying Manuel de Andrada and Antonio de Goda , is the group in the heading of a spy report copied in Cinq Cents de Colbert 33 (f. 113), Avisos que ha venido a dar David, traducidos de [fer] : Portugués*. Still open (contextual proposals only, asterisked in the key file): tum , fru , cor in A; hon (copyist: diligencia ; the sense wants licencia ), bor ( pero ?), gu , bu , com , ga ( armada ?), Jam , lo , bem , par in B; and a sixteen-group passage of B that the encipherer struck out and the copyist skipped.

Don Bernardino de Mendoça, del mi consejo y mi embaxador: vuestras cartas de 27 de jullio, 2 y 8 de agosto se han recivido estos dias, y no la de 30 de jullio que avisays en la de dos; y en tiempo de tanta confusion como por alla deve de haver, bien ha sido duplicar por muchas vias. La muerte del Rey mi hermano ha sido cosa de gran lastima, y assi me la ha causado a mi por todos los [?respetos] que se pueden considerar. Dios le perdone y ponga las manos en las cosas desse Reyno, dandoles el remedio que mas convenga a su servicio y al bien de la cristiandad. Estando todo lo de alla en la confusion que se halla, creo que con [?vuestro] buen zelo suspendierades el usar de la [?licencia] que teneys para salir desse Reyno antes no se os avisara de aca; porque siendo tan importante [?vuestra] [gu] en el [bu] para el buen assiento de las cosas, no puedo dexar de encargaros que en ninguna manera trateys de hazer ausencia de ay sin nueva orden mia, sino que atendays a lo necessario con el cuydado que soleys, y vays endereçando lo que mas conviniere al bien publico, que es solo el fin que yo tengo, y dandome aviso de todo para que se os avise lo que havreys de hazer. Gran falta ay por aca de avisos de [?Inglaterra] en lo que toca a sus [?designios] y lo que traman y traçan; que del camino con que bolvio su [?armada] y cosas destas bien se sabe por la lengua que han tomado algunos navios que a este [Jam] se embiaron, y por diversas particularidades. Procurad vos tener las [lo]s, y a menudo, de quanto passa por alla, y embialdo a la forma que el negocio pidiere; y de creer es que entre ellos y el de Bearne se deven andar urdiendo malas cosas en [bem] de la [par]. Todo importa entenderlo, y en particular sus armaçones. De San Lorenço a 7 de setiembre 1589. Yo el Rey. Don Martin de Idiaquez. Duplicada. Address: Por el Rey. A don Bernardino de Mendoça, del su consejo y su embaxador en Francia. Don Bernardino de Mendoza, of my council and my ambassador: your letters of 27 July and of 2 and 8 August have been received these days, but not that of 30 July which you mention in that of the second; and in a time of such confusion as there must be over there, it has been well to send duplicates by many ways. The death of the King my brother has been a thing of great pity, and so it has caused me [grief] for all the [?considerations] that may be weighed. God forgive him, and set His hands to the affairs of that kingdom, giving them the remedy most fitting for His service and the good of Christendom. All things over there being in the confusion in which they are, I believe that with [?your] good zeal you will have suspended using the [?licence] you have to leave that kingdom before you are informed from here; because, [?your] [gu] being so important in the [bu] for the good settlement of affairs, I cannot fail to charge you in no way to attempt to absent yourself from there without a new order from me, but to attend to what is necessary with your accustomed care, and to go on steering what is most fitting for the public good, which is the only end I have, and to give me notice of everything, so that you may be advised of what you are to do. There is a great want here of news from [?England] concerning their [?designs] and what they are plotting and scheming; for the route by which their [?armada] returned, and such things, are well known from the prisoners some ships have taken that were sent to this [Jam], and from various particulars. Do you take care to keep the [lo]s, and often, of all that passes over there, and send it in the form the business requires; and it is to be believed that between them and the man of Béarn evil things must be being woven in [bem] of the [par]. It all matters to understand, and in particular their armaments. From San Lorenzo, 7 September 1589. I the King. Don Martín de Idiáquez. Duplicate. Address: From the King. To Don Bernardino de Mendoza, of his council and his ambassador in France. Key: key_cg13_partial.tsv

A cryptogram printed in 1969 as a dispatch of Marshal Berthier to Napoleon, 22 December 1812, and listed as unsolved on Cryptiana, is a letter of King Joseph from Spain. Ilia Chirtulov found that the Great Cipher of 1812 reads it; Brice Dudout re-read it independently with the table of the Service historique de la Défense, whose cells he read on Jean-François Bouchaudy’s photographs: all 325 printed groups, 233 of 233 words, with a permutation control that none of 1,000 shuffled tables reaches. Joseph has no news of the Emperor and his last courier was seized near Valladolid; he encloses General Reille’s dispatch on the Army of the North. The plate ends mid-sentence. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 30 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) and Jean-François Bouchaudy (key or decipherment used) and Satoshi Tomokiyo (transcription) · Also credited · Ilia Chirtulov (earlier solution) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letter A dispatch to the Emperor, filed in the Archives nationales as a duplicate in Berthier’s cipher and printed as such in 1969. It is page 3 of a letter of King Joseph of Spain, written in Spain in December 1812. The cryptogram is a duplicate; only this page is published. Where Plate after p. 24 of J. Vilcoq, “Le Chiffre sous le Premier Empire”, Revue historique de l’Armée 1969 no. 4 (on Persée), captioned Archives nationales and dated 22 December 1812. The folder here is targets/napoleon/ ; it was catalogued as unsolved by S. Tomokiyo on Cryptiana. The cipher A numeric code of about 1,200 groups (2–1388): the Grand Chiffre of 1812, the code of the French armies in Spain, with several groups for frequent words. 325 groups are printed, 207 distinct, 132 of them used once. How it was read With the French deciphering table of the time (Service historique de la Défense, “B n° 30”), whose cells Brice Dudout read on Jean-François Bouchaudy’s photographs. French letter-sequence scores of the decode beat all 1,000 decodings with the table’s values shuffled. What it says Joseph has had no news of Napoleon since he left Paris, no returns of the Army of the North of Spain, and his last courier was seized near Valladolid. He sends the Emperor a dispatch of General Reille and begins to propose a remedy. Still open The rest of the letter: the plate ends in the middle of a sentence and the other pages are not published. In the 325 groups, five restorations from the sense and three probable readings. Credit Ilia Chirtulov was first to find the key and the writer (reported by S. Tomokiyo on Cryptiana, 12 October 2026). Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée ) then read it independently, working with Claude agents, and sent the reading in on 29 October 2026. The table is at the Service historique de la Défense; the photographs of it are Jean-François Bouchaudy’s.

Vilcoq printed one page of a ciphered dispatch in his 1969 article: three lines of archivist’s notes (“Duplicata”, “Chiffre du Prince de Neufchâtel”, “La Primata a été déchiffrée”), the salutation “Sire,”, then 22 lines of numbers. The caption calls it a letter of 22 December 1812 from Marshal Berthier, Prince of Neuchâtel, to the Emperor. On that basis the cryptogram was filed on Cryptiana among the unsolved. Page 3 of the dispatch: the archivist’s notes, the salutation and the first lines of the cipher, 918 1045 1100 493 359 … Image: J. Vilcoq, Revue historique de l’Armée 1969 no. 4, plate after p. 24 (Archives nationales), via Persée. The earlier attempt in this folder tried the opposite route. Berthier’s letters of December 1812 are printed in clear (Chuquet, 1912, from the same carton, AF/IV/1643), but the cryptogram has no frequency signal to match them with: 64% of its groups occur once against a book of about 1,200 entries, and the 325 printed groups do not align with Chuquet’s letter XXIII. That route stopped there and the result stood as not solved until the table was tried.

The Grand Chiffre of 1812 is the repertory of 1,200 numbers for letters, syllables and words that the French armies used, extended to 1,400 with additions for Spain (1211 the Army of the Centre, 1214 the English army, 1300 Lord Wellington, 1383 the Tagus). Frequent words have several numbers: here de is 13, 544, 710, 989 and 1060, que 69, 607 and 893. Words that are not in the book are spelled out in syllables (“depuis” is 544 de + 432 puis, “son” is 118 so + 718 n, “Paris” is 1135 pa + 1122 ri + 173 s). The group numbers run up to 1388, and 1202 (Valladolid), 1238 (the Army of the North of Spain) and 1388 (Salamanca) are Spanish additions: a first sign, before any sentence formed, that the table of Spain was the right one. A different cipher on this folder’s other item, a letter to Marshal Marmont in 1807, has no ciphertext published and no page.

Brice Dudout tried the ARCSI tables of Imperial great ciphers first: unrelated words. The Great Cipher of 1812 read from the first line: 918 je, 1045 n, 1100 ait, 493 aucun, 359 nouvelles. The 226 cells used were read from Jean-François Bouchaudy’s photographs of the SHD table and are in key_entries.tsv . The same table reads two letters of the French command in Spain in the sibling Jourdan and Marmont, 1812 , which has its own page. Control. A French 4-gram model trained on an independent text (Berthier’s December letters in Chuquet) scores the decode −2.11 per character. 1,000 decodings with the table’s numbers shuffled score −2.63 at the median and −2.43 at best: none reaches it. Tant’s tables score −2.72 to −2.82. The plate re-read. On Persée’s high-resolution image eight groups differ from the online transcription, and each correction makes its passage clear. This also settles the variant noted between the two Cryptiana pages: the plate reads 356, which the table gives as préjudice , while the sense requires 656, quel : a slip of the encoder or copyist. The sister letter. Joseph wrote to the Minister of War from Madrid on 23 December 1812 (Du Casse, Mémoires et correspondance du roi Joseph , IX): the same matter, the same phrases, Reille’s enclosed letter and “I knew well … but did not believe it so bad”. It is a confirmation of the content, not a word-for-word collation. Berthier was then with the remnants of the Grande Armée in East Prussia; the writer is Joseph, who wrote for the Emperor from Spain. Ilia Chirtulov found this first: his result reached S. Tomokiyo on 4 October 2026 and was reported on Cryptiana on 12 October. Brice Dudout’s reading was made independently of it.

The 22 lines read, with the elisions modernised (Brice Dudout’s running text): « Je n’ai aucunes nouvelles de Votre Majesté depuis son départ de Paris ; je n’ai aucune nouvelle directe de France depuis les lettres du Ministre de la Guerre du cinq octobre. Je n’ai jamais reçu ni compte ni rapport ni état de situation vraisemblable de l’armée du Nord de l’Espagne, quel[le]s qu’aient été mes demandes réitérées à cet égard. J’ai adressé à Votre Majesté impériale et au Ministre de la Guerre à Paris des quadruplicata de mes dépêches de Salamanque, mon dernier courrier ayant été enlevé avec toute la correspondance près de Valladolid. » “I have had no news from Your Majesty since your departure from Paris; I have had no direct news from France since the letters of the Minister of War of the fifth of October. I have never received any account, any report or any credible return of the state of the Army of the North of Spain, whatever my repeated requests. I have sent Your Imperial Majesty and the Minister of War in Paris quadruplicates of my dispatches from Salamanca, my last courier having been seized, with all the correspondence, near Valladolid.” The second paragraph, Reille’s dispatch, the concentration of forces and the “remedy” are in the full text below. It ends mid-sentence: “in the event that the war with Russia should continue and that Your Majesty…”. Nothing in the printed page names the king, and the writer is identified by the content, by the table of Spain and by the sister letter.

Count by the 95% rule, in words (elisions counted as two): 233 words, 225 certain, 3 probable, 5 restored from the sense, 0 unresolved. Probable: 559, table “Compagnie, s”, read com- ( compte ); 1086 sous ; 131 [q]ue . Restored: 851 ni and 1051 ité , both hidden by a fold of the table in both photographs; 356 read for 656, quel[le]s ; 495 table “car” where the word needs cen ( concentration ); 320 table “C” where exigéat needs t . 325 ( paix ) stands where a full stop (225) fits, probably a second slip. The rest of the letter. The cipher of the other pages is not published, and the Archives nationales original has not been consulted here. The letter is therefore read in the part that exists in print. The 1807 Marmont letter. No ciphertext is printed anywhere reachable; it has no page.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. King Joseph to Napoleon, Spain, December 1812 (the 325 printed groups, page 3 of the dispatch) King Joseph, with no news from the Emperor since he left Paris, reports that his last courier was seized near Valladolid, encloses General Reille's dispatch on the Army of the North and, shaken by it, begins to propose a remedy for the concentration of forces if the Russian war continues. The letter was filed as a duplicate in Berthier's name; its text breaks off at the end of page 3. Translation translation.md # Translation (English) "[Sire,] I have had no news from Your Majesty since your departure from Paris; I have had no direct news from France since the letters of the Minister of War of the fifth of October. I have never received any account, any report or any credible return of the state of the Army of the North of Spain, whatever my repeated requests in this regard. I have sent Your Imperial Majesty and the Minister of War in Paris quadruplicates of my dispatches from Salamanca, my last courier having been seized, with all the correspondence, near Valladolid. Your Majesty will find enclosed a copy of a dispatch from General Reille, which seemed to me worth placing before you. It is the first document of this kind that I have received; it enlightens me on the situation of the northern provinces; I know well that it was not good, but I did not believe it so deplorable, and I did not think that it would require sacrifices as great as the concentration in question. I nevertheless believe in the truth of Count Reille's report and in the uprightness of his intentions. I understand that a remedy must be found, and here is what I propose to Your Majesty in the event that the war with Russia should continue and that Your Majesty..." (End of page 3; the rest of the letter has not been published.) Key: key_entries.tsv

The one letter of Mary’s 1570 cipher correspondence with the imprisoned Duke of Norfolk that has no contemporary decipherment (BL Cotton Caligula C II f. 74r). Satoshi Tomokiyo’s key for the series, a simple substitution with word and name signs, was applied to a new transcription of all 23 lines; five signs and a few words stay open. Written after the Regent Moray’s murder, for which Elizabeth blames Mary. The cipher Mary’s private cipher to Norfolk, with nomenclator signs. How it was read Satoshi Tomokiyo rebuilt the key from the three deciphered siblings and decoded about the first half. Here the whole letter was transcribed and decrypted with his key, on new images from the British Library’s IIIF service. No key was recovered here. What it says Mary tells Norfolk to write to the B[ishop of Ross] of your part and thanks God for delyvring us of our [enemy] Murray . She ends yours feithful til death . Still open Five nomenclator signs have no value in the key. Two groups in line 1, the end of line 4 under a stain and a few single words are unread. Credit Much of the letter-level decoding is Tomokiyo’s; new here are the transcription, the continuous decipherment, the fill of his gaps, the names and the date.

Cotton MS Caligula C II is a volume of Scottish state papers from Burghley’s circle. Folios 66 to 75 hold Mary’s ciphered letters to Norfolk that were intercepted or surrendered, with deciphered copies. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana page on Mary’s ciphers ( mary.htm ) lists them this way: Folio Date on the letter Decipherment In print f. 66r “last of Januarie” [31 Jan 1570] transcription f. 67, decipherment f. 72 Labanoff iii p. 19 f. 69 “the xv of this instant” [15 Jan 1570] f. 70 Labanoff iii p. 11 f. 74r “the tventi of this instant” none none found f. 75 [18 Apr 1570] clear text f. 73, roughly corresponding Labanoff iii p. 35 Tomokiyo lists f. 74 as having no contemporary decipherment; he does not list it among open ciphers. He found no matching letter in Labanoff’s Lettres de Marie Stuart , vol. 3, or in Froude, and took the address my oun good lord as a sign that it too is from Mary to Norfolk. He then reconstructed the key from the deciphered letters (“Mary-Norfolk Cipher (1570)”, corrected 16 July 2023). With it he printed the first two lines as a paraphrase, “I have, my own good lord, your friendly [letter??] [with??] no [g?]entle satisfaction and for * I will never [do??] anything in hand …”, and left two further pieces of work that are not on the visible page. One is an HTML comment in the page source: a continuous transcript as far as about line 11 ( … in? deliveri[n]g us of our * the Queen of England … ). The other is an image, mary_CottonCaligulaCII_f74.png , with his decode written in magenta over each of the 23 lines, letter by letter. Unkeyed signs are shown as asterisks, doubtful letters as queries, and words are not divided. That overlay is the starting point, and it has to be credited. For most lines it already has the letters, including murton is gon to , Talbo and herkebus . This page adds the decipherment as continuous text. The letters are divided into words and made into sentences, and many of his asterisks and queries are filled. Line 8, which the comment leaves out when it runs and I shall be your sister scrup from the end of line 7 into line 9, is restored. The names are identified and the letter is dated. The verso, f. 74v, has no address. It carries only a short note written upside down relative to the text, with a mark above it; the note says Norffolke (or Northfolke ).

The British Library’s new viewer publishes the volume as a IIIF manifest ( bl.digirati.io/iiif/ark:/81055/vdc_100162985756.0x000001 , reached from the Search Archives record for Caligula C II). The image service claims IIIF level 2 but will not return an image more than about 1,024 pixels on a side. The full leaf is 7,144 × 10,328 pixels, so fetch.py and region.py ask for 1,024-pixel tiles and paste them back together. The text block of f. 74r is the region from x 1000 to 6500 and y 4900 to 9800, at full resolution. strips.py finds the centre of each line in five vertical bands from the ink profile and cuts 23 strips that follow the slope of each line, so a line can be examined at magnification from end to end. F. 74r, left half of lines 1–5: I have, my oun good lord, … / I will never take anithing in hand … / -ept I var sur it var to your veil … . The letters are separate signs written continuously. Word signs (the barred forms, the boxed cross ⊞ for for ) stand among them without spaces. Image: British Library, Cotton MS Caligula C II f. 74r, via the BL IIIF service (stitched from tiles).

The cipher is a simple substitution of one sign for each letter, with no homophones except f . Nulls are scattered through the text, even inside words. About twenty word signs and a handful of name signs complete it. This is Tomokiyo’s reconstruction. Before it was applied to f. 74, it was checked against f. 66r, whose contemporary transcription and decipherment survive (ff. 67, 72). The opening of f. 66r, My oun lord, I vret to you befor to knou your pleasur if I schould sik to mak an entrepryse , decrypts correctly with it. The control, f. 66r, lines 1–3: the letter of the last of January 1570, whose decipherment (f. 72) is printed by Labanoff. The same signs and word signs as f. 74r. English The English of the same partial reading ( texts/f74r_en.md ), with the same marks. I have, my own good lord, {3̲2} your friendly {ꝗ} {ʃ̊} no [?gentle] satisfaction; and therefore I will never take anything in hand {⊕} some very good may come of it to me, anything except I were sure it were for your weal as for mine; and if I might be so for us both, I would be sure all should not be in danger. For I have experience {⊔} that [?favour] that my own f[…]s […] but not, my own lord, that your {a—} and my [?friends] would not believe so to [?use] a way can in nothing content the Queen of England. I find that the cardinal is with [us], that is well minded to help me; {∨} for find means that our cause demean not for fault of solicitation: write to the [?b.] on your part, and I shall be the next to the […] friends; would also, as I can, persuade {⊘} to haste {o°} find means, by your sister Scrope or another, to cause {rʒ} know your mind, for I have no means that he may be sure of forces and have all friends in hand. {blot} I trust God he [?will] help us, as he began […] already in delivering us of our {o—} [?Murray]. The Queen of England has spoken […] courteously to the Bishop of Ross of you […] showed; and if I would cause her friend to be shot with a harquebus-shot, it would not hurt me, God be judge between us. I am assured that she [?gives] me the blame of Murray's death {ø}; but God knows if […] her mind would […], at least you know the truth of this. God will, I trust, prosper us both, the better that we […] {Ш—} […]les. The rumour is that Morton is gone to […]; but not for truth I write [?one] this: tonight Lord Talbot {∂} [told] me, not for truth, it comes from York. […] I will end, and pray you not to constrain yourself or hazard yourself to write yourself, but cause {⊗}, but write to any other in your name, [so long as] you are well; and remember your own. I desire no more, for if I hear nothing, I fear ever that some tales make you offended at me. I shall, God willing, never make cause, but since the last […] I am ever in doubt of the like. I pray him to preserve you from feigned friends, and send us more comfort; an[d] [?yet] we have had in this meantime, in weal or woe, I shall ever remain yours faithful till death. {Mary}. The twentieth of this instant. The names. The B. of Ross is John Leslie, bishop of Ross, Mary’s ambassador in London. Your sister Scrup is Norfolk’s sister Margaret Howard, wife of Henry, Lord Scrope of Bolton, who had been Mary’s keeper at Bolton in 1568. Murray is James Stewart, Earl of Moray, Regent of Scotland, and Murton is James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton, the leading man of the King’s party after him. Lord Talbot is the courtesy title of the Earl of Shrewsbury’s eldest son, and Shrewsbury was Mary’s keeper. The cardinal is not named; her uncle Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine, is the obvious candidate but the leaf does not say so. Veyt is Scots wyte , blame, and brut is bruit , a rumour. In for and I hear nothing , and means if . The re-reading of 23 October 2026 found that the sign before of your pert is a single φ, not the key’s sign for the Bishop of Ross, so the first mention is [?b.] ; the Bishop is named by his title only in the B. of Ross of you .

The letter gives only the day, the tventi of this instant , without a month or place. The content fixes it closely enough: After Moray’s murder. The Regent was shot with a harquebus at Linlithgow on 23 January 1570 by James Hamilton of Bothwellhaugh and died the same night. The letter trusts God for delyvring us of our {o—} [?Murray] , speaks of Murray death , and has Elizabeth talking of whether I would caus schut her friend a harkebus-schut . So the 20th is not 20 January. Elizabeth already knows, and blames Mary. Labanoff’s chronology puts Elizabeth’s receipt of the news, and her placing of the Bishop of Ross in the Bishop of London’s custody, on 10 February. Norfolk in the Tower. He was there from October 1569 to August 1570, which fits the warnings about writing and the talk of forces and meanes . Mary’s letters of January to April 1570 printed by Labanoff are dated from Tutbury. That leaves 20 February or 20 March 1570. One point leans towards February without settling it. Labanoff prints (iii, pp. 31–33) a decipherment of Mary to Norfolk dated the 19th of march which opens I have forborn this long time to write to you, in respect of the dangers of writing and grieves for Pembroke, who died on 17 March. A letter written the next day that says nothing of Pembroke would be odd. So would one written a day after she said she had not written for a long time. F. 74 says neither.

Thirteen unkeyed signs, each once. ⊕ (l. 2), ⊔ (l. 4), ∨ (l. 6), ⊘ and o° (l. 8), rʒ (l. 9), ø (l. 13), ⊗ (l. 17), ∂ after Lord Talbot (l. 16), three in line 1, and a family of letter signs with a long tail-dash ({a—} l. 5, {o—} l. 11, {Ш—} l. 15) that looks like a class of word signs. Our {o—} Murray would fit enemy by sense only; no value was adopted. Folios 66, 69 and 75, in the same cipher, have not yet been searched for them. Open spots. The opening sentence, the experiance sentence (l. 4, under a stain), lines 10–11 and line 15 do not build. Legible runs in lines 11 (after spokn ), 15 (after ve ), 17 and 20 are transcribed but not resolved ( texts/f74r_signs.tsv ). Demen in line 7 is what the signs carry, but its sense is not secure. Print. The Calendar of State Papers, Scotland, vol. iii (Boyd, 1903) was searched on 23 October 2026: it calendars the sibling letters but not f. 74. Word division and sense. The signs run on without spaces and nulls stand inside words, so the division into words is an editorial choice. In lines 5–6 and 9–10 the sentences are construed as closely as the words allow, and the paraphrase is one interpretation of them. The month. February or March 1570, as set out above. Nothing on the leaf decides between them. The hand. Tomokiyo remarks that the hand of the Norfolk ciphers looks like Mary’s own but differs in the h and in spelling from her autograph letters, and suggests comparing it with her secretary Raulet’s. That was not attempted here.

Mary Queen of Scots to Norfolk, 'the 20th' [Feb or Mar 1570], BL Cotton MS Caligula C II f. 74r decoded, not read Written after Moray's murder at Linlithgow (23 Jan 1570): Mary tells Norfolk she will undertake nothing unless it is safe for them both, urges him to write and to act through his sister Scrope or others, says Elizabeth gives her the blame ('veyt') for Moray's death, reports rumours of Morton and Lord Talbot, and begs him not to risk writing in his own hand. BnF fr. 3982 is one of the Mémoires de la Ligue volumes (fr. 3974–3995), which gather League correspondence, much of it ciphered, from the 1580s and 1590s. No. 22 runs from f. 46r to f. 50r with the address on f. 50v: nine close-written pages, about fifty lines each, dated “A Burgos le xiij septembre 1592”, signed “Vre bien humble et obeissant serviteur Pelissier”, and marked Tripta (the third copy sent). Clear French and cipher alternate within the same lines, and the cipher is written with a small repertory of letter-like signs, figures and marks. f. 46r: “Monsieur J’entreprins mon voyage de la court si a contre temps que arrivant a Valladolid ou le Roy avoit sejourné deulx moys…”, and then the first cipher. The small writing between the cipher rows is the contemporary decipherer’s. His glosses are few and scattered, and they are the letter’s whole “partial decipherment”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3982 f. 46r, via Gallica (btv1b9060543f, canvas 100).

Tomokiyo’s League page reconstructs the cipher Pelissier used in nos. 45 and 46 (Madrid, 27 October 1592) from their clean decipherment on f. 115. It is a homophonic alphabet with one to seven signs per letter. Some signs are two-digit numbers (24, 26, 28, 30, 33, 36, 44, 56, 60, 80). There is a sign for et , signs for the doubled letters rr , ss and uu , and six nulls. His table is not reproduced here; it is on his page. No. 22 is six weeks older and on the same key, with two additions: Code group 315 is the Béarnais , Henri IV: “le [315] ayant incontinant tourné la teste et s’estant campé pres l’armée catholique”, “les forces d’Allemaigne … iointes au [315]”. It occurs on four of the nine pages. Code group 310 occurs once, on f. 50r: “ne correspondront pas a ce que pretend [310], et l’ambassadeur … a esté renvoyé sans aultre esclaircissement sur ses demandes”, next to a passage on the governor of Milan. A claimant with an ambassador at Philip’s court and a Milanese connection is most likely the Duke of Savoy , Philip’s son-in-law, who had his own pretensions in France; the Duke of Lorraine is the alternative. Context only. Code group 441 occurs once, on f. 49v: “non seulement en [441] mais en toutes aultres regions de la Chrestienté”, which asks for France . Context only. The decipherer’s glosses check the key wherever they are legible. They agree on de , auisa , meschans , roy , les tirer , Noyon , a la main qu , n’auoit , en atendant , quar la bataille , mais le retour , de crainte , langaiges , Valentia , a gens matez des and (qu’ay)ant pleu a Dieu , among others. One gloss disagrees in an instructive way. Over “nos forces” the glosser wrote os a orc : he applied the table’s ϝ = a literally where the sense needs f . The hand that deciphered this letter in 1592 was working from the same table, and it slipped on the same sign. Calibration. Tomokiyo’s table gives each sign a letter; it does not say how to tell apart signs that look alike on a fast page, and that is where the first decryption stalled. The two letters he built the key from were therefore aligned with their clear text on f. 115, sign by sign: 835 signs of no. 45 (f. 111r) and 929 of no. 46 (ff. 113r–v). That settles the look-alikes with known plaintext: 4 : the plain closed 4 is n (and often m ), never t ; t is the 4 with a hooked lead-in off the crossbar, or with a curl. The first transcription had written both as 4, and a decode that let every sign take any letter wanted that 4 to be t 355 times. ⊤ : flat-topped is a ; with a hooked top and a descender, p ; with a tail, s . The lone hooked τ is g . δ : with a straight ascender o ; curling over into a long hook, c ; with a big open loop over a closed bowl, r . 56 : compact, y ; with the long hooked 5 and the 6 set high, c . 8 : plain, n ; crossed at the waist, q . + is h and ∐ is l , never e ; π is i , never s (the tailed ϖ is s ); the barred ӿ is u and the large plain ✗ a null; 7 is b , or h . The October letters and no. 22 were written by the same hand six weeks apart, and the page transcribers found a few further habits in no. 22 alone: an alpha-shaped sign and a barred 5 for g , a small box-shaped ∐ for e , the tall double long-s for rr , and a looped ℓ that stands for u or e by context. The whole guide, with exemplar crops of every form, is targets/pelissier1592/GLYPHS.md and cal/atlas/ . f. 46v. Clear text (“a l’arrivee du Roy en ce dict lieu de Burgos Je retornay treuver le seigneur Don Joan, lequel m’ayant donné une heure particulliere”) runs straight into cipher. The cipher opens “i’exposay pour fondement de mon discours qu’il n’est rien plus requis en un estat que la conservation de la reputation”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3982 f. 46v, via Gallica (btv1b9060543f, canvas 101).

Deciphered words are quoted as written, with the letter’s spelling. The page summaries below are in English. The full text, page by page, with gaps marked, is in targets/pelissier1592/READING.md . f. 46r. Pelissier reached Valladolid just as the court was leaving, and Don Juan de Idiáquez put business off to Palencia. In cipher, he says his credit is gone, “le credit m’est[oit] failly pour n’avoir satisfaict au payement des sommes qui m’ont esté prestées a Madrid”. He takes the King’s long silence for a refusal and asks leave to go home. He is told Philip has his own ministers in France. Philip’s answer to the rest is “yo lo creo”. Then comes the grant: “elle m’avoit ordonné cinq cens ducats, qui valent environ quatre cens cinquante escus, ou plus”, payable in Madrid, “ou je me pouvois retirer avec les ambassadeurs et aultres estans par deça de la part de princes estrangiers”, so that he can wait for news. f. 46v. At Burgos, Don Juan gives him a private hour. Pelissier’s theme is reputation, and his example is Parma’s army of 1592. While it flourished, “la plus part de la noblesse catholique qui suit ce party se retira chacun en sa maison” and towns began to treat. If it had wintered in France, the Béarnais would have been brought to “une ruine tres certaine”, and the Germans “n’eussent eu l’audace de sortir de leur pays pour l’assister”. Its return to the Low Countries undid everything: League towns afraid of being exposed if the enemy returned began their own dealings, and La Fère, Soissons and the places of Picardy, perhaps Corbie “pres d’Amiens” (a doubtful reading), were left in danger. ff. 47r–47v. The French “aymeroient mieux mourir touts l’un après l’aultre” than be forced, as the rising against “le dernier Roy” showed; mildness and benefits would win them to anything. The King asks whether Pelissier speaks on Mayenne’s orders. He has had no word since the armies faced each other at Caudebec. The Spanish answer is that no king had ever given such help, and any failure lay with those who received it. Pelissier’s reasons for putting off the Estates are taken for a trick. The minister recalls that Mayenne, in the time of the Cardinal de Bourbon, had pressed for everything else to be set aside for the Cardinal’s “deliurance”, and Pelissier is heard to say it would be “necessaire que l’on mist sus deux armées”. Yet the minister concedes that the League’s French would take it very badly if Spain delayed “la nomination d’un roy legitime pour l’opposer a l’heretique et tyran”. Of the Spanish ministers, Pelissier writes: “ilz ont les oreilles delicates”. f. 48r. He calls for a “troisiesme moyen”. This is the wrong time to hold the Estates: the people are exhausted, the clergy intimidated, and the nobility held only by its interests, and they would sooner accept “un accord qui creera un Roy pour l’opposer a celuy qui se pretend”. He foresees a war that may end only “par l’extermination de la race de l’un desditz deux Roys”. His remedy is the plan already put to Philip “de tenir deux armees en pied”. One army would drive the enemy from the Seine to the Loire. The other would take the Seine towns and free Paris and Rouen. He answers the cost, “pres de trois cens mil escus par mois”, by saying the effort need last only a few months. A war left to drag on would be “si sanglante” that, driven to despair, it would spare neither age nor sex: “ne pardonnant a aage ni sexe”. f. 48v. The army should be mostly French, “tant a pied qu’a cheval”, stiffened by “un corps de sept ou huit mil Alemans” and some Spaniards and Walloons “assistés de bons capitaines”. A victory would ruin the enemy. After a defeat, an army of Philip’s own nations “seroit preste pour recueillir les reliques de ceste deffaicte”. Piecemeal aid only ruins the provinces. And if Philip showed “quelque affection particuliere en la nomination du roy”, everyone would follow. f. 49r. The campaigns of 1591–92: Chartres, Noyon, the Prince of Ascoli’s relief, Caudebec, Henri’s daily offer of battle, and the retreat towards Château-Thierry. The clear text blames Parma for letting chances go by, which gave the enemy room to spread the rumour that Philip fights only to keep the French busy while he subdues his Low Countries rebels. f. 49v. What Frenchmen were saying: that Philip wanted France kept “en telle balance” so that he could take his share of a divided crown. Then the case for Navarre. God called him “comme par miracle a la succession”. He has lived “en perpetuelle peine et travail, pauvre et miserable”, and so he will want peace. If he turned on the Catholics, they would be “libres du serment de fidelite”. Such talk works on “gens matez des maux soufferts et plains de desespoir de mieux”. Philip alone can cure the malady, and would add to “Catholique” the names “tres chrestien” and “liberateur de la Chrestienté”. f. 50r. “Ilz vont minant l’authorité” of Mayenne: finances first, then command, then credit: “ilz luy diminuent le credit … l’abaisser le plus qu’ilz pourront. Dieu veulle que je me trompe”. Whatever [310] pretends to, its ambassador has been sent home without an answer, and Pelissier pleads for a union among the League so close that an offence to one would be felt by all. In clear, Pelissier stays “pour essayer de tirer une derniere resolution sur la partie de cinquante mil escutz”. A postscript describes a visitor sent to Palencia, whom the King received well enough to send him horses for his audiences.

Transcription by sign. Each page was cut into third-width bands at 1.5× from the full-resolution Gallica scan. Every sign was written as a token (a name for its shape) and every clear passage in full. Seven parallel agents did ff. 47r–50r; ff. 46r–46v were done here and served as the worked example. Decoding with the key. Each token carries the letter the key gives it, plus alternatives where two signs look alike. A 4-gram language model of period French chooses among the alternatives and supplies the word breaks. No solver changed the key. Second pass. For every row that did not decode to French, the signs were transcribed again at 2.5× and genuine misreadings were corrected on every page. A change was made only when the sign was visibly different on the leaf, never just because French would then appear. Each page’s decryption file lists the glosses and whether they agree. Calibration and third pass. The key’s own source letters were aligned with their clear text (section 02), the look-alike families were split into separate tokens, and every row of all nine pages was transcribed again against the scans with them. Open words fell from 413 to 256 and doubtful ones from 278 to 158. A failed approach. Twice, once per page and once over the whole letter, a solver (hill-climbing) adjusted the sign-to-letter map against the language model, starting from the key. Both times it drifted to a degenerate map in which every frequent sign is e , which a noisy transcription always rewards. The key was right. The errors were in the tokens, which had merged signs the key keeps apart: 56 with a flourish is c , and plain 56 is y . The plain δ is o , the δ with a long curling hook is c , and the closed-loop ∂ with a curled top is r . The flat-topped ⊤ is a , the hooked τ is p , and the small curled “Tz” is g . Among the barred I forms, the plain one is l , the bold-footed one is o , and the double-barred one is o as well (Ƒ). vv is et , and also ff . ϝ is a in the table and f in dozens of words. The calibration in section 02 corrects this: most of these splits are now tokens in their own right, confirmed on known plaintext.

Re-measured 5 October 2026. A fourth pass (5 October 2026, PASS4.md ) re-cropped and re-read every gap on all nine pages: 256 → 183 gaps. Counting doubtful words as unread, 90.9% of plaintext words give sense; counting them, 95.3%. The 183 left are legible signs that do not decode under the key, blots and empty-sign gaps. The recurring name groups z 6 z , z 6 1 , z 5 8 were tested at every occurrence; no single value is forced. Re-measured 24 October 2026. On the written-out reading ( READING.md ), with every marked gap and doubtful word as a hole, 92.2% of the words read: the letter builds coherent sentences, but under the 95% a complete reading needs. 256 words open , marked [?] , against 3,734 decrypted inside the ciphered stretches (94 %), and 158 more decrypted but doubtful, marked (?) . Every page’s decryption file lists its open rows with their tokens. They are single signs the eye cannot settle, a hole in f. 50r, and names. Nothing is supplied by conjecture. Grades. The key is H (in print, and confirmed on 1,764 signs of known plaintext and by the glosses). The decryption of the firm stretches is H; the (?) words are C. 315 = the Béarnais is H (it recurs, and “appeler [315] comme par miracle a la succession” fixes it); 310 = Savoy and 441 = France are M, one occurrence each; Corbie and Amiens on f. 46v are I. Names. The Dominican confessor on f. 50r decrypts to c-o-r-n-e | n-t-(u/e) across a line break, “Cornente” or “Cornete” if a heavily inked 4 is cancelled; not identified. A “don …” beside the governor of Milan, the visitor of the postscript, and a place in the 1592 campaign (f. 49r) are open. Everything is in the repository under targets/pelissier1592/ : the account in NOTES.md , the reading in READING.md and reading_46r.md … reading_50r.md , the token transcriptions t46r.txt … t50r.txt , the decoder beam.py with cands.txt , the sign vocabulary in TOKENS.md , the calibrated guide in GLYPHS.md , and the alignments of nos. 45 and 46 with their exemplar crops in cal/ .

DECODE R8565, catalogued as a letter of Francis Poyntz to an unknown recipient, is the second part of the three ambassadors’ despatch to Wolsey from Valladolid, 17 July 1527. Its short passages in the Lee–Worcester cipher were deciphered on arrival by Brian Tuke, and the decipherment is printed in Letters and Papers IV no. 3271. The letter was identified and the catalogue corrected. Valladolid → Cardinal Wolsey · Lee–Worcester cipher of graphic symbols, English · 17 July 1527 Ghinucci, Lee and Poyntz to Wolsey, Valladolid, 17 July 1527 to Cardinal Wolsey Go to the full text ↓ British Library, Cotton MS Vespasian C IV ff. 174–177; DECODE R8565. The catalogue listed a ciphered letter of “Fran. Poynts” to an unknown recipient, content unknown. It is the second part of the three English ambassadors’ report to Wolsey on their audiences with Charles V. Its few cipher passages were deciphered on arrival in 1527, by Brian Tuke, and his decipherment is printed in Letters and Papers IV no. 3271. Nothing was left to decipher; the work was identifying the letter from the calendar and correcting the catalogue. The five cipher passages and their contemporary decipherment were transcribed on 23 October 2026 from the full-resolution images (texts/R8565_reading.md) and checked against the signs with Tomokiyo’s key. The cipher The Lee–Worcester cipher of 1526–1529: graphic symbols for letters plus a small nomenclator. DECODE R8565 has eight images, 7 pages of text, status “Partially decrypted”, with inline cleartext and inline plaintext both marked “Yes”. The key linked to it is “Lee–Worcester Cipher (1526–1529)”. The public thumbnails (200 pixels wide) show: seven written pages under the Cotton running head “Hispania 1527”, mostly English in clear; about five short bands in which a line of cipher carries a line of decipherment above it (images 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7), which is DECODE’s “Partially decrypted” and “inline plaintext”; three signatures at the foot of image 7, as expected for Ghinucci, Lee and Poyntz; image 8, the address leaf with its endorsement. So the catalogue entry is wrong on two counts. The letter is not from Poyntz alone but from all three ambassadors, and the recipient is Wolsey.

The calendar prints the deciphered passages in italics. For this part of no. 3271 they are the following. The words are the calendar’s summary of Tuke’s decipherment, not the letter’s own spelling, except where the calendar quotes. … Perceive the French would not have brought him to show any demands. He professes willingness to do everything for the King , and we avoid giving him any token but that the King and your Grace are still wholly his . … Buclans asked if they restored Sforza, what security they should have that he would not give up the duchy to France, and suggested that the Emperor might give it along with the daughter of Portugal to the duke of Richmond . De Tarbes has now shown us the fourth instruction. Perceive well why he withheld it; for he is to say to the Emperor, before the English ambassadors, that they desire his amity more than that of any other prince . 17 July 1527. Signed. So the ambassadors kept three things out of reach of anyone who opened the packet. First, they were privately reassuring Charles that Henry and Wolsey were still “wholly his”, while they mediated alongside the French. Second, the Emperor’s side had floated a marriage: Milan and Maria, daughter of Manuel I of Portugal (the Emperor’s niece), for Henry Fitzroy, duke of Richmond, Henry’s illegitimate son. Third, the French envoy had been told to court Charles in front of the English. The companion letter no. 3272, from the same three men and “chiefly cipher, deciphered by Tuke”, continues in the same vein. It reports an intercepted despatch from Charles’s ambassador in France: De Tarbes could offer the Viceroy’s conditions undiminished; Lautrec had authority to conclude in Italy; Wolsey had pressed Francis to marry the Princess Mary. It also names a portion of 400,000 ducats for the Portuguese match.

This is the cipher Lee and Ghinucci used with Wolsey from 1526 to 1529: graphic symbols for letters, with further symbols for words and names (a small nomenclator). Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed it, and his table is attached on DECODE to R8566. It has already been checked against the interlinear decipherments of two sibling records. On R8566, the symbols under “possibilite” and “good” decrypt to p-o-ss-i-b-i-l-i-t-e and g-o-o-d. On R8567, the run under “can not” decrypts to c-a-n-n-o. On 23 October 2026 the key was applied to R8565 as a check: each of the five cipher passages was compared with its decipherment on the full-resolution images and every checked word agrees (sign 5 = “not” in two places is not in the table). R8565, f. 177r, the last cipher passage of the despatch: each line of Lee–Worcester signs has the contemporary decipherment written above it, that De Tarbes has now shown them the fourth instruction, which he is to use before the English ambassadors: that they desire the Emperor’s amity more than that of any other prince. That the King's Highness [and] your Grace are as wholly his as you ever have been. [?Whereas] he [?fears] that the French king will not be brought to reason, it shall therefore be as meritorious as it is an honourable and high deed to win them to peace and amity; and if the King's Highness and your Grace do not do it, we think it would be long before it were done. What surety shall we have that he will not render the duchy into the French king's hands? We cannot doubt but that he will. And therefore it is better that the Emperor bestow it on one of his friends, who knows none so great as the King's Grace; and therefore [?if he would give] the daughter of Portugal to the Duke of Richmond, and the duchy of Milan with her, what do you say, [?how] does this please you? Those things were better given to one of his friends than to this man, who is in no way fit for it. De Tarbes has now shown us the fourth instruction. He kept it from us because it [?is] a device that he shall say to the Emperor, when the ambassadors of England are by, that they desire his amity more than that of any other prince.

Uppsala UB C 513 (DECODE R4349) has a dating colophon in which every vowel is written as the next letter; the Uppsala catalogue printed the rule and the decipherment in 1992, and the colophon was transcribed and decoded to the same text. The six signs closing an Old Swedish note pasted on f. 1r, DECODE’s “six symbols”, are too few to decipher. Annp dpmknk mkllfskmp qxkngfntfskmp → Anno domini millesimo quingentesimo · a→b e→f i→k o→p u→x Strängnäs → Västerås · vowel shift and six signs · 1517 Two ciphers in the Strängnäs sequentiary of 1517: a dated colophon and a six-sign signature Go to the full text ↓ Uppsala University Library, C 513, f. 19v: a paper book of sequences with square notation, written for the Dominicans of Västerås. DECODE catalogues it as R4349, a ciphered letter from Strängnäs with “six symbols”, sender and recipient unknown. The book holds two ciphers. On f. 19v the scribe dated it in a colophon in which each vowel is replaced by the letter after it. The Uppsala catalogue printed the rule and the decipherment in 1992; here the colophon was transcribed and decoded with that rule, and the result matches the print word for word. On a slip pasted on f. 1r, a short Old Swedish note to one Anders Larsson closes with six signs. That is the note DECODE describes, and six signs are too few to decipher. Where Uppsala University Library, C 513; DECODE R4349 (catalogue entry 235), which has one placeholder image and a note about “a short ciphertext of six symbols”. The cipher In the colophon every vowel is written as the next letter of the alphabet (a→b, e→f, i→k, o→p, u→x); consonants stand for themselves. How it was read The rule and decipherment come from the 1992 catalogue of the Uppsala C collection. The folio was found in the Alvin scans, transcribed letter by letter (125 letters) and decoded word for word. What it says The book was written in 1517 in the Strängnäs convent for the convent of Västerås. The slip is an Old Swedish note sending herbs and cinnamon bark to Anders Larsson. Still open The six signs ending the f. 1r note are not deciphered: the colophon rule does not fit them and six signs cannot fix a key. 125 of 131 cipher tokens are decoded. Credit Andersson-Schmitt, Hallberg and Hedlund (1992) gave the rule and the decipherment.

Uppsala UB C 513, f. 19v: the ciphered colophon under its staves. The red-stroked initial A is the only plain vowel. Image: Uppsala University Library, C 513 f. 19v, via Alvin (public domain). C 513 is a sequentiary of 84 paper leaves in one early-16th-century cursive hand. The owner’s entry on the front pastedown reads Liber conuentus insulensis ordinis predicatorum . f. 19v closes the sequence Benedicta sit celorum regina with “…in celesti patria Amen”. The scribe then carried on in the same hand, on four more text lines under notation, in what looks like a garbled language. A red catchword Corda manibus , the incipit of the next sequence, closes the page. Annp dpmknk mkllfskmp qxkngfntfsk- mp dfckmp sfptkmp prfsfns lkbfr sf- qxfnckpnbrkxs fst scrkptxs kn cpnxfntx strfngfnfnsk prp cpnxfntx knsxlfnsk The rule is the old scribal trick of writing each vowel as the next letter of the alphabet (i and j, u and v counting as one letter each): plain a e i o u written b f k p x Consonants stand for themselves, and word division and doubled letters are kept. The rubricated capital A of Anno is left plain. Because b and p are also ordinary consonants of the text, the written b in lkbfr is a real b ( liber ) and the written p in scrkptxs , prfsfns and prp is a real p ( scriptus, presens, pro ). Everywhere else they stand for a and o. Context always decides, and no word stays ambiguous.

Anno domini millesimo quingentesimo decimo septimo presens liber sequencionarius est scriptus in conuentu strengenensi pro conuentu insulensi. “In the year of the Lord 1517 this sequentiary was written in the convent of Strängnäs for the convent of Västerås.” Insulensis is the Dominican house of Västerås, the owner named on the pastedown. The catalogue adds a small irony. A later reader at Västerås, who evidently could not read the ciphered date, wrote on f. 20v that the book was the work of Frater Gudmundus Benedicti “circa annum 1520”.

The slip is a second, unrelated cipher in a later hand, so its result is given apart from the colophon’s: the colophon 125 of 125 letters read with its known key, the slip 0 of 6 signs, not solved. Uppsala UB C 513, the slip pasted on f. 1r: a note to Anders Larsson. The last line ends liff oth sel and the six signs. Image: Uppsala University Library, C 513, slip on f. 1r, via Alvin (public domain). The catalogue notes only that a slip with a post-medieval Swedish text is pasted on f. 1r, and that “an Anders Larsson receives medicines”. Transcribed from the scan (uncertain words marked ?): thetta skal wal[?] larens? andhers hess? lass son wara andhers y brygghe stuffuan … kære hertans brodher andhers larsson h[elsa]? sändher yagh edher littit örther til edher brysth kanelbark men yak ffruchthar ath han är gammal kære brodher edhra [w]älgärningar? är yak ffor ringa til at betala hwilket yak tager then effuige gudh til help then yak edher beffaller til liff oth sel ÿ ɑ M ÿ u ꝺ “…to Anders Larsson in the brewhouse. Dear brother Anders Larsson, I send you a few herbs for your chest, cinnamon bark, but I fear it is old. Dear brother, I am too poor to repay your kindnesses, which I leave to the eternal God, to whom I commend you in life and soul.” Then come the six signs, where the writer’s name would stand. The clear text of the slip, with its uncertain words counted as holes, reads at 94.8% of its words, under the 95% a complete reading needs. The last line: liff oth sel , then ÿ ɑ M and ÿ u ꝺ . Image: Uppsala University Library, C 513, slip on f. 1r, via Alvin (public domain). The signs look like cursive letters of the same hand: ÿ as in yagh , and ꝺ the hand’s looped d, as in edher . They fall into two groups of three, each opening with ÿ, as a first name and a patronymic would. The colophon’s vowel shift does not apply, since none of b, f, k, p or x occurs. None of the 23 shifts of the alphabet on five readings of the signs gives a name or a formula, and nothing else in the book is in this hand. Six signs with one repeat cannot fix a substitution. They are not deciphered.

The DECODE record’s only image is a placeholder icon. Its attached PDF is the catalogue entry, which named the folio and the rule. A first pass took DECODE’s “six symbols” to be a garbled description of the colophon. All 175 Alvin images were then checked, and the slip on f. 1r turned up. The only other extra writing is clear pen trials on the back pastedown. Alvin’s scans of C 513 are public domain. f. 19v is attachment 42, and its full TIFF was cut into line crops and transcribed. The inverse rule was applied by a small script. It takes k as i and x as u (neither is a consonant in this text) and chooses a or b, e or f, and o or p by scoring the candidate words across the whole colophon with the project’s Latin n-gram model. A first pass word by word, with no context, took prp for oro . With the sentence as context, it chose pro , and the output matched the catalogue’s reading in every word.

The six signs closing the f. 1r note ( ÿ ɑ M ÿ u ꝺ ) are not deciphered. Too short, with no key and no sibling in the same hand. Probably the writer’s name. The colophon: all 125 cipher letters have a value, and all 19 words give sense (grade H). The note’s clear Swedish is a first transcription from the scan; the words of its first line are uncertain. In the transcription, the minims after the initial A could be read m or nn. The rule requires nn ( Annp ), as the catalogue has it. In the first cpnxfntx the n is carried by a stroke over cp . The catalogue cites earlier literature on the book: Collijn (1917), Moberg (1927) and Hedlund’s plate of 1977. Whether any of these printed the decipherment before 1992 was not checked.

Four clear letters of Leicester, Burghley and Walsingham, catalogued by DECODE as a cipher from an unknown sender. Code [3] = the Queen was identified from context; the other codes and a nine-symbol cipher run are not deciphered, as no key survives. The partie 776 + w5 ‡ 6 3 ∩ 6 remaineth here in London · He wisheth [3] to look well to Scotland · [3] = the Queen London ↔ Paris · name codes in clear letters · November 1572 Walsingham’s letter-book, November 1572: Burghley, Leicester and Walsingham from Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester → to Francis Walsingham BL Harley MS 260 ff. 367r–369v (DECODE R8361, catalogue 125), listed as “unknown sender to unknown recipient”. The six pages are a fair copy of four English letters of Sir Francis Walsingham’s Paris embassy. They are in clear except for a few name codes and one short cipher run. The cipher items were transcribed; [3] = the Queen was identified from context, and the rest are not deciphered for want of a key. No earlier decipherment is known. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 7 November 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The document Four letters of November 1572 in a fair-copy register: the end of Leicester to Walsingham, Burghley to Walsingham (7 November), and Walsingham to Smith and to Burghley (both 27 November). Where British Library, Harley MS 260 ff. 367r–369v; DECODE R8361 lists it as a six-page letter from an unknown sender to an unknown recipient, “short parts encrypted only”. The cipher Nine boxed name codes, a letter code H and one nine-symbol run: 21 tokens in all. All four letters are printed in Digges (1655), pp. 297–301, with the cipher as garbled figures. How it was tried The boxed code [3] is the Queen, the only value that fits all four places it occurs (context only, no key). No Walsingham–Burghley key of 1572 is known, and the sibling records have none. Still open Codes [7] and [9], H and the nine-symbol run are not deciphered. The originals at Hatfield or SP 70 might carry a clerk’s decipherment.

The page heads carry the running date “November 1572”. The letters are copied one after another with their addresses, in one hand, so this is a register, not the letters as sent. DECODE images P5 and P6 are in reverse folio order. f. 367r, Burghley to Walsingham, 7 November 1572: “written to Rome [9]”, then “The partie … 776 + w5 ‡ 6 3 ∩ 6 remaineth here in London”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 367r, via DECODE R8361 (image P1). Burghley, 7 November: “a person come, as he saith, from Florence [9] ” “letters which the partie hath written to Rome [9] ” “The partie 776 + w5 ‡ 6 3 ∩ 6 remaineth here in London … and yet I doubt the P. will smell of him”. This is a letter cipher, probably spelling the person’s name. Walsingham to Burghley, 27 November: f. 369r: “He wisheth [3] to look well to Scotland” and “If Steward himself, or the [9], shall learn any thing that toucheth [3]”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 369r, via DECODE R8361 (image P6). “delivered to Steward, for that Glasgow [7] was not here” “he biddeth me tell him as [3] that he is now without fear of danger” “He wisheth [3] to look well to Scotland, and that Manessier is sent but to abuse her Majesty with fair words” “If Steward himself, or the [9] , shall learn any thing that toucheth [3] , I shall be advertised” “within these 8 days … [7] protested that he should never be quiet so long as the exercise of Religion continued in any one place of Christendom” “both he and Spain shall, for the avoiding of suspicion of the Legate’s coming, entertain the [3] with good words” “I have requested H to be throughly advertised”

[3] = the Queen. In all four places the code stands for a person English policy turns on: someone warned to look to Scotland, someone news may “touch”, someone France and Spain mean to “entertain with good words”. The Queen fits every time, and no other candidate fits all four. Grade C (consistent context, no key). [7], [9], H. [7] follows “Glasgow” (the Bishop of Glasgow, Mary Stuart’s ambassador) and is also the man who swore never to rest while the Reformed religion survived. That points to the Cardinal of Lorraine or the Duke of Guise, but a code that follows a name may mark a title rather than a person. (This background is not from the sources and was not checked here.) [9] follows both “Florence” and “Rome” and then stands alone (“the [9]”). Its three uses do not settle on one person, so it stays open. The nine-symbol run. It mixes digits, a letter and graphic signs. Nine symbols of an unknown alphabet cannot be deciphered without the key. What was checked: the sibling records from the same volume (R8357, R8363) have no key. The pages carry no glosses. Tomokiyo’s survey of Elizabethan ciphers (Cecil–Norris, Throckmorton, Stafford) has no Walsingham key of 1570–73. CSP Foreign vol. x does not calendar these letters. Digges prints them without deciphering the codes.

The letter run “776 + w5 ‡ 6 3 ∩ 6”, f. 367r: too short, no key. Codes [7] (×2), [9] (×3) and H: no key material. Leads: the originals Walsingham sent (Hatfield or SP 70) may carry Burghley’s clerk’s decipherment, and Digges’s other letters of 1571–73 use the same boxed codes, so a full inventory of them could fix [7] and [9].

The work here covers the letters of 13 May and 20 November, where no decipherment was found. Where BnF fr. 2984 (Béthune 8509), pp. 29–31 and p. 105, on a Gallica black-and-white microfilm. The volume has eight ciphered items; about 106 lines lacked a decipherment. The cipher A monoalphabetic substitution with homophones, three nulls and three word signs. How it was read The key is Tomokiyo’s 2020 table, re-measured off the image after a first pass slipped one column. A control line decrypts glyph for glyph. 86 of the 106 lines were deciphered by hand. What it says The 13 May letter reports the Emperor’s side of the negotiation nine days before Cognac, with the plague in Rome. The 20 November letter turns on a pontificate that would be the ruin of a house. Still open The 13 May letter (pp. 29–31) is decoded, not read: about 13% of its letters did not resolve on the half-size crops used here, and Brice Dudout’s reading of the November letter shows the microfilm does resolve at full size, so it can be re-read. Two word signs and two names are unsettled. Credit Satoshi Tomokiyo published the key (2020); Mignet (1886) and Bourrilly (1901) noted or printed other parts. Brice Dudout read the ciphered end of the 20 November letter (p. 105 and the whole of p. 106) on 27 October 2026, with the key as re-measured here ( his edition ).

BnF fr. 2984 is volume 8509 of the Béthune collection, the Court’s file of correspondence from Rome in 1526. Gallica has it as a black-and-white microfilm (ark btv1b90598430 , 85 views, every canvas labelled “NP”). Tomokiyo set out the 1526 key in French Ciphers during the Reign of Francis I (2020) as an image: a header row of plaintext letters over up to four rows of cipher glyphs, the columns about 78 px apart. It is a monoalphabetic substitution with homophones, three nulls and three word signs. Assigning each glyph to its letter by eye is error-prone, and the first pass here slipped a column. Measuring the positions settles it. Locating the white header letters in the magenta band, then labelling the ink blobs below and assigning each to the nearest header column, every blob falls within 15 px of a column centre, a fifth of the column spacing. The measured table is: Every glyph cut out of the key image and labelled by the column it measures into. Three homophones for a and u/v , four for e , three for i , two each for l , o , p , r and s ; no glyph at all for x ; three nulls. Image: Drawn here from S. Tomokiyo’s key table, Cryptiana, “French Ciphers during the Reign of Francis I” (2020). The correction. l is the 9 , not the round s ; m is the round s , not the long f ; n is the long f . The first pass had these one place to the left. H measures under s , not under r where it had been put. Why it matters. That single shift is what produced dongUeaent for longuement , egsembde for ensemble and SonseigEur for monseigneur in the first machine draft. Every file derived from the shifted table was discarded. Confusable pairs. p has a T and a circle with a dash to its right; r has a 4 and a dash then a circle. The two are near mirror images and are the easiest pair on the leaf to confuse. The most frequent single glyph, a circle at the foot of a barred stem, is an e . Word signs. A looped L with a tail = con ; two small circles joined by a curve underneath = l’empereur ; a cursive y with a descender = le pape . The letter y is E , so a y-shaped glyph is the word sign, not the letter. The control. With the measured table, p. 29 line 20 decrypts glyph for glyph and leaves nothing over: ∧ λ n v ✕✕ 7 ∧ ℓ ꝛ I ℓ 7 f 9 o ⊡ ꝛ v 4 ℓ ϝ 7 ∧ o R ꝛ E ψ ny 7 ∧ ℓ T o 4 ℓ E T ꝛ v 4 R 7 f ✕✕ 4 I ⊡ E → s [null] qui estoit en la court de Savoye [null] est party pour venir icy The line uses a , c , d , three of the four e homophones, two of the three i , l , n , o , p , q , r , s , t , u/v , y , and two of the three nulls. That is the evidence the table is right.

The numbers written on successive Gallica views run 29, 31, 33, 35, 37, two apart. Taken as folio numbers that would mean half the volume’s openings were never filmed, and every letter in it half missing. They are page numbers, written on odd pages only: view n shows pages 2 n −4 and 2 n −3, 85 views cover about 167 pages, and the digitisation is complete. So the 13 May letter is three consecutive pages, 29, 30 and 31, and the 20 November one is p. 105. The text settles it independently. Page 29 ends … et n’est possible … monstrer plus a[ffe]- and page 30 opens -ction . Both halves of that join were deciphered glyph by glyph before the join was noticed.

The film is legible at about 2× but the ink is grey and the hand is small, so the difficulty is transcription. Three steps made it possible. One image per manuscript line, cut into four overlapping quarters and stacked, so a whole line fits in one view without losing magnification. Numbered tokens. Connected-component segmentation gives 5,629 glyph tokens; drawing each token’s box on the line and numbering it means a hand transcription is written as one character per token and lands aligned to the segmentation with no guesswork. Every line was checked against its token count before it was kept. Machine suggestions. A classifier over the token images, combined with a 6-gram language model of period French without spaces, proposes a letter for every token. It is right on about 85–90 % of them: enough to speed up hand transcription, too few to replace it. p. 30 line 8 with every segmented token boxed and numbered. The hand decipherment of this line is [null] respondu à ce que ce qu’on a envoyé d’icy et de V[null]enise par deu- , running on into line 9 as -ers ledict seigneur . Token 39, a K , is a null standing inside the word Venise . Image: Annotated here on BnF fr. 2984 p. 30 (Gallica btv1b90598430). How accurate the classifier is. The hand decipherments double as training data, so the classifier can be scored by leaving one hand-deciphered line out at a time: training data leave-one-line-out per-token accuracy the map’s own confident tokens only 0.840 + hand labels, weight 1 0.856 + hand labels, weight 8 0.901 (peak, at 32 hand-read lines) + hand labels, weight 30 0.860 This is why the text was deciphered by hand. At 0.90 per token a six-letter word survives at 0.53, which is why only about a third of the machine text segments into real French words however the decoder is tuned. The residual confusions are between glyphs that really are similar at this resolution: ψ (e) against 4 (r), the cursive ℓ (t) against 9 (l) against the lollipop (d), the caret (s) against the vee (u) against × (a). The key itself leaves none of these ambiguous. More labels will not fix that; better images would.

Nine days before the League of Cognac was signed. The clear close on p. 31 (transcribed here; no printed text of it was found) dates and signs it ( De Rome, ce xiij jour de may, 15c xxvj … Nicolas Rainse ) and reports that Rome expects Andrea Doria at Civitavecchia that day or the next, with six galleys and two brigantines . The three ciphered pages that precede it give, in part: … ne cessera jamais qu’il n’ayt destruict ledict seigneur … ; and, a line later, d’autres propo[s] … ains de vert[u] et mensonges . … ont receu … de Castille, qu’ilz disent … ; ensemble … les bourguignons ; and, of a great lord, les castilliens li[sent] au (con)traire que lesdessusdict[z] sont … … delib-eré prendre le chemin de Valence … à ceste fin, et qu’il ne voul-oyent qu’il feust … si grant seigneur. … et qu’il[z] seront cause de la destruction, de la part d’avoir faic-t capituler avec … ; the likeliest referent is the Treaty of Madrid of January 1526, though the letter does not name it. Ledict He[rr]er[a](?) doit partir de dans deux ou troys jours pour s’en retourner (the name is not settled); and …s qui estoit en la court de Savoye est party pour venir icy. p. 30: (L’empereur) est esbay de ce que … n’a escript autrement, aucune part deça, depuis son retour … en son royaume; et m’en a parlé plusieurs fois . … que mondict seigneur l’Admiral luy av-oit dict que seroit celuy qui y tiendroit. J’ay tousiours respondu à ce que ce qu’on a envoyé d’icy et de Venise par devers ledict seigneur … … deux ou trois fois qui a[voit] deu venir à Rome … disant prendre tout pour le mieul[x] … Bien est vray, monsei-gneur… p. 31: … la peste qui est au logis … ; …s foys escript des advis qui viennent aux imperiaulx par leu[rs] … ; … es grant dommaige en toutes les sortes qu’on pourroit … ; [il] y ayt grant obligation pour les dommaiges qu’ilz disent ledict avoir… and, near the end, a named man: …t un jour, en plaine place pres du palais, un nommé Pietro Anthonio … secretaire ou serviteur dudict, qui estoit icy pour luy … followed by propos … quel estoit cause de tout le mal … deux ou trois fois .

Two months after the Colonna raid on the Vatican, and five months before the Sack. The ciphered part turns on the Pope: … qui a … peust … faire s[e]cre[te]ment · et … pontif-icat seroit la cause de la totale(?) ruine de sa maison , de-… With, in the same passage, …me, et s’en fuire; et que encores … luy feist … la grace ; … et que … l’on penseroit … y respondre de part de nature ; …t jamais pensé que les choses … prinst, et le for[t]- ; sincerement … qu’il estoit … en besoing ; … et que l’i[n]convenient … peril à qu[oy] … ; and et aussi qu’il estoit … bien cler que n’estoit … dicte de . “Sa maison” is the Medici, and the pontificate is Clement VII’s. Read in full by Brice Dudout, 27 October 2026. The cipher does not stop at the foot of p. 105: p. 106 is a whole page of it, 35 lines, which this page had missed, ending in the clear postscript on the bull of monitory against Cardinal Colonna. Dudout read the lower 21 lines of p. 105 and all of p. 106 sign by sign on the full-size Gallica images (IIIF, about 7,900 pixels wide), with Tomokiyo’s table as re-measured here and frozen before reading: about 98% of some 610 words, the rest mostly word signs missing from the table. On p. 105 his text agrees with the decode made here on 95.6% of the letters, and fills most of its holes. It is his reading, not re-read here on the image. The Pope, says Raince, wishes for death: his pontificate would be “la cause de la totale ruine de sa maison”, the King would lose “le meilleur amy qu’il eut oncque au monde”, and His Holiness charged him to write it all to the King. The full text and translation are under Full texts.

Re-measured 5 October 2026. Every line was re-read from the image ( trans/reading_v3.txt ) and the reading scored for sense: p. 29 0.923, p. 30 0.877, p. 31 0.872, p. 105 0.781, all 0.870 (on the old reading the same measure gives 0.476). The circled cross is now identified as i. Open: about 13% of letters whose glyphs do not resolve on the black-and-white Gallica microfilm (worst p. 105 ll. 15–17, 20–21, p. 30 ll. 30–34, p. 31 ll. 1–2, 17, 23–24), and two word signs absent from Tomokiyo’s key (a bold two-crossbar stem, a person after son maistre , and ℓ°), about four occurrences each. Twenty lines of the 106 carry only the machine decode. They are kept, marked, in trans/reading.txt and left out of the edited text. Gaps inside the 86. The edited text leaves … wherever the glyphs did not resolve. Nothing is supplied by conjecture; a wrong confident decipherment would be worse than a gap. One glyph is in no published table: a bold vertical stem crossed by two horizontal bars, the lower one longer and projecting right. It occurs ten times across all four pages and every occurrence falls at a clause boundary: between plaisirs and qu’il , between lectres and qui est , or opening a sentence. It is not the barred-b g , not the barred-stem e , and not any of the three nulls. Most likely a point or a fourth null; it is written · in the edited text. The p. 29 / p. 30 join gives …monstrer plus a[ffe]- + -ctio?e , where the glyph after ctio measures as a plain triangle ( f ) rather than the n the sense wants. Left with a query. Two personal names are not settled: messire Ca?in , who appears twice on p. 30, and the agent transcribed as He[rr]er[a] on p. 29. What would finish it was thought to be better images. Brice Dudout’s reading of pp. 105–106 (27 October 2026) shows the black-and-white microfilm resolves at Gallica’s full size on crops of half a line at about three times magnification; the unresolved glyphs here came from the half-size crops. The 13 May letter, pp. 29–31, can be re-read the same way.

Key measured off the image. Header letters located in the key image, ink blobs labelled and assigned to the nearest column, every assignment within 15 px of a column centre. Contact sheet of every labelled glyph kept. Verified on the leaf against a control line that decrypts with nothing left over, using sixteen of the alphabet’s letters and two of its three nulls. Segmentation by connected components on a background-normalised binarisation, tokens assigned to lines by a y-histogram, x-overlapping components merged; 5,629 tokens over the four pages. Cluster-to-letter map fitted by hill-climbing against a space-free 6-gram model of period French, with each cluster restricted to the letters its glyph shape allows. Restricting the moves is what stops the collapse into a degenerate map that defeats an unconstrained solver on a stream with this much segmentation noise. Hand decipherment line by line against numbered-token images, one character per token, length-checked against the segmentation. Scoring by leave-one-line-out over the hand-deciphered lines, since a model trained on its own output otherwise scores itself. Everything is in the repository: the measured key and reading method in targets/raince/CALIBRATION.md , the account in targets/raince/NOTES.md , the hand labels in targets/raince/gold/labels.txt , the edited reading in targets/raince/trans/reading_edited.txt , the line-by-line text with each line marked hand or machine in targets/raince/trans/reading.txt , and the clear close of 13 May in targets/raince/trans/p31_clear_close.txt .
