Raince to Montmorency, Rome, 13 May 1526 (BnF fr. 2984 no. 7, pp. 29-31): ciphered part, reading by Brice Dudout A letter written nine days before the League of Cognac was signed (22 May 1526): the ciphered part fills the lower half of p. 29 (after ten lines glossed at the time), the whole of p. 30 and the top of p. 31; the plain close announces Andrea Doria’s arrival at Civitavecchia with six galleys and gives the date “De Rome, ce xiij jour de may 15c xxvj”. Raince reports the quarrels at Charles V’s court after the release of Francis I, the complaints of his Roman contact that the King has sent nobody to the Pope, and the leaks running through the Duke of Ferrara’s men to the Imperialists. 105 lower part and p. 106, reading by Brice Dudout Two months after the Colonna raid on the Vatican, Clement VII summoned the French king’s agent and spoke “sighing so deeply that there is no heart so hard that it would not have felt the greatest compassion in the world”. He thought of abandoning Rome and fleeing, blamed France for not breaking with the enemy “over there”, and predicted that people in France would soon say: “the Pope has run away”. Nicolas Raince put it all into cipher for Anne de Montmorency, Grand Master of France. The end of page 105 and the whole of page 106 had never been deciphered. I inform you, Monsignor, that all the trust and hope of His Holiness, in whatever necessity and tribulation he may find himself, rest entirely and wholly on the said lord and lady, and that he is quite sure that you too hold him in very good regard. As for the secret understanding of which he has again been spoken to, etc., he is still of the mind I wrote to you, and freer than ever to do whatever is wished in it, by good means. Moreover, I have again spoken to him about the bulls concerning the tenth, to which he is well disposed; you will have seen what I wrote to you lately of what he had ordered in the matter: good effect will be seen from it. the Castilians and "les bourguignons"; a plan to "prendre le chemin de Valence"; a capitulation already made, which "il[z] seront cause de la destruction … de la part d'avoir faict capituler"; an agent Herrera(?) who "doit partir … dans deux ou troys jours pour s'en retourner". Rome's own despatches are described as going "d'icy et de Venise par devers ledict seigneur", and the Emperor "est esbay de ce que … n'a escript autrement". The Admiral of France is quoted at second hand ("mondict seigneur l'Admiral luy avoit dict que seroit celuy qui y tiendroit"). The plague is in Rome ("la peste qui est au logis"), advices reach the Imperials through their own people ("des advis qui viennent aux imperiaulx par leurs …"), a named man — Pietro Anthonio, secretary or servant of the same — was taken "un jour, en plaine place pres du palais", and there is talk of "grant obligation pour les dommaiges qu'ilz disent ledict avoir …". The clear close of the same letter, on p. 31, expects Andrea Doria at Civitavecchia within a day with six galleys and two brigantines. The 20 November letter, two months after the Colonna raid on the Vatican, turns on the Pope: a pontificate that "seroit la cause de la totale ruine de sa maison" — Clement VII and the Medici — with talk of doing something "secretement", of flight ("s'en fuire"), of "le peril à quoy", and of what "l'on penseroit". Three (R852, R912, R922) are French reports sent to him from Danzig or “au quartier”; R483, his own letter from Lwów of 27 June 1711, is in a different cipher and was split off on 14 October 2026 (rakoczi1711). Monseigneur, j’ay receu la lettre que V. A. m’a fait l’honneur de m’escrire le 26. X bre . Je feray passer au S r Groffey celles qui estoient pour luy … V. A. peut luy donner directement les ordres, outre que je vous respons encore une fois de sa fidelité … J’ay veu une ou deux fois un imprimé latin intitulé Mercurius hungaricus . Il seroit tres important pour le service de V. A. qu’on imprimast regulierement toutes les semaines une feuille de cet imprimé … il n’y a point de gazetier allemand ny hollandois qui ne detruise à son ayse le Roy me d’Hongrie … On croioit encore à Berlin qu’il n’y avoit plus de Hongrois depuis l’action. The ciphered page is followed by its clear copy, transcribed here from the image, and by a short clear note offering to keep a register of M. de Bonnac's letters and bills of exchange. The writer is at Danzig and speaks of Groffey in the third person. The cipher's letters and syllables agree with R639, but its word codes do not: 144 is de and 254 is la , where R639 has beaucoup and jusque . It is an earlier issue of the table.

Monseigneur, je me suis privé [?pendant] quelque temps de l’honneur d’escrire à Vostre Altesse … faite à Madame la Palatine de Belz … une copie authentique de cette vente au sieur Kray … autant qu’il a esté possible, par mon credit et par mes avances … pour joindre le Roy de Pologne … l’avantage de luy continuer mes services à la Cour de Pologne … Je suis avec tout le respect possible, Monseigneur. From the reading of 23 October 2026 ( texts/R922_reading.md , English R922_en.md ): the decode with the corrected R639 table divided into words and normalised by hand, the table’s words read for their sound (161 con , 395 son , 188 dont ), doubtful places checked on the image. Holes: groups 9, 873 and 574, one “?” group and one short run; 18 letters rest on a look-alike figure. The letter concerns a sale for the Palatine of Belz (Elżbieta Sieniawska), orders for carbines, and the sieur Kray. On page 2 it turns to money and to someone who is a prisoner. A contemporary hand deciphered only the first two lines, between the lines: the date and “je me suis privé pendant quelque temps de l’honneur d’escrire à Vostre Altesse”, 37 of the 722 groups. Everything after them was deciphered here with R639 alone.

Monseigneur, ayant eu l’honneur de marquer à Vostre Altesse le 29 du mois dernier que le Roy Stanislas … le Palatin de Belz … charge de grand Général … la pacification … une nouvelle élection en Pologne … le Czar … la lettre qu’elle avoit escrite au Maréchal Rheinschild … Monsieur le Palatin de Russie … avec un profond respect et un zèle parfait. From the reading of 23 October 2026 ( texts/R912_reading.md , English R912_en.md ). Page 1 follows the 1707 interlinear decipherment read on the image ( texts/R912_interlinear_p1.txt ), checked against the figures, with seven figure corrections seen there (473 is 493 les Polonois , 501 is 301 …); the rest is the R639 decode, divided and normalised by hand. Page 1 and the end of page 3 build fully. Page 2 keeps runs of holes (ll. 3–7, 14–22, 26–31), where the groups as transcribed give no French under R639 and a second look at the image is still due. A survey of Polish and Swedish politics that includes the Rehnskiöld affair of R902. It also covers a regiment asked of Rákóczi, which King Stanisław and the Germans hold against him, and Tököly. What was deciphered at the time. A contemporary hand wrote the plaintext between the lines of page 1 over every line except the end of one and the two below it (659 of the page’s 713 groups), over the first four lines and the start of the fifth on page 2, and over the first line and the start of the second on page 3: about 780 of the letter’s 1,630 groups. DECODE’s transcription records these interlinear lines. The opening, the Palatine of Belz, the grand général, the pacification, the new election, the Tsar and the letter to Rehnskiöld quoted above all lie under it. The rest of pages 2 and 3 carries no decipherment on the leaves and was deciphered here with R639 alone: the Palatine of Ruthenia, the regiment, Stanisław and the Germans, Tököly and the closing formula. So were the three lines of page 1 that the decipherer left. Those three lines finish a sentence about the King of Sweden, “ce Prince s’est voulu réserver un prétexte de rester cet hiver en Pologne pour ne pas s’éloigner de l’Allemagne”, where the interlinear stops (added 30 September 2026): … ni perdre de veue les affaires générales de l’Europe. Aussy publie-t-on comme une chose presque certaine qu’il n’entrera en Moschovie que la campagne qui vient. ‘… nor lose sight of the general affairs of Europe. So it is given out as an almost certain thing that he [Charles XII] will not enter Muscovy until the coming campaign.’ He did invade Russia only in the campaign of 1708. Of the 54 groups, 44 read directly with R639 (H), four are fillers or nulls (589, 619; 115, 97), and six need comment: publie : the group is 327 = pu . Its last figure has the open top of this hand’s 7 (as in 257 and 297), not the round bowl of its 9 (349, 149). It had been transcribed 329 = pas (M). une : the group is 87 = U. Its first figure closes in a loop at the foot, like the 8 of 87 in “un homme” higher on the page, not the open hooked 5. It had been transcribed 57 = Et , here and by DECODE (M). veue : 427 426, both ve in the key. The key has no separate v (its alphabet runs T, U, X), and a line higher the contemporary decipherer wrote ue over 427, so the pair reads ve-ue (M). presque : 343 350, présent que in the key. The writer used 343 for the pré- of prétexte two lines higher, where the decipherer also wrote pre (M). campagne : 58 = ns on the image and in the key, read as a slip for 88 = M (M). vient : 534 46, Vienne and T. The place code is used for its sound, as 266 leur gives the l’Eur- of l’Europe in the same line (M). The first transcription also had 509 ( France ) at the end of the last line. The image has 589, a filler, as DECODE reads it, so R912 has 1,585 keyed groups, not 1,586.

Monseigneur, je me suis privé [?pendant] quelque temps de l'honneur d'escrire à Vostre Altesse, ne voulant pas le faire que je ne pusse luy marquer que l'affaire de Jaroslau estoit finie, que la vente ou donation en avoit esté faite à Madame la Palatine de Belz. Ce fust mardi dernier; je remettray une copie authentique de cette vente au sieur Kray, et je me contenteray de feliciter ici Vostre Altesse de la belle acquisition qu'elle a faite. Nous avons reglé avec le sieur Kray les comptes de ce qui a esté dépensé depuis son départ. Elle verra dans le raport qu'il luy en fera que j'ay évité autant qu'il a esté possible, par mon credit et par mes avances, le préjudice que le service de Vostre Altesse pouvoit recevoir du peu d'ordre avec lequel le Comte Bertoti faisoit ses traittes, malgré la manière dont il s'est comporté en cela, dont la [?veuve] [...] ni moy ne pouvions estre guère contents. A l'arrivée du sieur Kray, afin [...] tout cela, je luy ay communiqué les ordres de Vostre Altesse pour les nouvelles carabines; c'est luy [à qui] on a donné les ordres pour les premières, à l'emplette desquelles je n'ay eu aucune part. Je compte de partir au premier jour pour joindre le Roy de Pologne. Tout sera reglé avant mon départ d'une manière dont Vostre Altesse aura lieu d'estre satisfaite, et qu'elle n'aura qu'à adresser ses ordres au sieur Kray pour ces sortes de choses, me reservant seulement l'avantage de luy continuer mes services à la Cour de Pologne, si elle juge à propos de m'employer en quelque chose. Je me suis expliqué amplement avec le sieur Kray au sujet des sieurs de Chassan et du Boucard. J'ajouteray seulement ici que le premier, manquant de tout dans sa prison et m'asseurant qu'il n'a [873] receu directement de la part de Vostre Altesse depuis qu'il est prisonnier, comme je juge que c'est parce qu'elle manque de correspondans en Autriche, et que je puis luy faire toucher directement de l'argent d'ici, j'espère [qu'elle] aura agréable que je le [?fasse]. My Lord, I have denied myself for [?some] time the honour of writing to Your Highness, not wishing to do so until I could tell you that the Jarosław business was finished, that the sale or donation of it had been made to Madame the Palatine of Bełz. That was last Tuesday; I shall hand an authentic copy of the sale to Mr Kray, and I shall content myself with congratulating Your Highness here on the fine acquisition you have made. We have settled with Mr Kray the accounts of what has been spent since his departure. You will see from the report he will make to you that, as far as possible, by my credit and by my advances, I have averted the harm that Your Highness's service could have suffered from the disorder with which Count Bertoti drew his bills, despite the way he behaved in this, with which the [?widow] [...] and I could hardly be satisfied. On Mr Kray's arrival, so that [...] all this, I passed on to him Your Highness's orders for the new carbines; it is he who was given the orders for the first ones, in whose purchase I had no part. I expect to leave any day now to join the King of Poland. Everything will be settled before my departure in a way with which Your Highness will have reason to be satisfied, and you will only have to address your orders to Mr Kray for such matters, while I keep only the privilege of continuing my services to you at the Polish court, if you see fit to employ me in anything. I have explained myself fully with Mr Kray about Messrs de Chassan and du Boucard. I shall only add here that, since the first, lacking everything in his prison, assures me that he has [873] received directly from Your Highness since he became a prisoner, and as I judge that this is because you lack correspondents in Austria, and as I can have money paid to him directly from here, I hope [you] will approve my [?doing] it. C. Fasc. 39, pp. 312-314) ## Reading Du 5 9bre 1707, au quartier du Roy de Suède à [?Slupce], le 5 Novembre. Monseigneur, ayant eu l'honneur de marquer à Vostre Altesse le 29 du mois dernier que le Roy Stanislas a osté à Monsieur le Palatin de Belz la charge de grand Général de la Couronne et qu'il l'a donnée au Palatin de Kiovie, [...] depuis qu'il n'a fait cette démarche que par ces considérations et ses intérêts, parce que le Roy de Suède l'a voulu, celuy-ci ne voulant point s'exposer à l'embarras où il auroit esté, comme son ministre le dit, d'ôter à un homme qui se seroit venu rendre à son devoir une charge dont il falloit nécessairement le priver pour le punir, et n'avoir plus rien à craindre de ses [?engagemens] avec les Moscovites. Les Polonois croient que le Roy de Suède, en apportant un aussy grand obstacle à la pacification des troubles de la Pologne que la proscription de Monsieur le Palatin de Belz, a des veues sur ce Royaume tout opposées aux intérêts [...] dont il s'est si souvent vanté. Il est, à mon avis, plus vraysemblable que ce Prince s'est voulu réserver un prétexte de rester cet hiver en Pologne pour ne pas s'éloigner de l'Allemagne, ni perdre de veue les affaires générales de l'Europe. Aussy publie-t-on comme une chose presque certaine qu'il n'entrera en Moschovie que la campagne qui vient. L'on dit à présent à la Chancellerie Suédoise que, en effect, Vostre Altesse n'a pas accepté la Couronne, mais [...] la mettre sur la teste, mais dans l'espérance que l'embarras d'une nouvelle élection en Pologne et la nécessité de faire une puissante diversion en Allemagne contre l'Empereur détermineroient le Roy de Suède à la satisfaire sur les choses qu'elle luy avoit si souvent demandées, de sorte que je vois déjà du changement de ce costé là. Aussy m'a-t-on dit que, comme ce Prince, dans la situation présente de ses affaires, n'estoit point en estat de rendre service à Vostre Altesse, nous [?pouvions] estre asseurez qu'il n'estoit pas non plus dans la disposition de [?luy] nuire, veu que depuis la lettre qu'elle avoit escrite au Maréchal Rheinschild il [...] estoit pas arrivé une seule fois de parler [d']elle; je ne désespérois pas que vous ne le fissiez songer à vous, Monseigneur, [?d'une manière] qui pourroit avoir quelque bonne [?suite], si, comme j'ay eu l'honneur de vous le [?marquer] dans ma dernière, vous luy escriviez, ou bien à son ministre, pour expliquer les motifs [...] de vostre commerce avec le Czar, dans le [...] dont j'en ay [...]. La Cour de Pologne [...] plus retirée. Le Roy Stanislas prétend [...] que vous [...] pas encore, Monseigneur, [...] de vostre amitié capables d'effacer les impressions qu'une démarche pareille à [...] a faites sur son esprit, et croit ne devoir pas estre satisfait du renvoy des [...] de Monsieur le Palatin de Russie, à cause que Vostre Altesse, [...] escrivant sur ce sujet à leur père, [...] en mesme temps fait ressouvenir de la perte [...] son régiment de [?Bielck]. Je ne vous arresteray point, Monseigneur, par le récit de tout ce que j'ay représenté sur ce sujet, ni à vous faire remarquer ce qui paroit de soy mesme, à scavoir que le Roy Stanislas [...] les Allemans [...] obligez pour ne pas satisfaire Vostre Altesse au sujet du régiment. J'auray seulement l'honneur de vous dire que, lorsque j'ay demandé quelles preuves on souhaitoit que vous donnassiez, Monseigneur, pour persuader le Roy de Pologne de la sincérité de vos sentimens, [...] vous attendre sur le dédommagement du régiment, on m'a répondu au premier [...] qu'il falloit que Vostre Altesse s'abandonnât [...] le Palatin et [...] la Palatine de Belz [...]. [...] dans un estat à pouvoir satisfaire présentement Monsieur le Palatin de Russie, qui me parle tous jours des obligations qu'il a à Vostre Altesse, m'a encore demandé comme un moyen de disposer les choses au rétablissement d'une bonne intelligence [...] que le Roy son maître demandoit une [...] de la part de Vostre Altesse à ce Prince. [...] de vous dire, Monseigneur, [...] les obligations qu'il vous a [...] de retraitte que vous avez donnée à Tekeli [...] qu'il ne vous en doit aucune [...]. Ne pourroit-on pas dire que la Cour de Pologne suit dans son propos [...] de Vostre Altesse que de Monsieur le Palatin de Belz [...] pour les intérêts de l'Empereur? Je ne scavois mesme si elle ne scauroit pas [...] le Roy de Suède à chagriner Vostre Altesse par le motif de ses liaisons avec Monsieur le Palatin de Belz. Je puis me tromper, mais je croi ne devoir pas cacher ma pensée à Vostre Altesse, afin qu'elle prenne les mesures qui luy seront convenables. Je suis avec un profond respect et un zèle parfait, [...] ## Notes - Page 1 (713 groups): the 1707 interlinear covers it to l. 16 and again from l. 19; ll. 16-18 read from the figures (NOTES, 30 Sept 2026). Same holes. --> # R912, an agent with the Swedish army to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 5 November 1707 ## Translation 5 November 1707, at the King of Sweden's quarters at [?Slupce], 5 November. My Lord, having had the honour of informing Your Highness on the 29th of last month that King Stanisław has taken from the Palatine of Bełz the office of Grand General of the Crown and has given it to the Palatine of Kiev, [...] since he took this step only out of these considerations and his own interests, because the King of Sweden wished it; the latter not wishing to expose himself to the embarrassment he would have been in, as his minister says, of taking from a man who had come back to his duty an office of which he had of necessity to be deprived in order to punish him, and to have nothing more to fear from his [?commitments] with the Muscovites. The Poles believe that the King of Sweden, by putting so great an obstacle to the pacification of the troubles of Poland as the proscription of the Palatine of Bełz, has designs on this kingdom quite contrary to the interests [...] of which he has so often boasted. It is, in my opinion, more likely that this Prince wished to keep a pretext for staying in Poland this winter so as not to move away from Germany, nor lose sight of the general affairs of Europe. So it is given out as an almost certain thing that he will not enter Muscovy until the coming campaign. It is now said in the Swedish Chancery that Your Highness has in fact not accepted the Crown, but [...] to put it on your head, but in the hope that the embarrassment of a new election in Poland and the need for a powerful diversion in Germany against the Emperor would bring the King of Sweden to satisfy you on the things you had so often asked of him; so that I already see a change on that side. I have also been told that, as this Prince, in the present state of his affairs, was in no condition to do Your Highness a service, we [?could] be assured that he was no more disposed to [?do you] harm, seeing that since the letter you had written to Marshal Rehnskiöld he had not [...] once happened to speak of you; I did not despair that you might make him think of you, My Lord, [?in a way] that could have some good [?outcome], if, as I had the honour to [?tell] you in my last, you wrote to him, or else to his minister, to explain the motives [...] of your dealings with the Tsar, in the [...] of which I have [...]. The Polish court [...] more withdrawn. King Stanisław claims [...] that you [...] not yet, My Lord, [...] of your friendship able to efface the impressions that a step like [...] has made on his mind, and he believes he need not be satisfied with the sending back of the [...] of the Palatine of Ruthenia, because Your Highness, [...] writing on this subject to their father, [...] at the same time recalled the loss [...] his regiment of [?Bielck]. I shall not detain you, My Lord, with an account of all I represented on this subject, nor point out to you what appears of itself, namely that King Stanisław [...] the Germans [...] obliged not to satisfy Your Highness over the regiment. I shall only have the honour of telling you that when I asked what proofs they wished you to give, My Lord, to persuade the King of Poland of the sincerity of your feelings, [...] expect you on the compensation for the regiment, I was told at the first [...] that Your Highness should give yourself up [...] the Palatine and [...] the Palatine of Bełz [...]. [...] in a position to satisfy at present the Palatine of Ruthenia, who speaks to me constantly of the obligations he owes Your Highness, has again asked me, as a means of arranging matters for the restoration of a good understanding, [...] that the King his master asked for a [...] on Your Highness's part to this Prince. [...] to tell you, My Lord, [...] the obligations he owes you [...] of the refuge you gave Thököly [...] that he owes you none [...]. Could one not say that the Polish court follows in its intent [...] of Your Highness as of the Palatine of Bełz [...] for the Emperor's interests? I did not even know whether it might not [...] the King of Sweden to vex Your Highness by reason of your ties with the Palatine of Bełz. I may be mistaken, but I believe I must not hide my thought from Your Highness, so that you may take such measures as seem fitting to you. I am, with a deep respect and a perfect zeal, [...] R852, Dantzig, 22 Jan 1706 The writer acknowledges Rákóczi's letter of 26 December, vouches for Groffey, and asks for a weekly Latin paper like the Mercurius hungaricus, since the German and Dutch gazetteers 'destroy the Kingdom of Hungary'. Its text is the letter's own contemporary clear copy (R852_clear.txt); R852 uses a variant issue of the table, so R852_key08_read.txt (R639 applied to DECODE's transcription) is a comparison only. [?] and [y] as there. --> # R852, to Prince Ferenc II Rákóczi, Dantzig, 22 January 1706: English translation of the contemporary clear copy At Dantzig, 22 January 1706. My Lord, I have received the letter that Your Highness did me the honour of writing to me on 26 December. I shall pass on to the sieur Groffey those that were for him. I am sure that he will make good use, for Your Highness's service, of the orders that you are pleased to give him. I shall help him on my side in everything that depends on me. Your Highness may give him orders directly; besides, I answer to you once more for his fidelity. He is very prudent and will never make anything but good use of them. I am waiting impatiently to learn that the sieur Roth. has finished with the sieurs [?], so as to come and join me. I have seen once or twice a Latin print entitled Mercurius hungaricus. It would be very important for Your Highness's service that a sheet of this print be printed regularly every week and that one or two copies at least be sent to me. There is no German or Dutch gazetteer who does not destroy the Kingdom of Hungary at his ease and turn your affairs upside down as he pleases. A similar paper would serve to prevent the bad effect that those of your enemies produce. In Berlin they still believed that there were no more Hungarians since the action of Kubo? when the letter of M. Rada[y] was received. M. de Bertoti could easily have the news printed and send it to me by way of Cracow. Key: key.md , DOC_R639_D2752_2752.txt

Where Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 1.01.02 Staten-Generaal inv. 7407; DECODE R1039, images 5450–5452 (cipher) and 5448–5449 (decipherment). DECODE transcribed the decipherment as cleartext and the record was catalogued as having none. The cipher A numerical code of three-digit groups; the marks over single digits are part of the code. How it was read The decipherment, headed Ont cyfferde Missive , repeats the last group of each cipher row in its right margin, so the clerk keyed it line by line. It is transcribed in full. The key was not rebuilt. What it says On De Swart’s advice Rechteren withheld his letter to Grand Duke Paul, contrary to his instructions. He is sure every letter is opened, and asks to send couriers and to be answered in cipher. Still open The cipher was not aligned group by group with the decipherment. The pair is the largest known-plaintext sample of this code, whose key blocks the first 1,928 groups of De Swart’s 1787 letter (R1040); the code is in inv. 158, not online. From the 1785 decipherment, original spelling: Hoog Edele Gestrenge Heer! Bij mijn arrivement alhier sprekende met de Heer De Swart over mijn eerste audientie, vraagde mij die Heer of ik ook een Brief aan den Groot Vorst had, waarop ik geantwoord hebbende, raade mij zijn Ed: het zeer af, deezen over te geeven, als niets anders als jaloutsie aan het Hof kunnende verwekken; daar bij voegende, dat zulks de zaaken van den Staat tort zoude doen, en dat ik het gerust konde laaten, alzo er een geval met den Heer Meinertshaagen had plaats gehad, die ook zijn Brief aan den Groot Vorst had te rug gehouden. De langduurige ondervinding van den Heer de Swart, en de kennis die hij van dit Hof heeft, gepaard met de geruststelling, dat hij er voor verantwoorde, hebben mij dit gedeelte van mijn Instructie niet laaten executeeren. Ik hoop niet, dat mij zulks ten kwaade zal worden geduid, alzo er niets anders als de vordering van ’s Lands belangen meede beoogt, en ik buiten dat wel occasie zal hebben, den Groot Vorst van de goede intentie van Haar Hoog Mog: te verzekeren. De zekere overtuiging, waarin ik ben, dat alle mijne Brieven geopend worden, zal mij zeer geneeren in mijne depeches, wanneer er eens mogelijkheid is, om de negociatie te hervatten; wes halven verzoek te mogen weeten, of ik, wanneer de zaaken een absolut geheim vereischt, en de publiciteit van dezelve aan de belangen van den Staat, en het vertrouwen dat men in deszelfs Minister behoord te stellen, eenige belemmering zou te weege brengen, of ik alsdan, doch niet als in de hoogste noodzaakelijkheid, een Courier aan U Ho: Ed: Gest: mag afzenden, het welk te meer noodzaakelijk is, alzo in den begin van deeze mijne Commissie meer omzigtigheid als ooit moet gebruiken. Ik verzoek hierop een spoedig antwoord in Cyffer, alzo een ongecijfferd de ontdekking van het cyffer zou faciliteeren. Ik heb de Eer &c. St Petersburg 23 Sept: / 4 Oct: 1785. In English. When I arrived and spoke with Mr De Swart about my first audience, he asked whether I also had a letter for the Grand Duke. I said I had, and he strongly advised me not to hand it over. It could only rouse jealousy at Court and would harm the affairs of the State. I could safely keep it back, as Mr Meinertzhagen had done with his own letter to the Grand Duke. De Swart’s long experience and his knowledge of this Court, and his assurance that he would answer for it, led me to leave this part of my instructions unexecuted. I hope it will not be held against me: I had only the country’s interest in view, and I will have other occasions to assure the Grand Duke of Their High Mightinesses’ good intentions. I am certain that all my letters are opened, and this will hamper my despatches whenever the negotiation can be resumed. I therefore ask whether, when a matter needs absolute secrecy, I may send a courier to Your Honour, though only in the utmost necessity. I need all the more caution at the start of my mission. I ask for a prompt answer in cipher, since an uncoded answer would help them discover the cipher. The Grand Duke is Paul, heir to Catherine II, who kept him out of affairs, which explains De Swart’s warning. (This background is not from the sources and was not checked here.) Karl de Leeuw cites this letter as the Russian example of envoys complaining that their post was opened. He does not print its text.

The record came from DECODE with the saved session cookie: images and the 2020 transcription ( DOC_R1039_D3590_3590.txt ). That transcription marks images 5448–5449 as <CLEARTEXT> , with gaps in most lines. Transcribed from the scans, they are the decipherment. The dates, the Secreet mark and the margin groups tie it to the cipher. The 310 words of plaintext against 424 groups is a normal ratio for a nomenclator that also spells syllables. As a side test, two partial Rechteren-family keys reconstructed for De Swart 1787 from the 1784 and 1786 crib pairs (R2051, R2052) were tried with the marks removed. They do not produce Dutch and disagree with each other, which confirms that the marks carry meaning.

The key was not rebuilt, and the cipher was not aligned group by group with the decipherment. The text given here is the 1785 clerk’s decipherment (grade C for the few words hard to make out in the scan, H otherwise). The alignment is worth doing for another target. R1039 is a 424-group known-plaintext pair in Rechteren’s code, and that code blocks the first 1,928 groups of De Swart’s letter of 29 Nov 1787 (R1040). The code itself is Nationaal Archief, legation in Russia, inv. 158, which is not online.

Seven ciphered records of BnF fr. 3053, catalogued with no sender, and a letter in fr. 3071 are letters of Charles Hémard de Denonville, cardinal of Mâcon, ambassador to Paul III, to Anne de Montmorency, all in “Mascon’s cipher”. Tomokiyo reconstructed the key from fr. 3053 and Lasry tabulated it in 2023, without publishing any plaintext; it was applied, corrected from contemporary glosses, and about 95% of the cipher letters are decrypted. DECODE gives the sixteen fr. 3053 records a recipient (Anne de Montmorency), a place (Rome, twice Orvieto) and no sender. Tomokiyo’s page on the French ciphers of Francis I names the volume for what it is: letters of 1535–37 from the bishop, later cardinal, of Mâcon, ambassador in Rome, to Montmorency. The records confirm it in clear. R4240 ends “A Orviette le deux[iesme] jour de septembre 1536”, signed “Vostre treshumble et tresobeissant serviteur Charles e. de Mascon”; R4247’s second letter is dated Orvieto, 1 September 1536 and signed the same way; R4239 ends “A Rome le vj e jour d’apvril 1537”, signed “E. Card[ina]l de Mascon”. The promotion of 22 December 1536 falls between the two. (This background is not from the sources and was not checked here.) That also settles the key. Lasry’s table of 5 November 2023 for BnF fr. 3071 f. 9 is called “Mascon’s cipher” and identified with fr. 3053; the letter it decrypts, Rome, 11 April 1537, is five days younger than R4239, and it was decrypted first (18 September 2026, then filed with the other letters of catalogue item 6). Since 14 October 2026 it is on this page, with the other letters in the same key ( section 08 ). The same key serves throughout, with the corrections set out below.

DECODE’s “Decrypted” marking on this volume means that the cipher system is known: no transcription or plaintext file is attached to any of the sixteen records.

The clearest of the letters, and the one with the best control: a contemporary hand glossed its last cipher lines in the margin, and the gloss and the decryption agree word for word. Mâcon has learned “de bon lieu” that Vergerio, nuncio under Clement VII and kept on by Paul III, carried word from Ferdinand to the Germans that the Pope and the College were content that, coming to the council, they might there « dire et faire ainsi qu’ils seroient inspirez par le Sainct Esperit »; on that assurance they resolved to attend, hoping for a decisive peace. But the Pope, judging this would be « la totale ruine de l’Eglise et sainct siege apostolique », has sent an auditor to summon them on the old law and custom instead. The Germans will not consent, Mâcon hears: they say the morals of pope, cardinals and bishops must be reformed, and that cannot be done without them. Then the clear text resumes, and the ambassador leaves his master to draw the conclusion: « Je vous laisse a penser sur cela, monseigneur, que ce sera de l’assemblee dudict concille. »

Andrea Doria had written to the conte dell’Anguillara to hold his galleys ready to join his own when sent for. Since Doria’s cousin Antonio had lately taken one of Anguillara’s fustas, and since Anguillara’s galleys are in the Pope’s service, Mâcon inferred a reconciliation made at the Pope’s command, and therefore a secret treaty with the Emperor — and put it to Paul III to his face. The Pope answered that Anguillara had indeed shown him the letter and that he marvelled at it, given the seizure of the fusta; that he did not think Doria content with him, having last year made him pay for three months for his three galleys and pay besides for the dispensation for his wife’s son to marry Antonio de Leyva’s second daughter; and that he was wholly ignorant of the cause. Mâcon replied that it could not be so without either a treaty with the Emperor, which he could not believe, or Anguillara having taken Doria’s service; the Pope said only that he knew nothing of it. A second block of the same letter has a man sent by cardinal Ennio Filonardi of Veroli sound the ambassador out: could the King be brought to consent that the duchy of Milan pass, from the Emperor, to the son of Pier Luigi Farnese, or else to the young Sforza? Mâcon answered that neither the King nor Messeigneurs his sons would ever consent, and that as long as the crown of France reigned it would not suffer Milan to go into other hands than its own, being their true inheritance, so it was time lost for the Pope. The second letter of 1 September 1536 (R4247) carries the count of Pitigliano’s advice: if the Emperor winters in Milan, strike at Naples, discontented and with no strong places but on the coast, and Sicily « ne fauldroit, avec peu d’ayde, de se revolter ».

The bearer of the letter is sent by the Sienese fuorusciti to press Francis I to an enterprise against Siena. Mâcon sees no prospect in it, but did not stop the journey; his fear is that if the exiles are left to themselves they will go over to duke Alessandro de’ Medici, who is working to win them and so « s’impatroniser de l’estat du dict Siennes ». In the same letter a German at Rome, who says he is of King Ferdinand’s chamber and knows his secrets and wants to enter the King’s service, gives him letters for a lansquenet captain serving with count Wilhelm von Fürstenberg; Mâcon suggests having them translated in Paris before they are delivered.

The January letter (R4233) runs over the pourparlers on marriages for Pier Luigi Farnese’s children, with cardinal Trivulzio’s view on how to stop them; the imperial ambassador and Venice; cardinals Trani, Cesi and Pisani. If the French cardinals were at Rome, Mâcon writes, they could steer a conclave should some mishap befall the Pope, who is « septuagenaire et plus » and failing — and meanwhile the King has done no favour to any of the Pope’s servants, so little goodwill can be expected from them. The Pope is sending cardinal Verulano’s secretary, « ung tres mauvais garson », into Switzerland, and means to take the legation of Parma and Piacenza from Salviati and give it to Verulano; behind it Mâcon suspects « quelque dessaing sur le duché de Millan ». In Piedmont the French captains are quarrelling among themselves, Guido Rangone among them, and the grain is nearly gone. The letter of 15 February (R4235) holds the most direct statement in these letters, and it is one of the three checked word for word against a contemporary margin: « j’ay sceu de bon lieu que le dict [pape] vouloit entretenir le [roy] de mariage, et ayant de ce dudict seigneur bonne[s paroles], pour ce s’en prevaloir vers le dict [Empereur], pour parvenir a son intendit. » Keep it from everyone but the King, he adds, and keep the secret of the envoys’ charge — above all from the bishop of Verona, who passes for more devoted to the King than to the Emperor because he holds benefices of him. The long February letter (R4234), almost wholly in cipher, is now decrypted throughout; its reading builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.1% of its words, under the 95% a complete reading needs. Its first pages turn on the same business: the Pope means to wrong someone through an intermediary and to bring the King to consent; cardinal Cesarini writes in the same sense; the bishop “de Lodes” — Lodi, then at Venice, whose see had passed to cardinal Simonetta (first taken here as Rodez) — holds that the King should never consent. Later pages report the marriages of Pier Luigi’s sons and the match of his house with Cosimo de’ Medici, “sworn several times over”, and then his arming: so many thousand escuz paid at his departure from Rome, two thousand more assigned at Parma and Piacenza, and a levy of six thousand Italians, five thousand Swiss, five hundred light horse and a hundred men-at-arms. The rest of the letter, decrypted in a third pass, is the fullest account in the volume of the Farnese design on Milan. Pier Luigi’s horse under Giovanni Battista Savelli is to be ready this month and the foot by March; a Sienese gentleman in his service, questioned by Mâcon, says the troops are held in Parma and Piacenza « soubz umbre et couleur de vouloir garder » them, ready to garrison the towns and fortresses of the duchy of Milan if the Farnese marriages persuade the Emperor to sell it to Pier Luigi for a great sum; and the Pope, « qui est fin », will meanwhile make a show of keeping his neutrality. Mâcon weighs the report as possibly a plant by the Imperialist cardinals Veroli and “Cesane”, but the Pope’s own admissions give him « grant presumption »; and Contarini, « imperial pour la vie », has become the Pope’s familiar. The last cipher pages (one of them with a clear copy slipped in beside it) call messire Ambroise « corruptible plus que tous les hommes que je congnoisse », fear that the King’s new demand for three tenths on the French clergy, with the calumny of the Turk, will give the Pope his pretext to declare against him, and end on Andrea Doria, whose talk of going to Spain Mâcon takes for a feint. The rest of the 15 February letter has the Pope angling for the fortresses of Milan and saying the idea came from the King’s side; Mâcon denies it, and counsels not driving the Pope to despair. A later passage, checked against a contemporary clear copy bound in beside it, sets out the French hope: « si le Roy est fort en Italie du costé de Lombardie, facillement ledict estat de Florence se pourra reduire en l’ancienne liberté et devotion dudict seigneur Roy ».

The last and longest of the deciphered letters. Paul III talks to the ambassador of the marriage of his grandson Ottavio Farnese to the Emperor’s daughter Margaret — the match celebrated in November 1538 — and insists on his neutrality while pressing for peace. A contemporary hand glossed one line of the second letter, “quant au faict de florence”, and it opens a passage on the intrigues at Rome of the exile cardinals Salviati and Ridolfi in the months after the murder of duke Alessandro de’ Medici on 6 January 1537; the clear text around it has Mâcon setting a spy on Salviati’s household. The main business of the letter is a bid for the Pope’s son. The Imperialists have offered Pier Luigi Farnese the investiture of Novara and are pressing him to take it; Mâcon counters with « quelque honneste estat en France », arguing from the Pope’s age and from Pier Luigi’s need of an « occasion d’en eschapper » once his father is dead. Pier Luigi answers neither yes nor no: he will take nothing without the Pope’s knowledge, and now the King’s. Around it the clear pages carry the news of the season: Bohemia’s grant to the King of the Romans against the Turk, a Lutheran diet in Saxony, and the death of the marquis of Saluzzo and count Philippe Torniello by arquebus shot before the castle of Carmagnola in Holy Week. The pages decrypted in the third pass fill in the middle: the duke of Urbino tells Ridolfi’s envoy Albizzi of « estroicte praticque » between the Pope and the Emperor’s ministers, the Emperor wanting tenths and crusade money and a league of the Italian princes; Mâcon asks for a ciphered article he can show the Pope, « afin que si la raison et l’honnesteté ne le desmeuvent des dictes praticques, que la peur l’en peust divertir »; and Novara was offered to Pier Luigi at the Pope’s own command. Meeting him in the Pope’s antechamber, Mâcon is told, « sans accepter ne refuser », to write nothing of it to the King.

The cardinal’s letter of 11 April 1537 is in another volume, BnF fr. 3071 (no. 4, ff. 9–10), and alternates clear and cipher. Its code numerals, which neither published table explains, were first identified from this letter: 20 is the Emperor (“se precipiter a la devotion du dict 20”, “se declarer partial de 20”), 30 the Pope (a contemporary hand has written “le dict pappe” above it on f. 9r), and 40 the King . What the cipher says: Pier Luigi Farnese, the Pope’s son, has sent men to take possession of a place decrypted as Novarre , and has approached the captain of a fortress to see whether he can be bought. (The Farnese were invested with Novara only in 1538, so the decryption of the name is one of the few that need checking. The 1538 date is not from the sources and was not checked here.) The Pope has been offered the marriage of his granddaughter, Pier Luigi’s daughter Vittoria, with Cosimo de’ Medici. Mâcon thinks that if it goes the Pope’s way he will throw himself wholly to the Emperor. Through Latino Giovenale, the Pope sends word that if the marriages are refused “il aura occasion de se declarer partial de l’Empereur: ce qu’il vous plaira considerer”. “La confederation du Roy avec le Turc se verifie clerement.” If the Pope declares, it is “a craindre que les Venitiens le suivissent entierement”, since it is said that “le Roy avoit promis au Turc de faire passer grosse puissance en Italie, et qu’il s’amuse en Picardie”. In April 1537 François was campaigning at Hesdin. The French ambassadors at Venice, the bishops of Rodez and Lavaur, are trying to win over Alessandro Vitelli, who held the fortress of Florence and was angry with the Emperor. Mâcon holds back so as not to spoil their practique . He fears that if Cosimo marries the Pope’s granddaughter, Vitelli will follow, “car le dict pape a moyen de le contenter es terres de l’Eglise mesmes, de la ville de Castelle, dont il commance a se faire tirant”. The control. Fr. 3071 f. 9bis is a slip pasted into the volume, a contemporary decipherment of the f. 9v cipher: De quoy j’ay adverty mess rs de Rodez et de Lavaur qui m’ont escript avoir bon moyen envers luy de le practiquer … The f. 9v cipher was transcribed and decrypted glyph by glyph before the slip was compared, and the two agree almost word for word. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3071 f. 9bis, via Gallica btv1b9060315f view 18. In the clear text, the duke of Mantua will not host the council summoned to Mantua for May 1537 without a paid guard. His brother, Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga, said so “en plain consistoire” (those three words are in cipher), and the Pope is thinking of moving the council. The dispatch goes by way of Venice to save the cost of a courier. In this letter a dotted r is a null in most places but must be r in partant , and the R sign is easily mistaken for the C sign. Still open: seven signs on f. 9r ll. 27–28, the word before puissance , a damaged name on l. 8, and the decryption Novarre ; the clear text, in a fast secretary hand, is transcribed only loosely.

The system is homophonic substitution on digit-like graphic signs, one sign per letter, with special signs for doubled letters, two nulls, and exactly three code numbers: 20 = l’Empereur, 30 = pape, 40 = roy. No other number occurs in any of these letters, so no part of these letters is hidden behind an unknown nomenclator. What stays undecrypted does so because of the hand. Work proceeded record by record from the DECODE page scans, cropping a line at a time at full resolution, writing each line as a string of ASCII aliases, decoding it with the table built in targets/rome1536/macon_key.md (made for the fr. 3071 letter), and then interpreting the output as French. Six contemporary decipherments turned up in the volume, marginal on R4233, R4235 and R4240, interlinear on R4235, R4239 and R4240. Three of them agree with the decryption word for word; they are the control this write-up rests on. One of them also corrected the published table: over the line ꭓ£+7G 8ꭓ ǂ3Δ4G 5o ǂ10D27o74g a contemporary wrote “quant au faict de florence”, which makes the big curly X Q and U , not N as the working table had it, and shows the QUE group written three ways indifferently. Other values fixed here: the plain saltire is N as well as L; 4 is C, R and sometimes T; 7 is N, R and B; the triple bar on a stem is RR (proved by PIE-RR-E, three times); ω is PP and the hooked ʃ is H, both in eschapper . F. 38v, the postscript to R4239 (Rome, 6 April 1537): clear French with runs of the Mâcon signs, and a contemporary decipherment written over them, “mandé de […] pape pour me faire entendre les propoz que verrez … par Sa S[ain]cteté”. The key decrypts these runs with 2 errors in 64 letters. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3053 f. 38v, via Gallica. What limited the first passes to between 55 and 85 % was one family of signs. The barred crosses — ǂ , £ , the long ƒ — stand for F, P, O, U, V and D, and at first they seemed separable only by context. The limit was palaeographic; the key itself was known.

After the first passes about a quarter of the letters were still doubtful, and nearly all the doubt sat on one family of barred signs. Cutting 1,262 glyphs out of the pages and grouping them by shape showed why: what the transcribers had written as one sign ǂ is four or five different signs of the key: a long hooked f for O, a £ with a looped foot for U, a two-barred stroke for P, a looped p-top for F, a barred q for M, each distinct once the line is seen at full size. Every record was then transcribed again, sign by sign, from the BnF’s own full-resolution scans on Gallica, with each warped line straightened first, and decoded by the key and a sixteenth-century French language model. Two more contemporary clear copies turned up in the process: ff. 37r–v, bound after R4239, are the clerk’s clear text of that record’s whole second letter, and Mâcon’s companion letter to the King of the same February day (BnF Dupuy 44, ff. 30–38) carries its own decipherment. Against every clear text the new readings differ by 3–8 % of letters, and most of that is spelling ( pappe for pape , Loys for Luis ). About 95 % of the cipher letters are now decrypted. The lines once called faded at the foot of R4247 are sharp on the Gallica scan: « il seroit icy fort difficille de recouvrer gens de cheval ne artillerie; bien trouverroit on tant de gens de pied, et bons, qu’on vouldroit, et beaucoup de gentilz homes forussiz, qui serviroient pour peu de chose. » R4234 now names Stefano Colonna to lead Pier Luigi’s foot and Giovanni Battista Savelli his horse; R4240 names the auditor sent to the Germans, “Vuorst”, apparently Peter van der Vorst.

About 5 % of the letters, inside lines that otherwise decrypt: runs where the signs 7 (N or B), 4 (C or R) or the O/U pair stay ambiguous and no clear copy covers them. The ink is legible; nothing on these pages is physically lost. A few short runs in R4239 (the postscript’s margin, whose contemporary gloss does not fit the signs under it) and some names: a Sienese gentleman, a count “Mer[?]le”, two German captains, “Cesane”, “Palmier”. The fr. 3071 letter: the spots listed in section 08. Its reading ( fr3071_no4/macon1537_reading.md , 23 October 2026), which follows the contemporary slip f. 9bis for f. 9v ll. 4–16, reads at 94.2% of its words; R4234 reads at 94.1% (both measured 24 October 2026, under 95%).

Assembled as one text for the first time. **Cipher**: f. 9r ll. 3-25 from the glyph-by-glyph decode in `fr3071_no4_macon.md`, ll. 26-34 from `macon_9r_26-34.md`, f. 9v from `macon_9v.md` (Lasry's 2023 table, `../macon_key.md`); f. 9v ll. 4-16 follow **the contemporary decipherment on the slip f. 9bis** (transcribed in full here, `macon1537_slip_f9bis.txt`), which agrees with the decode word for word except *car* / *ce que* (l. 7) and *peine* / *peur* (l. 8), where the reading follows the figures. **Clear text**: re-read on the Gallica images (openapi.bnf.fr IIIF, ark btv1b9060315f views 16-19, full size), f. 9v ll. 2-4 and 17-30 and f. 10r for the first time line by line; the fast secretary hand leaves single words doubtful, marked. Conventions: plain = carried by the figures, the slip or the clear hand; `[?word]` partly carried; `[word]` supplied; `[…]` unread. Spelling as written (cipher words as the figures spell them); *nre. sainct pere* expanded. ## Reading Monseigneur, vous verrez par la longue lettre que j'escriptz au Roy ce qui est survenu et les propoz que j'ay euz avec nostre sainct pere depuis la depesche que je luy fiz et a vous du [?vj] de ce moys par ung courrier que je despeschay en [?partie], le dict pape […]. Oultre ce vous advise que le seigneur Pierre Loys a envoye prandre possession de Novarre, et devers le capitaine de la [?Rocque] de [?Pise] pour veoir s'il le pourra corrompre. Il fust parle au dict pape du mariage [?de Cosme] avec sa niepce, fille du dict Pierre Loys. Aussi, qu'il me semble, si […] son vouloir sur les dicts mariages, le dict pape est pour entierement se precipiter a la devotion du dict Empereur; mais, faignant ne les trouver mauvais, Sa Saincte pourra demourer plus retenue, esperant avoir support et faveur du dict seigneur. Suyvant [?ma lettre], messire Latin […] a ainsi dict […]. Et davantaige […] de Lyon quant dernierement […] a [?Castillon] […] trouve toutes […] monsr le Cardinal de Tournon. La confederation du Roy avec le Turc se verifie clerement. Ce que je ne croy, mais est chose que je pense que le dict pape m'a faict dire par le dict Latin, pour me donner a entendre que, la [?facon] trouverra les dicts mariages [?nies], il aura occasion de se declarer partial de l'Empereur: ce qu'il vous plaira considerer, [et estre] advise par vostre bon et prudent conseil d'induyre le Roy a ce […] [?marchans]. Aussi, se declarant le dict [?pape], il [?sera] […] a craindre que les Venitiens le [?suivissent] entierement, joinct que j'ay [?sceu] de bon lieu […] seullement le Turcq et [?promectant] […] tousjours avec l'Empereur, ce qu'ilz [?esperoient] obtenir, actendu qu'il se dict que le Roy avoit promis au Turc de faire passer [?grosse] puissance en Italie, et qu'il s'amuse en Picardie. Partant ne luy tient promesse. C'est chose certaine. Et Alexandre Vitelli n'est content de l'Empereur pour ce qu'il ne luy a voulu faire responce par l'homme qu'il luy avoit envoye, lequel luy a seullement rapporte que le Conte de [?Cifuentes] avoit charge de la [?guerre]. De quoy j'ay adverty messieurs de Rodez et Lavaur, qui m'ont escript avoir bon moyen envers luy de le practiquer, ce qu'autrement j'eusse mis peine faire de ma part; mais j'ay eu peur de gaster la practique des dicts sieurs. Toutesfois, ou ils fauldront de leur coste, je feray apres ce que je y pourray faire, ou mieulx; combien que je crains que, se faisant le mariage de Cosme avec la niepce du dict sainct pere, le dict Vitelli suive ceste voye, car le dict pape a moyen de le contenter es terres de l'Eglise, mesmes de la ville de Castelle, dont il commance a se faire tirant. Je escripvy derrenierement au Roy que le duc de Mantoue ne vouldroit [?bailler la ville] pour l'assembler du Concille, ce que depuys le Cardinal son frere a faict entendre a nostre sainct pere et a tous messrs les Cardinaulx en plain consistoire, [?despensant] le dict duc sur la [?demande] des nations qui pourroient assister au Concille, et le temps de [?garder] ou [?mesme] [?sommer], offrant neantmoins sa dicte ville pourveu qu'on luy [?donnast] souldoyer ung bon nombre de gens de pied et de cheval. Le dict sainct pere a envoye devers luy en diligence pour sçavoir plus clerement son intention. Mais le dict Cardinal m'a dict que ce n'est temps [?perdu], et qu'il n'estoit point pour persuasion quoy qu'on luy [?peust] faire bailler sa dicte ville, chose que j'estime proceder du commandement de l'Empereur, actendu mesmement que le dict duc a difficulte de […]. Toutesfoys on pense que le dict sainct pere, voulant donner a entendre qu'il ne tient a luy que le Concille ne soit celebre, apres la responce du dict duc se soit pour transferer le Concille a [?Pavye], Plaisance ou Boulongne et y aller en personne: chose qui me semble mal a propoz. Car, comme vous ay derrenierement escript, je suys si pouvre que je n'ay moyen d'en [?conduyre], pour estre debiteur de tous. Et si j'eusse eu argent, j'eusse despesche ung courrier expres pour advertir le Roy de ce que je luy escriptz. Mais j'ay aussi advise, pour eviter despence, envoyer ceste depesche a Venise pour, par le premier courrier que despescheront messieurs de Rodez et Lavaur, la vous faire tenir. Vous suppliant, Monseigneur, pour l'honneur de Dieu, ayant pitie de moy, me faire payer de ce qui m'est deu, dont mon homme a les acquictz; mais je vous [?mande] qu'il est impossible d'en trouver argent. Aussi me faire donner quelque bien par le Roy, autrement il est impossible que je puisse demourer par deca. Sur ce, je me recommande tres humblement a vostre bonne grace, suppliant le Createur, Monseigneur, vous donner en sante longue vie. A Rome le xj jour d'avril 1537. Vostre treshumble serviteur et perpetuel oblige, Car. de Mascon. ## Notes - Cipher spots still open: f. 9r l. 3 end (*le dict pape* then a sign); l. 8 the name group (*?seu de ?iosme*, read *de Cosme* on the strength of the slip, which names Cosme); l. 10 middle (`… X o 5 A s L M N l o 6 f 7`, decoded *le dis im n le son*, not understood: the hole before *son vouloir*); l. 16-17 after *messire Latin* (`t?e`) and the last word of l. 17 (*fraeeure*); l. 27-28 seven signs between *le dict pape* and *a craindre*; l. 33 the word before *puissance*. - Clear text: *[?Cifuentes]* (*Gifuentes* on the image; Fernando de Silva, count of Cifuentes, the imperial ambassador in Rome); l. 26 *[?marchans]*; ll. 29-31 of f. 9r (the clear words between cipher runs about the Venetians) and the f. 9v Mantua passage hold several single doubtful words. - *se precipiter entierement* is the figures' order *est pour entierement se precipiter* (f. 9r l. 11-12). Translation macon1537_en.md # BnF fr. 3071 no. 4: the cardinal de Mâcon to Montmorency, Rome, 11 April 1537 — English Translation of `macon1537_reading.md`. Same holes. My lord, you will see from the long letter I am writing to the King what has happened and the talks I have had with our Holy Father since the despatch I made to him and to you on the [?6th] of this month by a courier I sent in [?part], the said Pope […]. Further, I inform you that lord Pier Luigi [Farnese] has sent to take possession of Novara, and to the captain of the [?citadel] of [?Pisa] to see whether he can corrupt him. The said Pope was spoken to about the marriage [?of Cosimo] with his niece, daughter of the said Pier Luigi. It also seems to me that if […] his will over the said marriages, the said Pope is set on throwing himself entirely into the Emperor's devotion; but, pretending not to find them bad, His Holiness can remain more reserved, hoping to have the support and favour of the said lord. Following [?my letter], messire Latino [Giovenale] has said so […]. Moreover […] of Lyon when lately […] at [?Castillon] […] found all […] the lord Cardinal of Tournon. The King's confederation with the Turk is clearly confirmed. Which I do not believe; but it is a thing that I think the said Pope had told me through the said Latino, to give me to understand that, if the said marriages are [?refused], he will have occasion to declare himself partisan of the Emperor: which you will be pleased to consider, [and be] advised by your good and prudent counsel to induce the King to this […]. Also, the said [?Pope] declaring himself, it [?will be] […] to be feared that the Venetians [?will follow] him entirely, seeing that I have [?learnt] from a good place […] only the Turk and [?promising] […] always with the Emperor, which they [?hoped] to obtain, seeing that it is said that the King had promised the Turk to send a [?great] force into Italy, and that he amuses himself in Picardy. Therefore he does not keep his promise to him. It is a certain thing. And Alessandro Vitelli is not content with the Emperor, because he would not answer him by the man he had sent him, who only reported to him that the Count of [?Cifuentes] had charge of the [?war]. Of which I have informed Messieurs de Rodez and Lavaur [the French ambassadors at Venice], who have written to me that they have a good means of working on him, which otherwise I would have taken pains to do on my part; but I was afraid of spoiling the said lords' dealings. However, if they fail on their side, I will afterwards do what I can there, or better; although I fear that, if the marriage of Cosimo with the Holy Father's niece is made, the said Vitelli will follow that way, for the said Pope has the means to content him in the lands of the Church, even with the town of [Città di] Castello, of which he is beginning to make himself tyrant. I wrote lately to the King that the Duke of Mantua would not [?give the town] for the assembly of the Council, which since then the Cardinal his brother has made known to our Holy Father and to all the lords Cardinals in full consistory, the said Duke [?weighing] the [?demand] of the nations that might attend the Council, and the time of [?keeping] or […], offering nevertheless his said town provided he were [?given] a good number of foot and horse in his pay. The said Holy Father has sent to him in haste to learn his intention more clearly. But the said Cardinal told me that it is not time [?lost], and that he was not for any persuasion whatever to be made to give up his said town, which I judge to proceed from the Emperor's command, seeing especially that the said Duke has difficulty in […]. Yet it is thought that the said Holy Father, wishing to show that it is not his fault that the Council is not held, after the Duke's answer will be for transferring the Council to [?Pavia], Piacenza or Bologna and going there in person: which seems to me ill-timed. For, as I wrote to you lately, I am so poor that I have no means to [?manage], being in debt to everyone. And had I had money I would have sent a courier on purpose to inform the King of what I write to him. But I have also decided, to avoid expense, to send this despatch to Venice, so that it may reach you by the first courier Messieurs de Rodez and Lavaur send. Begging you, my lord, for the love of God, taking pity on me, to have me paid what is owed me, of which my man has the receipts; but I [?tell] you it is impossible to find money. Also to have some benefice given me by the King, otherwise it is impossible for me to stay here. Whereupon I commend myself most humbly to your good grace, praying the Creator, my lord, to give you long life in health. At Rome, 11 April 1537. Your most humble servant and perpetually obliged, Cardinal of Mâcon. Key: macon_key.md , catalogue.md , catalogue_additions.md , BnF_fr3071_f9.png , francisMacon.png

Roosevelt Three lines of digits above a threat to the President, reproduced by William Friedman; no decipherment of the digits has been proposed since 1935 Transcribed from the sharpest available copy, the digits are the numbers 1 to 52, each written once, in an order with the statistics of a hand-written list. Thomas Ernst noticed the permutation in 2017 and called the block a doodle; this page confirms it and tests the cipher interpretations that can be tested at this length. There is no ciphertext and no message. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 16 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not a cipher Credits · Thomas Ernst (earlier solution) · Gerd (earlier solution) closed At a glance Not a cipher The document A sheet received by the Secret Service on 24 April 1935 and sent to President Roosevelt: three lines of digits, a transposition line, and “OR ELSE YOU DIE!!”. Friedman reproduced it in 1959. Where Figure 2 of The Friedman Legacy (NSA, 1992), via the Internet Archive; the original is in the William F. Friedman Collection at the NSA. The cipher The number block is a permutation of 1 to 52: nine single digits, 43 tick-joined pairs, and eighteen zeros in groups of 6, 6, 3 and 3. How it was tried Transcribed glyph by glyph, then tested against a fair shuffle. Ordered-homophone and rank-key readings were attacked by annealing, with matched 52-letter controls recovered. What it says Nothing: the block has the statistics of a hand-written “random” list (sixteen rising chains where a shuffle gives about 26), and the ordered-key readings fail. Credit Thomas Ernst noticed the permutation in 2017 and called it a doodle; Marc Gutgesell noted the loose digits are 1 to 9. Still open An unordered one-time key cannot be tested. The question reopens only with the original sheet or a second message from the same hand.

A sheet received by the Secret Service on 24 April 1935, according to the receiving stamp on its face, headed “Secret Service” in a looping hand, with a diagonal “261” top right, three lines of digits, two lines of block capitals, and a skull and crossbones above a dagger driven through a boot. William Friedman reproduced it as figure 2 of the first of his 1959 lectures, printed by the NSA as The Friedman Legacy (1992), with one sentence: an authentic example of a transposition cipher, sent to President Roosevelt, which the Secret Service asked him to decipher, and which to his chagrin said “Did you ever bite a lemon?” That decipherment takes every second letter of NDOIMDEYLOAUEETVIEBR?; the line under it, OR ELSE YOU DIE!!, is in clear. Friedman said nothing about the digits. Klaus Schmeh posted the letter in 2015 and again in December 2017 as number 17 of his Top 50 list. In the comments Marc Gutgesell observed that no tick-joined pair repeats and that the loose digits are 1 to 9; Thomas Ernst listed the 43 pairs, found they were exactly 10 to 52, and concluded the block was “a doodle, if not a fake”, perhaps made to give Friedman a lemon to bite. No decipherment has been proposed since.

Two copies exist: Schmeh’s 614-pixel scan and the figure in the NSA book. The Internet Archive holds a 300 ppi scan of the book, and its figure, cropped here, is the sharpest copy of the block that can be had without the original. Figure 2 of The Friedman Legacy , NSA Center for Cryptologic History, 1992. Image: NSA Center for Cryptologic History, The Friedman Legacy (1992), fig. 2, via the Internet Archive. The “apostrophes” of the standard transcription are short ticks written between and above two digits, and the two digits under a tick are one number. Digits without a tick stand alone. Transcribed that way, the block is: 1 7 2 10 15 17 19 21 26 8 32 33 20 37 000000 16 27 12 34 38 28 22 39 40 41 42 48 44 000000 9 3 13 000 18 4 23 24 000 46 29 35 51 5 43 47 000 6 11 36 50 52 30 49 45 25 31 14 — The 43 pairs are the numbers 10 to 52, each exactly once. The nine loose digits are 1 to 9, each exactly once, in the order 1 7 2 8 9 3 4 5 6. The eighteen zeros come in groups of 6, 6, 3 and 3. That is the whole content of the block: a permutation of 1 to 52 with four separators. Friedman’s or the Secret Service’s pencilled trial letters under the digits, which two commenters noticed, are not recoverable from either scan.

A permutation of 52 numbers can be tested against a fair shuffle. This one fails in four ways at once. statistic observed fair shuffle of 52 p (200 000 shuffles) rank correlation of value with position +0.39 0 0.002 neighbours differing by exactly +1 5 about 1 0.003 rising chains (values whose positions increase) 16 about 26.5 below 1 in 200 000 neighbours summing to 53 4 about 1 0.018 The rising chains are the strongest signal. Follow each value to the next: 1 2 3 4 5 6 appear in that order along the block, so do 7 8 9, 21 to 25, 26 to 31, 32 to 36 and 37 to 43. The writer worked upward through the unused numbers in several interleaved passes, fell back for the ones skipped, and when fresh numbers ran short wrote 39 40 41 42 straight off. Every anomaly in the table is of that kind. Three of the four pairs summing to 53 straddle a zero group (37|16, 44|9, 47|6), which Gerd noticed in 2017; it is a mild excess and not a structure anything else depends on. The one object that comes in 52 is a deck of cards, so the block was also tested as a riffle-shuffled deck. Sixteen rising chains is what four riffles produce, but a deck riffled four times does not also drift upward by 0.39 and run four consecutive cards: the joint event has probability 0.003 under the Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model at four riffles and 0.023 at three. A hand-written list explains the block better than a deck does. Neither contains a text.

A block in which every number appears once can be a cipher in only two ways: a homophonic substitution with 52 homophones each used once, or a transposition key derived from a 52-letter phrase by ranking its letters. With an unordered key either reading can produce any 52-letter text at all, so neither can be tested or refuted; one commenter demonstrated this by fitting an arbitrary sentence. With an ordered key, homophones assigned to the alphabet in order or the phrase recovered from the inverse permutation with letters nondecreasing along the ranks, the plaintext is fixed by 51 boundary choices, about 66 bits, against roughly 70 bits of redundancy in 52 letters of English. That is testable, just. The test used simulated annealing over nondecreasing maps from 1 to 52 onto the alphabet, scored by a character 5-gram English model, in six readings (sequence order and inverse permutation, alphabet forward and reversed, zero groups as word breaks or ignored), with 60 restarts of 60 000 steps each. The controls were 52-letter passages of Dickens and Melville enciphered with ordered homophonic keys and attacked identically. reading best score, nats per letter best candidate sequence, alphabet a to z −3.02 abadefillbookofmdoomloorstsbadfallsnowassadovyouslod sequence, a to z, zeros as word breaks −2.70 abadefillbooko endoonloorsus dad falltoowast adovyouslod sequence, alphabet z to a −3.18 uttooooonsnnolonominoffeedertootooenlatedtoldandenno inverse permutation, a to z −2.63 derssteeretiryehereheissuehistwehisthinnootrustoutst inverse permutation, z to a −3.03 ttheeetsiteseatstetstreeatssedassseesspooneibeendeed controls, 8 passages −1.48 to −1.97 7 of 8 read at 88 to 100% of letters; one at 46% Nothing from the block comes within 0.6 nats per letter of a recovered control, and no candidate holds a run of English longer than a chance word. The block’s own structure works against an ordered key: under a forward alphabet the nine single digits must all become a, b or c, so every candidate opens “aba”. The ordered-key interpretations are excluded at the strength the controls allow; the unordered ones cannot be tested, and a block that is only consistent with an untestable key is not distinguishable from a doodle.

Ernst’s count is correct, and the permutation has the statistics of a hand that wrote 1 to 52 once each in a made-up order, then added runs of zeros. The letter lines below it are a transposition so simple that Friedman deciphered it at sight; the number lines above imitate a cipher and encode nothing. Whether the sender meant it as a hoax on the Secret Service, as Ernst suggests, or simply copied out what he thought a cipher looked like, the block has no decipherment because it encodes nothing. An unordered one-time key remains possible in principle and is indistinguishable from a doodle. The question would reopen with the original sheet in the William F. Friedman Collection at the NSA, whose reverse carries a typed text and whose face carries the pencilled trials, or a second message from the same hand.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 21 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letters Johann Joachim von Rusdorff to Axel Oxenstierna, The Hague, 1628: three letters, at least one in German. Where Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Oxenstierna collection (volume E 701, Ser. B); DECODE R4333–R4335, “Riksarkivet_Rusdorff_Oxenstierna_1628-1” to “-3”, with no decipherment recorded. Formerly part of catalogue item 207. The cipher One- to three-digit numbers (8 to 107) separated by dots, set among clear words. Not the cipher of Rusdorff’s London letters of 1625. Whether the three letters share one key is not known. How it was tried Not yet: the letters were opened on 21 September 2026, described and set aside. Still open Everything: transcription, Rusdorf’s own copybook of these letters in Kassel, the printed Oxenstierna correspondence, the key records of the same archive. These letters were filed on this site until 14 October 2026 with nine other Riksarkivet records of catalogue item 207. They are different ciphers, each with its own page: the archbishop of Bremen’s letters of 1631 (deciphered), R4282 (deciphered by George Lasry), R4284 , R4306 (deciphered in part by George Lasry) and the E 708 letters of 1633 . Two more records first filed here, R4336 and R4337, are Rusdorff’s letters from London of February 1625 in a different cipher, with their own page: George Lasry recovered their key on 21 October 2026. That key does not fit these three: R4333 uses numbers from 8 to 107, and the 1625 table runs from 16 to 87 with codes from 187.

A short German note on the first image of R4333, with a run of eight figure groups in the middle of the sentence. Image: Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Rusdorff to Oxenstierna 1628, letter 1, image 1, via DECODE R4333. Rusdorff, the Elector Palatine’s envoy, wrote from The Hague. DECODE has the year 1628 and nothing else: no sender, recipient or language. Its symbol set is “Numerical” for R4333 and “Alphabet” for R4334 and R4335, which may mean a second system or only a different cataloguer. The archive’s own description says many of them carry notes that the cipher was never worked out.

All the cipher passages of the three letters. They have not been transcribed. Ten records catalogued as ciphertexts to an unknown recipient are Sánchez’s despatches to the Emperor in his 1522 cipher, and Tomokiyo’s key applies unchanged. Seven were calendared by Bergenroth in 1866 from the contemporary decipherings. Of the three August letters not in the Calendar, Sánchez’s own of 16 August was transcribed and its code groups decoded; its spelled runs are deciphered in part. dom pud · vera · por la capitulacion · ho · nuf · gad · suf vuestra magestad · vera · por la capitulacion · que · no · se · ha Venice → Charles V · homophonic alphabet with a three-letter nomenclator · May–August 1523 Alonso Sánchez at Venice to Charles V, May–August 1523 to Charles V Go to the full text ↓ Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid, Colección Salazar y Castro 9/28 (A-28), ff. 18–574; DECODE R9670, R9671, R9672, R9674, R9677, R9689, R9690, R9767, R9769, R9770. The catalogue listed these as ten ciphertexts with no decipherment, to an unknown recipient. They are the imperial ambassador’s despatches to Charles V from the months when the Venetian league was negotiated. Their key is Tomokiyo’s reconstruction of Sánchez’s 1522 cipher, applied unchanged. Bergenroth calendared seven of them in 1866 from the contemporary decipherings; the two August letters not in the Calendar were transcribed here in full from contemporary decipherments found on neighbouring leaves (23 October 2026). The cipher is the one Sánchez used in 1522. Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed it in 2025 from a letter with its decipherment attached, and the 1522 write-up extended it. It has an alphabet of cursive signs whose shapes are not their values, three nulls opening each paragraph, and a nomenclator of consonant–vowel–consonant groups assigned in alphabetical order of the plaintext. On R9670, R9671, R9672, R9677 and R9767 the groups decode coherently with that key and nothing contradicts it: xig de, vog en, ho que, nuf no, dom pud vuestra magestad, vum … lal esta [re]publica, gub rac señor infante, tum frances. The ambassador did not change his key between the two volumes.

From the reading of 23 October 2026 ( R9767_reading.md , English R9767_en.md ): the clear text, and the two cipher passages read from the court decipherment on f. 567r (DECODE R9768), checked group by group against the figures of f. 563r ( R9767_cipher_align.md ): Pues por la que en comun escrivimos el prothonotario Caraciolo e yo vera vuestra magestad todo lo que occorre, no dire en esta salvo que recebi la de vuestra magestad de xv del passado, y quanto al entretener a este nuevo Duce hare lo que pudiere, ahunque a dezir a vuestra magestad verdad en el se conoce que no es mal frances; pero espero en dios que poco podra danyar, ahunque es bien toda via entretenerle. Vuestra magestad vera por la capitulacion que no se ha expremido ninguna causa porque dan los desta republica el dinero a vuestra magestad; antes [?diversas] vezes en el tractar con ellos les diximos que vuestra magestad le pedia porque les dava una paz perpetua y no por otra causa, mostrando siempre que ni por el Imperio ni por la casa de Austria no se les havia de dar mas drecho del que tenian, y assi lo vera vuestra magestad en todas nuestras escrituras, pareciendonos que assi sera mas servicio de vuestra magestad. Pareciendo nos lo mismo que vuestra magestad escrive, no quisimos obligar al señor Infante a la liga defensiva, pues estos no querian obligarse contra el turquo. Lo de la navegacion para los subditos del archiducado de Austria no se ha podido acabar con estos; estarse han como hasta aqui. Nuestro señor la imperial vida y estados de vuestra magestad prosperamente guarde con cumplimiento de la monarchia. De Venecia a xvj de agosto de mil D xxiij. Sánchez refers the Emperor to the joint letter and acknowledges the imperial letter of 15 July. The new Doge “no es mal frances”, but can do little harm and should still be humoured. The capitulation expresses no reason why the Signoria pays the Emperor money: the ambassadors always said it was for a perpetual peace, not for any right of the Empire or the house of Austria. The earlier partial reading had the gist right but not this argument. The clear postscript on the defensive league and the Turk, and on shipping for the Archduke’s subjects, is not in the Calendar abstracts. The decipherment also corrects two code readings: the group read as yol is yoh causa , and mal is spelled out, not a code. The joint letter, R9769/R9770. Caracciolo and Sánchez’s letter of the same day is transcribed in full, with its cipher paragraph read from the decipherment on f. 574r ( R9769_reading.md , English R9769_en.md ): the news of the peace and league concluded with Venice, the departure of the English ambassador and of the Infante’s ambassador, and prisoners released by the Signoria.

R9767 and R9769/R9770: closed on 23 October 2026 from the court decipherments on ff. 567r and 574r; a few uncertain words in the joint letter ([?xxix], [?possessiones]). R9670–R9690: not edited. Their content is in Bergenroth’s English abstracts, and a full Spanish edition would be transcription against the contemporary decipherings, not decipherment.

Salazar. A. 28. ff. 40-44. 549. Alonso Sanchez, Imperial Ambassador in Venice, to the Emperor. His negotiations with the Republic have been somewhat interrupted by the illness of Georgio Cornaro, who is one of the commissioners and a good Imperialist. The Doge, who was ninety years of age, died on the 7th, and it was necessary to wait for the election of another Doge. That was another cause of delay. On the 8th he and the ambassador of the King of England went to the Signory, and said they knew that the Doge had died, but as in Venice affairs of state are not interrupted by such an event, they begged them to give their definite answer about the alliance (between Venice, the Emperor, and the King of England). They answered that they would send them their commissioners. Fears that ... (fn. 1) Knows very well that until a new Doge is elected nothing will be done. Fears that the Venetians, under the pretext that they must first elect a new Doge, will delay their answer until they know whether the French will invade Italy, and until the Infante has sent his answer. The Pope has exhorted the Republic to conclude peace with him, and the English ambassador has done all he can to bring the affair to a speedy conclusion. Has had letters from the Infante. Has replied to them. Does not know what decision the Infante will make. Does not think that the exiles will pay the 18,000 ducats in one instalment, as they have promised. The Venetians answered the French in general words about their aid in case a French army should invade Italy. The French were not satisfied with the answer. Cardinal of Auch, &c.—Venice, the 8th of May 1523. Addressed : "To his Sacred, Imperial, and Catholic Majesty the Emperor and King, our Lord." Indorsed : "To the King. 1523. Venice. Alonso Sanchez. Vuestra magestad vera por la capitulacion que no se ha expremido ninguna causa porque dan los desta republica el dinero a vuestra magestad; antes [?diversas] vezes en el tractar con ellos les diximos que vuestra magestad le pedia porque les dava una paz perpetua y no por otra causa, mostrando siempre que ni por el Imperio ni por la casa de Austria no se les havia de dar mas drecho del que tenian, y assi lo vera vuestra magestad en todas nuestras escrituras, pareciendonos que assi sera mas servicio de vuestra magestad. Pareciendo nos lo mismo que vuestra magestad escrive, no quisimos obligar al señor Infante a la liga defensiva, pues estos no querian obligarse contra el turquo. Lo de la navegacion para los subditos del archiducado de Austria no se ha podido acabar con estos; estarse han como hasta aqui. Nuestro señor la imperial vida y estados de vuestra magestad prosperamente guarde con cumplimiento de la monarchia.
